detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered the boardroom through strategic presentations, risk and regulatory reviews, technology updates, investment requests, mergers and acquisitions, workforce planning, and questions about competitors' activities. For some boards, AI now appears on every meeting agenda. Others have established dedicated AI committees, expanded the mandates of existing committees, recruited directors with technology expertise, or asked management to return with clearer plans for addressing AI-related issues. Nevertheless, most directors we interviewed described their boards as being at an early stage of AI-governance maturity. This exploratory qualitative study draws on semistructured interviews with 20 corporate directors to examine how boards are progressing from general AI awareness to structured oversight. The interviews suggest that the principal board-level challenge is institutionalization, which requires clearly defined decision rights, enterprise-wide visibility, governance of AI investment portfolios, secure tools, director training, and measures of business value and risk outcomes. detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in everyday decision-making, their influence extends beyond improving task performance or responding to existing preferences. Although many AI systems are not intentionally designed to reshape users’ goals, prior research shows that AI-generated recommendations can unintentionally alter what users value, prioritize, or pursue. This raises an important question: can AI systems be designed to deliberately shape user goals toward beneficial ends? We conceptualize persuasive AI as a class of goal-shaping systems constructed to guide users’ goals. We argue that the effectiveness of persuasive AI depends not only on prediction quality but also on the communicative presentation, or persona, through which the system conveys its role, intent, and social orientation. Drawing on persuasion and social cognition theories, we distinguish two theoretically grounded personas: Authoritative AI, which emphasizes competence and legitimacy; Altruistic AI, which emphasizes warmth and shared values. We test these personas through a randomized field experiment in a business hotel, where guests were assigned at check-in to one of four conditions: a no-AI control, Neutral AI, Authoritative AI, or Altruistic AI. We use the same XGBoost model to generate expected water-usage predictions in all experimental groups, with variation only in the persona-related AI presentations. The water consumption record from 936 guests shows that persuasive AI can reduce usage, but its effectiveness is conditional on persona design. Authoritative AI significantly reduces water consumption, while Altruistic AI has limited effects. Further analyses suggest that model confidence cannot explain these differences. SHAP-based attribution patterns reveal an important boundary condition: Altruistic AI becomes more effective when predictions rely more on external features. Our findings contribute to human-AI interaction research by theorizing persuasive AI as a goal-shaping technology and highlighting the joint importance of predictive content and persona design in deploying AI for sustainability and prosocial outcomes.

detail.abstract:
This scoping study examines the emerging links between information and communication technologies (ICTs), climate change and development.  Reviewing the literature to date, it traces the evolution of the debate through three strands – sustainable development and the environment, mitigation, and adaptation and strategy – noting that most existing work reflects high-income country priorities (particularly emissions mitigation via smart grids, dematerialisation and intelligent transport) while developing-country perspectives remain underexplored.

The study makes three main contributions.  First, it maps the "big picture" of ICTs and climate change and the phases that have shaped the debate.  Second, it develops a conceptual model organised around four core components – the role of ICTs in mitigation, monitoring, adaptation and strategy – to identify the main trends, challenges and research gaps at the intersection of the three fields.  Third, it draws on examples from Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, where applications based around mobile phones, the internet and community radio support livelihoods, natural resource management, information access and awareness-raising as part of climate change responses.

detail.abstract: The Fuck Around-Find Out (FAFO) Principle was introduced as a model of adaptive information seeking in techno production: intervene, observe, compare with history, then retain, reject or branch [1]. This report applies the same loop to law and power. It distinguishes two uses of the phrase. FAFO as threat announces that someone else will learn through punishment; the verdict comes first. FAFO as inquiry commits the speaker to learning through evidence; the verdict comes last. Between September 2025 and September 2026 the first use became an official register of the United States government. Meanwhile the American legal system, whose structure is FAFO as inquiry, received the results. The report compares that structure with the Polish civil-law tradition, follows the Atlantic dispute over platform regulation and "censorship", and traces a line from the Pentagon-funded Georgetown-IBM translation experiment of 1954 to the Pentagon's contracts with AI companies in 2026. Its one claim is that a channel closed to an adversary on reflex blinds the one who closes it: refusing to read, hear or trade with the other side does not shrink uncertainty about them, it fills the gap with guesswork and force. Every fact is dated and sourced, and contested ones are marked reported, alleged, or disputed. Every interpretation is labelled as such. The report ends with a manifesto for open exchange of language, knowledge and science.

detail.abstract: While most attention on quality assurance today goes to models, not data, that assurance is only as reliable as the data it relies on. Widely used validation rules miss the revealers of these data issues: unintentional data entry mistakes, instances incorrectly labeled for the wrong categories, schema drift, duplicate or conflicting data, or incremental changes in data distribution; all often pass the validation test and go on to manifest themselves in the deployed systems as either decreased accuracy or unfair outcomes, or safety incidents that exceed the cost of the data problems to uncover. We propose and assess an adaptive data-quality intelligence (ADQI) framework that integrates the statistical profiling, validation by schema, unsupervised anomaly detection, and drift-sensitive monitoring components into a feedback-driven pipeline, directly before model training. Unlike traditional rule-based model approaches, the framework learns its own and updates its own detection thresholds from the detected error patterns and generalises across the structural, label, statistical and semantic error classes in general. A taxonomy of hidden pre-training errors is developed based on existing literature in the data quality and datacentric artificial intelligence domains, and a controlled evaluation is carried out to compare the adaptive framework with the rule-based overall pre-training error validation and with pre-training error detection based on domain-specific statistical profiles in the four categories. The adaptive framework gave the greatest F1 scores in all 4 error categories and best relative gains for label and semantic errors that were mostly missed by conventional schema-based tools. The results motivate the transition from a modelcentric to data-centric approach to quality assurance and provide machine learning practitioners with a structured framework for integrating adaptive error detection in the machine learning operations pipelines. Computational complexity, sensitivity requirements and the use of only partially labelled validation data are also highlighted as constraints, as are directions for future research for explainable, self-calibrating data quality systems.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping a wide range of business activities, with the search engine ecosystem emerging as a prominent domain of transformation. The increasingly popular practice of placing AIgenerated summaries at the top of search results, exemplified by Google's AI Overviews, can enhance users' information processing. However, these AI summaries may also divert traffic away from publishers and challenge traditional pay-per-click monetization strategies for search engines. This study examines the impacts of integrating AI overviews into search engines on different stakeholders. Based on a theoretical model, we find that AI overviews motivate users to conduct more searches (search-stimulation effect) but make fewer clicks (click-suppression effect). The two opposing forces jointly shape publishers' contentcreation and participation incentives as well as the profitability of search engine platforms. For publishers, although AI overviews reduce traffic, they can incentivize more high-quality publishers to create content and make it discoverable through the search engine under certain conditions. In contrast, the number of participating low-quality publishers always decreases. Together, AI overviews increase the proportion of high-quality content. For the search engine platform, AI overviews induce greater advertising intensity. However, profit increases only under restrictive conditions: a low click suppression intensity resulting from AI overviews, a low share of high-quality publishers, a large quality gap between publishers, and a moderate level of information-synthesis capability in AI overviews. Interestingly, although user surplus increases monotonically as the AI overview's information-synthesis capability improves, a sufficiently high capability is detrimental to publishers and the search engine platform. Our results offer important new insights into how AI overviews may disrupt search engine platforms' click-based business model and reshape the decisions of publishers who rely on search engine platforms for traffic and revenue.

detail.abstract:
Organizational research on hybrid work has largely treated proximity bias as a behavioral
or managerial failure — a bias to be corrected through leadership training or policy redesign.
This paper argues that proximity bias is better understood as an information-equity problem: a
structural asymmetry in who has access to the informal, high-bandwidth channels through which
trust, opportunity, and organizational knowledge actually circulate. Using Microsoft's 2022-2024
hybrid work transition as a case, this paper traces how formal communication infrastructure —
meetings, memos, digital collaboration tools — systematically fails to carry the same
information that in-person, informal channels do, producing measurable disparities in visibility
and advancement between co-located and remote employees. Drawing on information behavior
theory alongside organizational behavior frameworks, the paper reframes two commonly
proposed interventions, participative decision-making and structural redesign, as
information-channel interventions rather than purely managerial ones, asking of each whether it
redistributes access to information or merely reorganizes who delivers it. The paper closes by
situating this case within a broader question: as organizations increasingly route information
through AI-mediated systems, will those systems inherit, correct, or obscure the same access
asymmetries that shaped Microsoft's hybrid transition.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is changing the task content of professional work and may also change the credentials employers use to screen workers. This paper examines whether degree requirements have declined more rapidly in U.S. occupations with greater exposure to artificial intelligence. We conduct a secondary empirical analysis of publicly reported U.S. job-posting aggregates from PwC's 2025 Global AI Jobs Barometer, which is based on Lightcast data and draws on 406,046,340 U.S. job advertisements in the underlying country sample. Occupations are classified by the AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) measure, and degree requirements are defined as the share of postings that explicitly state a degree requirement. Between 2019 and 2024, the degree-requirement share in the top half of AI-exposed jobs fell from 63% to 53%, a 10percentage-point decline, compared with a one-point decline from 13% to 12% among the bottom half. The resulting two-period difference-indifferences contrast is-9 percentage points. The decline is especially pronounced for jobs classified as more exposed to AI automation, where degree requirements fell from 56% to 41%, versus 68% to 60% for AI-augmented jobs. These patterns are consistent with a credential-substitution mechanism in which AI reduces some knowledge and task barriers, although highly exposed jobs remain substantially more degree-intensive. The results are descriptive rather than causal because the public aggregate data do not permit occupation-level fixed-effects or statistical inference.

detail.abstract:
When an autonomous financial agent makes a consequential decision, three questions must be answerable retroactively: which agent acted, was it operating within its authorized scope, and is there a verifiable record? The challenge compounds in multi-hop delegation chains, where a human authorizes Agent1, which in turn delegates to Agent2. In these H2A2A (Human-to-Agent-to-Agent) configurations, no existing regulatory framework specifies which principal bears accountability at each delegation hop, or what calibration requirements govern agents that receive delegated authority rather than direct human authorization. The Financial Stability Board's June 2026 consultation on Sound Practices for Responsible AI Adoption (P100626) requires all three attribution elements but specifies no technical protocol for how they are cryptographically authenticated and transmitted to supervisors. The resulting gap is not organizational. It is infrastructural.

This paper names and analyzes that gap. The core distinction it introduces is between data-layer attribution (proving a record was not modified after issuance) and authorization-chain attribution (proving an agent was authorized to act within scope at the time of a specific decision). These are different infrastructure requirements; the first is largely solved by blockchain and cryptographic hashing; the second has no established standard. Analysis of thirteen regulatory documents spanning six geographic jurisdictions confirms that Multi-Agent Attribution (the specification of accountability for delegated authorization chains) scores 0/12 across all Category A governance frameworks (pre-adjudication inter-rater reliability κ = 0.6507). The proposed framework, AIF v0.1, addresses authorization-chain attribution through three components: W3C Decentralized Identifier and Verifiable Credential specifications for agent identity and delegation-chain attestation, and a 13-field Calibration Reporting Standard (CRS) applying privacy-preserving verification to calibration governance disclosures.

The framework is grounded in practitioner evidence from three operational contexts: autonomous content policy enforcement at Meta (2017-2019), e-invoicing attribution infrastructure at a digital asset infrastructure organization in Abu Dhabi (2026), and autonomous fraud and Sybil detection at OKX (2023-2024). An implementation path for FSB member jurisdictions is proposed, with a proportionality mechanism tied to the materiality assessment framework in Sound Practice 5.

detail.abstract: Since the emergence of Bitcoin in 2008, many studies and regulatory discourse have examined the recurring crypto crisis events primarily as a failure of crypto products and its financial system. However, the "positive" implications of the recurring crypto winters have remained considerably understudied and continues to impact how regulators, policymakers, and even researchers, evaluate the credibility and maturity of the crypto economy. This Article provides a new dimension in the evaluation of crypto crisis cycles from a maturing financial system's perspective. It makes a critical contribution to ongoing discourse on crypto economy's viability, by presenting the first examination of the recurring crisis events, not as a failure of a financial asset or institution, but as evidence of a maturing ecosystem adapting its core narratives and strengthening its infrastructure to meet the fast-evolving needs of its market. Furthermore, the Article provides a comparative analysis of selected jurisdictions actively competing, through innovative use cases and regulatory policy implementations, for the status of "digital assets global hub" to evaluate the level of global success and persisting fragmentations contributing to challenges, especially on regulatory arbitrage, in the new phase of global crypto regulatory and policy implementations. This analysis identifies the growing frictions in transnational regulatory cooperation and advocates for the engagement of international financial centers (IFCs) as enablers of coordinated supervision and harmonized capacity building in the increasingly leveraged and fast-evolving financial system.

detail.abstract: Generic substitution is impeded not only by fiscal incentives on the demand side but also by switching costs stemming from psychological resistance and informational frictions. This paper examines whether counseling by pharmacists raises generic adoption by leading patients to compare the two drugs. To explore this, we exploit a reform introduced in Japan in April 2022 that strengthened reimbursement incentives for pharmacies to promote generic use. Using monthly administrative dispensing data, we compare outcomes before and after the reform and show that generic adoption increased substantially in drug categories with greater scope for substitution. These findings are consistent with pharmacists inducing patients to weigh a generic alternative they would otherwise never have considered, and with the predictions of our model of provider-patient interaction. More broadly, the results highlight that provider-side involvement is a key determinant of generic uptake, beyond demand-side financial incentives.

Information sciences as a field diverged a while ago from pure librarian work, and graduate degree holders in LIS now go on to pursue a host of professions, many of them concerned directly with data. detail.abstract: This paper investigates the post-COVID inflation surge in the euro area, combining three features: decomposition of long-term trends and business-cycle dynamics-such as potential GDP, trend inflation, output-gap, and inflation-gap; time-varying volatility and fat-tailed distributions to accommodate extreme observations; and structural shock identification, distinguishing shocks by their persistence (permanent-vs.-transitory) and domain (globalvs.-domestic, demand-vs.-supply, or energy-specific). title: Aging Economies and AI Adoption: Firm Level Evidence from the World Bank Enterprise Service
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Aging Economies and AI Adoption: Firm Level Evidence from the World Bank Enterprise Service
detail.abstract: How do demographic trends shape the adoption of AI and automation technologies? This paper provides the first large-scale cross-country firm-level test of the demographic–automation hypothesis using World Bank Enterprise Surveys data covering 89,380 firms across 144 countries from 2022 to 2025. I classify adopters by applying a large language model to firms’ open-ended process innovation descriptions, identifying 1,656 AI and automation adopters (1.9 percent of the sample). A ten-percentage-point increase in the old-age dependency ratio raises process adoption probability by approximately 0.6 percentage points, after accounting for countries’ income levels, digital infrastructure, firm size and sector, and broad regional and time differences. The result is robust across specifications and supported by an instrumental variable strategy based on predetermined demographic cohort structure. Heterogeneity analysis shows the effect concentrates in manufacturing, large firms, and developing economies for the broad adoption measure; restricting to firms with explicit references to AI reverses the sector pattern, with services firms significantly more likely to adopt than manufacturing firms, pointing to distinct sectoral profiles for software-based AI and hardware-based automation. Aging also predicts firms’ development of AI-enabled products across both manufacturing and services. The results indicate that demographic aging shapes AI and automation adoption through both process and product innovation channels: firms substitute technology for increasingly scarce and costly labor in production, and separately develop AI-enabled products for labor-constrained customers.

detail.abstract: A brand name change is a strategic decision that extends well beyond visual identity, carrying implications for brand equity, consumer perception, regulatory compliance, and product competitiveness. This conceptual paper develops a framework that integrates marketing theory and public policy perspectives to analyze how brand name changes affect product competitiveness. The discussion draws on brand equity theory, brand repositioning, brand architecture, and brand transition strategy to explain the mechanisms underlying identity change, while regulatory analysis is used to identify policies that may either facilitate or constrain the rebranding process, particularly with respect to intellectual property protection, business competition, and consumer transparency. The synthesis yields three conceptual propositions. Adaptive rebranding is expected to strengthen competitiveness through improved brand recall, recognition, and engagement, whereas sudden-death rebranding carried out without transitional communication is likely to weaken competitiveness by generating brand confusion. Regulatory compliance and transparency are positioned as factors that reinforce the longterm sustainability of product competitiveness.

detail.abstract: Contextual advertising is increasingly discussed as an alternative to user-level behavioral targeting, but a contextual system is not automatically privacy-preserving. This paper presents AdNexusIO 0.2.0, a working contextual affiliate-advertising prototype whose ad-selection path uses page content and coarse request context without requiring third-party cookies or a persistent cross-site behavioral profile. The contribution is threefold. First, we document the system at a functional architecture level while intentionally withholding proprietary source code, scoring equations, coefficient values, lexical rules, thresholds, and deployment secrets. Second, we perform a privacy-surface audit that separates reduced dependence on cross-site identity from stronger anonymity claims: the evaluated implementation still processes page/context metadata and uses a transaction-scoped click identifier for downstream conversion attribution. Third, we report controlled technical evaluations. The internal classifier regression suite yields 30/32 correct decisions (93.75% accuracy; macro-F1 0.944), and a local microbenchmark reports a mean 1.067 ms per deterministic classification on the evaluation host. In a paired Monte Carlo comparison across 200 randomly generated CPA offer portfolios, with the exploration setting held identical between policies, the revenue-aware policy yields a median simulated lift of 15.2% over a legacy click-centric baseline (95% bootstrap CI 11.6%-20.5%) and higher simulated revenue in 76.5% of portfolios. These results are engineering evidence from an internal benchmark and synthetic simulation, not production-effectiveness or legal-compliance claims. The paper concludes with a concrete privacy-hardening and independent-validation agenda.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether Bitcoin is a safe-haven channel in the economic crisis by investigating the time-varying dynamic correlations between Bitcoin and other assets, including stock markets (proxied by the S&P 500, MSCI Europe, MSCI Pacific, and MSCI World), bond markets, commodities (comprising oil and gold), and the VIX. detail.abstract:
This working paper examines a recurring moral and relational error: the assumption that privacy, reserve, or selective
disclosure is inherently deceptive. It argues that biblical truthfulness does not require total exposure, universal access to
personal information, or disclosure to every person who asks. Scripture and Christian moral theology instead require the
right ordering of information: truth must be spoken without falsehood, but information must also be governed by charity,
justice, legitimate authority, confidentiality, safety, reputation, proportionality, and the recipient's genuine right to know.
The paper distinguishes privacy from secrecy, secrecy from deception, confidentiality from concealment of wrongdoing,
discretion from evasion, testimony from gossip, accountability from surveillance, and transparency from indiscriminate
exposure. It integrates biblical-theological analysis with interdisciplinary work on privacy regulation, communication
privacy management, contextual integrity, self-disclosure, family privacy, secrecy, trust, and digital information flow. The
study proposes a 12-gate Privacy, Information, Non-Deception, Disclosure, and Responsibility Assurance framework
(PINDRA-12G) for evaluating whether withholding or disclosing information is truthful, proportionate, and morally
ordered. The resulting account rejects two opposing errors: secrecy absolutism, in which privacy becomes a cover for
deception, abuse, or evasion of legitimate accountability; and transparency absolutism, in which every boundary is treated
as suspicious and disclosure itself is mistaken for virtue. The central conclusion is that privacy can be truthful, secrecy can
be either legitimate or illicit, disclosure can be either charitable or wrongful, and moral discernment depends on who is
entitled to know what, for what purpose, under what conditions, and with what foreseeable consequences.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates potential effects of AI adoption on firms' ethical decision making. Here I focus on variation in models' partiality, defined as the weight given to the party it serves relative to a third party. Study 1 applies an established instrument from computer science, administering 5,000 autonomous-vehicle dilemmas to each of fifteen frontier models and recovering a measure of moral partiality. Models differ sharply. All favor third parties over their principal, but by very different amounts. Some are nearly indifferent, while others will let up to five passengers die rather than kill a single pedestrian. Study 2 casts the same models as business advisors choosing, across 260 pairs, between projected firm revenue and jobs created outside the firm. From each model's choices, I estimate how much revenue it will give up per job. Twelve models pay for community employment, at rates from $923 to $7,066 per job; two place no measurable weight on it; and one, xAI's Grok, requires additional revenue before it will accept community jobs at all. Partiality in the vehicle dilemmas predicts how much revenue models give up for community jobs (ρ = .725, p = .002). AI thus introduces a new source of variation in how firms balance their objectives, and which model a firm adopts is a decision about whose interests the organization will prioritize.

detail.abstract: The USPTO publishes every US trademark application since 1884 with its prosecution history. We re-parse all 13.99 million case files into 242 million dated events, separating maintenance deadlines that terminal status codes conflate. Dating each cancellation makes the sworn five-year proof of continued use a product-level survival outcome: whether a registered mark's goods were still sold. We then build a two-sided measure of vocabulary position: a topic model reduces each goods/services description to themes, and each theme mix is compared by Kullback-Leibler divergence with its own class's filings in the five years before and after. Their average is atypicality, how unusual the language is; their difference is lead, whether it ran ahead of or behind the industry. Rescored under three vocabulary partitions, two reference weightings, five window constructions, a refitted model, and duplicate-text removal, lead survives every variation and predicts cancellation at the five-year proof (+1.4 points with design controls, t = 8.3); atypicality's effects belong to the partition or to a control. Two hazards follow: scoring words rather than themes measures description length (r = -0.64), and firm-level correlations built on word scoring dissolve under theme scoring. Corpus, scores and code are public.

detail.abstract: The idea that emotions in biological systems are analogous to intrinsic colored noise is advanced and justified. A model describing the dynamics of operation of biological networks under the influence of colored noise is suggested. The agents of a biological network can be represented either by biological species, such as humans and animals, or by neurons of the brain, or by the nodes of a neural network. Operational actions, or decisions, in a biological noisy network are based not only on the evaluation of utility of alternatives, but also on the agents emotions. The model is probabilistic, with the choice of alternatives characterized by the related probabilities. At the initial step, the agents make decisions individually and then start exchanging information with each other and imitating the actions of other agents, thus forming a biological network of interacting agents. Numerical simulations are accomplished for a heterogeneous society consisting of three groups of agents, one group possessing long-range memory, the other group, short-range memory, and the third group of super-rational agents acting strictly on the basis of utility, being deprived of emotions. Dynamics of opinions in different groups can be smooth, oscillatory, or chaotic. Altogether, eight types of operation are found, depending on the dynamics of group decisions. Under strong imitation effect, there appears chaotic motion in the evolution of decision choice. It is shown how the Ellsberg paradox can be resolved and how the exchange of information influences the dynamics of this paradox.

detail.abstract: Energy variables are often treated as unusually credible economic indicators because they are physically grounded. This paper shows why physical connection alone is not enough: the target being inferred must also be stated and validated. It evaluates three candidate classes against a common standard of physical grounding, economic specificity, temporal stability, timeliness, and operational relevance. Reconstructed crypto regressions are mostly null or unstable. The original 2023-2026 stablecoin-supply/M2 coefficient reproduces exactly (β = 8.86, p = 9.17×10^-16, N = 42), but severe residual persistence, adverse or lag-sensitive stationarity tests, and weaker dynamic alternatives limit the defensible interpretation to fragile short-run liquidity co-movement. U.S. electric-utility output growth is associated with the Weekly Economic Index (β = .588, p = 8.6×10^-6, N = 222), but the timing runs from the WEI toward electricity at short lags and the benchmark partly contains electric-utility output itself. Taiwan's semiconductor-manufacturing electricity sales are physically specific, yet an external target check changes their interpretation: electricity-sales growth is positive in every year from 2022 to 2025 while official electronic-parts production growth ranges from-17.36% to +24.92% and integrated-circuit production growth from-17.41% to +27.60%. The series is therefore better treated as evidence of the sector's structural electrical footprint or capacity use than as a validated short-run output proxy. The broader result is target-specific: statistical significance, physical grounding, sector specificity, and forecasting validity are distinct claims.

detail.abstract: Why do Indian citizens consistently choose private service providers despite significantly higher costs? This paper examines the structural gap between public provision and citizen preference across education, healthcare, and administrative grievance systems in India using primary government and institutional data spanning 2004-2026. Drawing on National Sample Survey (NSS) health rounds, Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) data, CPGRAMS administrative records, and official government policy and expenditure data, the analysis identifies recurring cross-sectoral patterns. Private hospitals consistently accounted for the majority of inpatient care despite treatment costs several times higher than those in government hospitals; rural private school enrollment has risen substantially over two decades, despite a temporary COVID-era reversal; and citizen satisfaction with public grievance redressal remains inconsistent. The paper argues that this preference is driven less by ideology than by perceived reliability, accessibility, and accountability of services. At the same time, India’s Digital Public Infrastructure demonstrates that government systems can achieve mass adoption and behavioural acceptance when designed for speed, simplicity, and responsiveness. Based on this evidence, the paper proposes actionable reforms to strengthen public service quality, accountability, and citizen trust. The findings contribute to ongoing debates on state capacity and public service delivery by providing a unified, evidence-based explanation of India’s public-private service gap and a practical reform pathway grounded in existing policy frameworks.

detail.abstract:
Venture-backed startups allocate equity among founders, investors, employees, and other stakeholders through preferred and common stock, warrants, and options. This structure creates a fragmented residual claim whose value is realized only upon exit. In intangible-intensive firms, where contracts cannot fully protect key assets such as human capital, equity ownership aligns incentives and limits knowledge spillovers. Venture-backed startups therefore function as “optional firms.” Participation is voluntary, and optionality runs throughout the capital structure: staged financing and preemptive rights give investors the option to commit additional capital; convertible preferred stock allows a shift between debt- and equity-like payoffs; liquidation preferences turn the common-stock claim into a call option on the firm’s residual value; and founder reverse vesting, together with employee stock-option vesting, ties human-capital retention to that same residual. Although these arrangements reflect distinct forms of optionality, each derives at least part of its value from a direct or contingent claim on the value of the common stock.

The Article develops the concept of “contingent shared ownership” as a unified framework for startup governance that synthesizes principal-agent and team-production theories. By treating the capital structure as a single ownership architecture, it argues that protecting the common-stock residual claim sustains a dual selection process through which both financial capital and human capital are continuously reallocated toward higher-value firms. The Article further identifies the startup board’s central task as allocating residual claims between financial investors and human-capital providers and interprets corporate law’s protection of the residual claim as essential to maintaining this selection process.

detail.abstract: This paper documents a two-phase research program to identify statistically defensible trading edges in foreign exchange markets. Phase I conducted an exhaustive, rule-based search for structural and fundamental factors-real yield differentials, Commitment of Traders (COT) positioning, sessionbased liquidity patterns, and inter-market correlations-explicitly excluding conventional technical indicators, and subjected 18,681 candidate strategy/parameter combinations across 22 research phases to a four-stage validation gauntlet (in-sample/walk-forward testing, Monte Carlo Permutation Testing, Bonferroni correction, and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio). Zero candidates passed the complete gauntlet, a null result interpreted as evidence of the pipeline's capacity to reject data-mined artifacts rather than a failure of the research program. Informed by this result and by a review of external reference material, the program subsequently evolved into Phase II: a fundamentals-driven machine learning architecture combining gradient-boosted ensemble models (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest) trained on macroeconomic (FRED) and cross-asset (Yahoo Finance) data, hidden Markov model-based regime-strict filtering, walk-forward cross-validation, and a production deployment layer with explicit risk controls. This paper documents both phases, compares their methodological standards-including a materially different statistical significance threshold between phases-and outlines the audits and extensions needed before any Phase II strategy is promoted to live trading.

detail.abstract: Industrial air pollution varies over short distances and time scales that sparse regulatory networks may not resolve. Low-cost sensors and geographic information systems (GIS) can increase monitoring density, connect measurements to sources and populations, and produce maps that support community action. GIS adds interpretive power through land use, meteorology, source inventories, terrain, buildings, mobility, and population data, but it does not repair invalid measurements. detail.abstract: Recognition claims can influence affiliation, event investment and athletes' expectations before their institutional consequences are clear. detail.abstract: The transition toward circular apparel systems depends not only on technological advances in textile recycling but also on the ability of supply-chain participants to recover post-consumer garments before they enter conventional waste streams. Consumer decisions regarding donation, resale, repair, take-back participation, recycling, and disposal directly influence the quantity, quality, and recoverability of textile materials available for circular use. However, consumer behavior and post-consumer textile recovery are frequently examined separately from downstream apparel supply-chain decisions. This study develops an integrated consumer-informed framework for evaluating post-consumer textile recovery within circular apparel supply chains. The proposed framework connects consumer disposition behavior with garment condition, product age, material composition, perceived residual value, collection accessibility, recovery cost, reuse potential, recycling suitability, and downstream demand. Alternative recovery pathways including direct reuse, resale, repair, refurbishment, fiber recovery, recycling, and final disposal are evaluated according to their ability to preserve product or material value while reducing unnecessary textile waste. Multiple post-consumer textile scenarios were constructed representing differences in garment quality, consumer participation, collection efficiency, secondary-market demand, material recoverability, and processing capacity. Comparative analysis examined how changes in these conditions influenced the proportion of textiles directed toward higher-value circular pathways rather than disposal. Performance was assessed through indicators including recovery rate, reuse potential, material-retention rate, avoided disposal, circular value retention, collection efficiency, and pathway utilization. The research was completed using secondary literature, publicly available consumer and textile-waste information, and simulated post-consumer textile populations without requiring proprietary industry data. Scenario analysis and sensitivity testing were used to evaluate the stability of alternative recovery strategies. The study provides a transferable framework linking consumer behavior with operational textile-recovery decisions and supporting more effective collection, reuse, and recycling strategies within circular apparel systems.

detail.abstract: We study the local welfare value of trading opportunities in a pure exchange economy, using no trade as the reference point. Under smooth interior regularity, the budget hyperplane is tangent to both the offer surface and the initial indifference surface. With a common normal orientation, the signed second fundamental form of the offer surface is twice that of the indifference surface. At no trade, endowment revaluation cancels first-order income effects; hence, the offer derivative coincides with the Slutsky matrix. The second-order displacement between offer and compensated choices is proportional to the Marshallian income response vector. We compare the maximum income reduction consistent with initial utility under full reoptimization with the corresponding reduction when non-numeraire quantities are fixed at their offer choices. Their difference is exactly the Bregman divergence generated by a graph representation of the initial indifference surface. The first possible nonzero discrepancy is fourth order in price changes, with an explicit income response coefficient. In many goods, the discrepancy divided by the squared reoptimized income reduction converges to a direction-independent limit for a fixed numeraire. These results connect local offer curves and surfaces to welfare measurement.

detail.abstract: River sediments integrate natural weathering and human-derived metal inputs across catchments, but distinguishing anthropogenic contamination from geological variation remains methodologically difficult. This structured critical review examines how geochemical and statistical techniques can be combined to assess anthropogenic heavy-metal inputs into river sediments. It synthesizes evidence on catchment source inventories, representative sampling, grain-size and mineralogical effects, analytical extraction, local background definition, enrichment and contamination indices, multivariate statistics, spatial analysis, source fingerprints, and effects-based benchmarks. The literature shows that no single concentration threshold, index, principal component, or interpolated map proves anthropogenic origin. Enrichment factor and geoaccumulation index depend strongly on the reference background and normalizer; correlation, principal component analysis, clustering, and factor analysis identify patterns but not unique sources; and spatial gradients can reflect hydrodynamic sorting as well as discharge. Strong attribution therefore requires convergence among source plausibility, hydrological connectivity, normalized enrichment, element associations, land-use patterns, and, where feasible, mineralogical or isotopic evidence. The paper proposes TRACE-MET: Target question and conceptual model; Reference and normalization strategy; Analytical quality and comparability; Catchment source inventory; Exploratory geochemical analysis; Multivariate and spatial modelling; Evaluation of uncertainty and validation; and Translation to management. This framework treats source attribution as a transparent weight-of-evidence inference rather than a deterministic output of statistical software.

detail.abstract: Practitioners without academic training face a flood of management and self-development frameworks (from SWOT to Lean Startup to Grit), each marketed as evidence-backed. This paper operationalizes a heuristic a practitioner-author proposed independently, later recognized as resembling the classical positivist and behaviorist explain-predict-control schema: a framework's evidential standing can be graded by whether it only explains a phenomenon after the fact, also predicts it prospectively, or has been shown, through causal designs, to improve outcomes when its own prescription is applied. We make this ladder explicit as a four-level codebook (L0: no testable causal claim; L1: explanatory or correlational support only; L2: prospective predictive support; L3: causal or interventional support), with decision rules for retrodictive evidence, single-study results, and cross-study heterogeneity, then apply it to eighteen well-known frameworks. Two independently prompted coders, both instances of the same large-language-model family (Anthropic's Claude) working from a shared structured evidence review, reached substantial agreement (exact agreement = 0.83; quadratic-weighted κ = 0.72; unweighted κ = 0.70 across n = 18), with five disagreements resolved by adjudication. The final classification shows a pronounced popularity-evidence gap: fourteen of eighteen frameworks (78%) receive only L0 or L1 support despite wide adoption, two reach L2 with caveats, and only two reach L3 causal support for their own prescription. We situate the ladder within its philosophical and management-science lineage rather than claim novelty for the three-rung idea, and discuss its narrow contribution as a screening instrument alongside its limits as a substitute for context-specific judgment.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: On-demand food delivery (OFD) platforms compete on speed by committing to tight estimated-time-of-arrival (ETA) targets. Tighter promises can restrict couriers' opportunities to accept orders across neighborhoods, and ultimately reducing the capacity available for matching even with the same fleet. How should platforms account for this loss of capacity sharing when setting ETA commitments?

Methodology/results: We develop a steady-state model where couriers choose bundle sizes and switch between restaurant clusters in response to ETA commitments. Larger bundles improve service efficiency per order, while feasible continuation between restaurant clusters enables capacity sharing by enabling couriers to move across the region to activate the network effect. A mean-field queueing approximation links these responses to matching delays and fleet requirements. Within this approximation, we establish conditions under which ETA relaxation reduces the fleet required to meet a given matching-delay target. We define the price of urgency as the marginal increase in this sufficient fleet bound when the ETA is tightened and we show that the price of urgency follows a mild--sharp--mild decline as ETA increases, around a threshold where this marginal cost falls most rapidly. Numerical simulation calibrated by OFD company reports support this trend and the network effects.

Managerial implications: Platforms should account for the capacity-sharing cost of faster delivery promises when planning their courier fleets. Theoretical and numerical studies show that, the threshold identifies an ETA range where further tightening rapidly raises marginal staffing costs, helping platforms assess the fleet consequences of shorter delivery promises. This gives platforms an operational reason to reconsider aggressive time promises even when their dispatching algorithms can meet them.

detail.abstract: Why does the same verified, correct piece of information change one person's decisions and leave another's untouched? This paper argues that accurate information has no fixed value: realized value depends on the recipient, not on the information's correctness. Using a thought experiment built on the historically contested anecdote of Gauss summing the integers from 1 to 100, we separate the objective, decision-theoretic value correct information carries for an idealized rational agent from its realized value for a specific person, and propose a three-stage serial filter governing the gap between the two: receptivity (humility and openness to revise prior beliefs), inquiry (active pursuit and personal reconstruction of the information), and enactment (converting reconstructed understanding into action). We integrate three established individual-difference literatures, learning agility, intellectual humility and actively open-minded thinking, and growth mindset, under this filter, and draw on the absorptive-capacity, knowing-doing-gap, and implementation-intentions literatures to explain why even receptive, inquisitive individuals routinely fail at the final, enactment stage. We do not claim a new psychological construct: the three-stage structure closely parallels the learning-agility construct family, and our contribution is limited to two things: the accuracy/realized-value distinction motivated by the Gauss illustration, and a re-operationalized, individual-level self-diagnostic checklist adapted from these literatures for practitioners outside organizational leadership-assessment settings. A short illustrative section, non-evidentiary by design, applies the filter to two independently documented historical cases and one first-person practitioner episode. The paper closes with boundary conditions and the empirical validation future work must supply.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: Healthcare is increasingly delivered through multi-facility networks, yet forming a network changes ownership and governance without changing configuration: someone must still decide which services are delivered where, in what roles, with what capacity, and under whose authority. Contemporaneous reconfigurations built on similar clinical logic have diverged sharply, indicating that the configuration process itself, not the clinical case for change, often determines success. Operations management (OM) currently offers no integrated decision architecture for this problem. Methodology/results: We define clinical service configuration (CSC) as a distinct operations-design problem and develop a generic two-layer framework grounded in a taxonomy of the couplings that bind care activities and services together, each treated by an explicit separate-or-retain decision. A pre-processing layer applies this treatment to construct the design space by scoping services and their decision rights, representing pathways, grouping activities into modules, and clustering coupled services. A five-stage backbone then develops the configuration from topology selection through to iterative stress-testing. A form-and-origin classification of networks determines which configuration levers are available and which performance requirements bind as enforceable constraints. Applying the framework, we explain one major reconfiguration that succeeded and diagnose one that failed, and show that the OM literature is strong in optimizing over pre-specified design spaces but thin in constructing them. Managerial implications: The framework unpacks reconfiguration labels (e.g., centralization, hub-spoke, hot-cold split) into explicit, auditable design choices, identifies governance and implementation risks before decisions are locked in, and yields a research agenda spanning virtualization, pandemics, integrated care, and governance.

detail.abstract: Rebranding has become an important strategy for companies in responding to changes in the business environment, technology, competition, and consumer expectations. This paper aims to develop a conceptual framework that integrates marketing theory, consumer behavior, public policy, and product competitiveness to explain the process of brand transition. The analysis was conducted through a literature review and comparison of rebranding cases, including BreadTalk to MAKO in Indonesia, Burger King to Hungry Jack's in Australia, Carrefour to Transmart, Facebook to Meta, and Dunkin' Donuts to Dunkin'. The discussion shows that rebranding is not merely a change of name or logo, but a strategic process that affects brand equity, consumer relationships, corporate identity, and competitive positioning. Public policy plays a role as a facilitator of certainty regarding trademark rights, as well as a regulator of competition and consumer protection. This paper proposes Equitable Brand Transfer (EBT) as a managerial proposition for transferring the value of an existing brand to a new identity. Future research is recommended to empirically examine EBT by measuring changes in Top of Mind awareness, brand recall, customer loyalty, and product competitiveness following rebranding.

detail.abstract: Problem Definition. In online retail, cart contents can generate such increases through promotional rules or seller assignment. We examine how these within-cart price increases affect shopping and purchasing behavior across carts and over time, and when platforms should absorb them by preserving earlier displayed prices at their own expense. Methodology/Results. We conduct three randomized field experiments with 1000Farmacie, an Italian online pharmacy marketplace, combining purchase outcomes with event-level clickstream data. Relative to absorption, pass-through reduces new-customer conversion by 9.95 percentage points and lowers expenditure. Conversion losses are greater for lower-value carts, particularly at larger price increases. Clickstream data show that pass-through increases initial removals of affected products, with much of the conversion loss involving customers who first remove a product and then abandon the purchase within minutes. Beyond the focal purchase, pass-through reduces subsequent purchasing over 90 days. Among recurring customers, conversion also falls, but less so for those who previously completed a purchase involving a within-cart price increase. Managerial Implications. We develop a selective-absorption framework, now implemented at 1000Farmacie, that uses initial cart information to determine which increases to absorb. The fitted rule maximizes predicted profit, including future customer value. In an out-of-sample experiment, the rule yields higher estimated profit and revenue than always passing through and higher estimated profit than always absorbing. We extend the framework to generate policies that trade some profit for additional revenue, allowing management to select the extent of absorption according to its profitability and growth objectives.

detail.abstract: Adolescents sometimes identify a non-parent adult, relationship, or place as safe during an acute protection concern before any caregiving arrangement has been established or formally assessed. This paper terms that antecedent event youth-identified adolescent refuge and examines it as a pre-classification governance and information-integrity problem. A structured cross-regional evidence synthesis integrates peer-reviewed studies, official administrative reports, international child-protection guidance, and statistical classification documents. The evidence establishes component conditions rather than the prevalence or effectiveness of the complete pathway: adolescents identify consequential nonparental and nonkin adults; informal care and hidden mobility can remain administratively incomplete; informal hosts can provide substantial support while bearing material burdens; institutional translation can flatten source, chronology, and relationship context; placement instability and uncertainty are associated with adverse mentalhealth outcomes; and adult participation responds to governance conditions. From this synthesis, the paper develops OARS-Signal, Function, Claims, Evidence, Risk, Bias Check, and Routenot as a validated intervention but as the assessment spine of a proposed, testable policy architecture for immediate and interim refuge. The architecture adds Full-Braid information preservation, source-preserving interpretation, proportionate assessment of the youth-identified adult (Adult X), a designated adolescent liaison and advocate, time-bounded procedural accountability, multidisciplinary integration, monitoring, reassessment, and governance oversight. OARS is designed to make the interval between an adolescent's refuge signal and durable disposition observable and auditable. A staged multi-site pilot is proposed to test feasibility, information integrity, reliability, equity, implementation burden, safety, adolescent experience, system performance, and unintended effects; failure to demonstrate benefit would require revision or rejection of the model. detail.abstract: Why does income inequality repeatedly rise and fall over long periods, sometimes even in the absence of major shocks? This paper develops a theory of endogenous inequality waves driven by the interaction between technological progress and human capital accumulation. Technological change raises the demand for skills but also erodes the adaptability of existing human capital, while human capital accumulation fuels innovation. I derive a closed-form decomposition of labor income inequality showing that the Gini coefficient can be written as the product of labor fractionalization and a nonlinear function of the skill wage premium. This result unifies two central mechanisms in the inequality literature: the Kuznets structural transformation and the race between education and technology. The model predicts recurrent movements in the skill premium, labor composition, and inequality, as well as stronger inequality responses to technology shocks in economies with lower initial adaptability. I test these predictions using U.S. CPS wage data, citation-weighted patent measures from PatentsView, and long-run international inequality series. The between-groups component of wage inequality closely follows the model-implied decomposition. Citation-weighted technology shocks are followed by increases in the skill wage premium and, with attenuation, in between-groups wage inequality. State-level evidence shows that these responses are stronger in initially less adaptable states, especially through labor composition. Long-run historical series show persistent inequality phases and reversals that do not systematically coincide with major shock windows. The results suggest that inequality waves can arise from endogenous labor-market forces, not only from exogenous shocks or institutional breaks.

detail.abstract: When a company collapses, the cause named is almost always a shortage of money. This is an observer error: money runs out at the end of every trajectory, regardless of what happened earlier. This paper separates three mechanisms of degradation that share an identical ending and require opposite interventions: resource depletion, delay in the management loop, and an open feedback loop. Each is presented with its equation, the units of every quantity, and a full calculation on a single running case — with dates drawn from a customer-request log and a log of organizational changes. The main result concerns the second mechanism: the four-delay rule states that the full period of organizational reversals equals four times the delay between a problem arising and a decision taking effect. The second mechanism consumes reserves and terminates in a resource collapse, which is why it is systematically mistaken for the first; additional funding in that state increases losses. The canonical early-warning signals are shown to be derived for the first mechanism and to produce systematic false negatives on the other two. The paper provides a diagnostic procedure based on documents that organizations already keep, seven refutable propositions, and an explicit list of limitations.

detail.abstract:
Most household product-choice models are evaluated as if a prediction should be issued for every eligible purchase event. This working paper studies a different operational question: can pre-event purchase history identify which household × product events are predictable enough to answer at all? The task is deliberately narrow. Conditional on a household making a purchase within a fixed six-SKU choice set, the target is the SKU selected on that occasion; the study does not model purchase incidence or the composition of a full next basket. 

Three predictors were developed in a nine-product panel. A market-prior baseline (B0) achieved 37.28% accuracy, a household-history model (B1) 64.53%, and a behavior-fusion model (B2) 65.52% across 17,408 forward-test events. In a separate 26,659-event practical-complexity study, B2 exceeded B1 by 1.2604 percentage points, with positive household-and week-cluster bootstrap intervals, but remained below a predeclared 3.0-point material-gain threshold. The public system therefore retains B1 as the simple predictor. 

The study then freezes P1, a parameter-free pre-event household-stability score based on history maturity, choice concentration, entropy, switching, and recent concentration, together with three operating cutoffs. In a first newproduct batch, the frozen rule achieved 39.16% coverage at 76.18% accuracy, 21.49% at 83.55%, and 11.50% at 88.14%. In a second untouched representative batch containing 40,474 events from 99 evaluable product groups, the corresponding results were 41.08%/77.17%, 22.00%/84.78%, and 11.01%/90.06%. A separate department challenge reached 79.33% accuracy at 40.22% coverage, versus 61.18% for B1 on all events. The evidence supports a simple selective-prediction architecture: use pre-event household stability to decide when to make a conditional SKUchoice prediction and ABSTAIN otherwise. The current evidence grade is CONFIRMED_WITHIN_PANEL_CROSS_PRODUCT; independent retailer replication remains the next test. The result also defines a staged research and application agenda: external replication first, followed by tests of purchase incidence, promotion and price response, decision value, and only then broader commercialization.

detail.abstract: Convenience stores compete locally through discounts they fund themselves, yet acquisitions of individual stores fall below merger reporting thresholds. Using transaction-level discount records for 275 acquired stores, we examine how acquisitions affect that margin. Acquirers cut retailerfunded discount value by 53 percent where they already operate a store nearby. The reduction scales with the customer overlap between the two stores, which the distance between them does not account for. Therefore, local consolidation imposes a consumer cost on a margin merger review does not measure as an outcome.

detail.abstract: Product name changes are strategic decisions that can influence consumer perceptions, brand equity, and product competitiveness in the market. This conceptual paper aims to analyze the mechanisms explaining how name changes can generate both opportunities and risks to competitiveness. The discussion uses the perspectives of product competitiveness, brand equity theory, and consumer behavior theory to explain the relationship between brand identity, consumer responses, and competitive position. The synthesis results show that name changes have the potential to increase competitiveness through differentiation, relevance, increased appeal, and adjustments to positioning in response to market developments. detail.abstract:
Japan obliges private employers above a size threshold to employ disabled workers at or above a statutory rate, and it raises that rate periodically. The rate went from 1.5% when it was introduced to 1.6% in 1988, 1.8% in 1998, 2.0% in 2013, 2.2% in 2018, 2.3% in 2021 and 2.5% in 2024, with a further rise to 2.7% in July 2026. The covered firm size has fallen with each step, from 67 employees at the 1.5% rate to 37.5 at the 2.7% rate, because the statutory threshold is the reciprocal of the rate.

The published count is not a headcount. Workers with severe disabilities count double, short-hour workers count as fractions, and the categories eligible for each treatment have been revised repeatedly. Every figure in this paper is therefore reported in quota-equivalent units, the quantity the statute actually regulates, and the paper never treats a change in that quantity as a change in the number of people employed.

Each annual release prints, beside the published figure, the same figure recomputed under the previous year's rules. Using those recomputations, the paper builds a series free of definitional jumps. Between 1977 and 2025 the published count multiplies by 5.49, but the definition-consistent count multiplies by 4.63: roughly 110,000 units of the 2025 headline, or 15.6%, reflect changes in what is counted rather than in what employers do. In the most recent change year, 2024, the mechanical component is 37.8% of the year's increase.

Against that corrected background the paper documents five further patterns. The realised rate was below the statutory rate in every year of the panel except 2023, when 2.33% just exceeded the 2.3% then in force. After the 2024 increase, the share of covered firms meeting the quota fell from 50.1% to 46.0%, and it fell most among the largest firms. The gap between the largest and smallest size classes widened from 0.62 to 0.75 percentage points. Non-compliance sits at the extensive margin: of the 65,033 firms below the quota in 2025, 37,262, or 57.3%, reported no quota-equivalent units at all, and that aggregate share has moved only between 57.3% and 58.6% across the six waves. Counted units classified as mental disability grew by 91.5% over the panel against 5.0% for physical disability.

None of this identifies a policy effect. The paper has no untreated group, the size cells are repeated cross-sections rather than a firm panel, and the quota moved at the same time as the counting rules and the coverage threshold. Its contribution is an accounting: what changed in the measured quantity, and how much of it was the measure.

The findings indicate improved compliance without evidence of a generalized shift toward cash, qualifying the hypothesis that greater observability of electronic transactions necessarily induces migration toward less traceable payment channels. detail.abstract:
Energy security law rests on a premise it has never had occasion to test, namely that unconventional production has made conventional Gulf supply substitutable. This Article tests that premise against the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed since February 28, 2026, and remains closed as this Article goes to press on September 21, 2026. The closure is treated as a crucial case, because if the substitutability thesis were to hold anywhere it would hold here. American output stood near a record, prices ran far above the new-well breakeven, and Washington urged producers to drill. The thesis nonetheless failed. Gulf shut-ins averaged some 9.4 million barrels a day from March to June, whereas American crude output in the second quarter of 2026 stood below its level in the last quarter of 2025, and the oil rig count fell to 410 in April before a late and partial recovery. Net supply from producers outside OPEC did not rise. Inventories and forgone consumption closed the gap.

The consequences run across fields that seldom speak to one another. The transit guarantee of the Law of the Sea Convention has no mechanism capable of restoring passage in real time. Iran’s attempt to convert the Strait into a toll road fails against Article 26 and against the settlement that redeemed the Danish Sound Dues in 1857. Stockholding obligations calibrated to volume and duration have left the Strategic Petroleum Reserve near its lowest level since 1983. And where the substitute fails, extractive pressure returns to jurisdictions whose only effective regulator is a foreign court. Shale is a price hedge and not a supply guarantee, and the difference now stands on the record.

title: Convergence from Above: When Global Catch-Up Reflects Falling Back
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Convergence from Above: When Global Catch-Up Reflects Falling Back
detail.abstract: Convergence is usually interpreted as evidence of catch-up: poorer economies grow faster because they are moving toward richer ones. This paper argues that the same empirical pattern can arise from a different source. If country-specific long-run trajectories shift over time, narrowing income gaps may reflect not only upward movement from below, but also adjustment from above. We develop a framework in which economies converge toward evolving rather than fixed steady-state paths, and construct empirical proxies for these paths using cross-country data. Economies above their predicted trajectories subsequently grow more slowly and are more likely to move downward within the world income distribution. Supporting evidence links positive overshooting to selected downside-adjustment episodes, especially banking-sector distress and loss of frontier position. The evidence suggests that observed convergence partly reflects compression from the top, not only catch-up from below.

detail.abstract: We use LLMs to extract sentiment around labor markets, inflation, and monetary policy from FOMC statements. The LLM-extracted sentiment predicts unemployment and inflation when controlling for the professional forecaster consensus, suggesting that the sentiment contains additional information. Monetary policy sentiment affects Treasury yields and inflation compensation gradually over 10-15 trading days and is nearly uncorrelated with high-frequency monetary policy surprises. Markets immediately price discrete rate decisions but may process the qualitative framing and narrative through a distinct, gradual channel.

detail.title: Market Power in Mexican Industries
detail.abstract: This paper studies market power in Mexican industries over the period 2008-23 using establishment-level data from the Mexican Economic Census. We document a substantial increase in the average price markup over marginal costs, from 12 percent in 2008 to 27 percent in 2023. The sources of this increase vary across sectors and time: services, particularly wholesale and retail trade, account for most of the increase in markups until 2018, while manufacturing, led by transportation equipment and export-oriented industries, plays a larger role in more recent years. Rising markups in services are associated with greater local labor market concentration, suggestive of increasing monopsony power. In manufacturing, markup growth is linked to higher capital expenditure, consistent with firms sustaining larger markups to recover higher fixed costs. Moreover, rising markups in manufacturing are positively associated with total factor productivity, whereas in services they are uncorrelated with productivity. Overall, these findings suggest that while market power has increased over time, its underlying drivers have shifted from monopsonistic power in labor markets to higher fixed costs, with more favorable efficiency implications in recent years.

title: Commodity Booms, Productivity, and Misallocation: Evidence from Chile's Administrative Data
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Commodity Booms, Productivity, and Misallocation: Evidence from Chile's Administrative Data
detail.abstract: We study how commodity booms affect productivity using administrative microdata from Chile combining firm exports by product and destination, employer-employee records, and firm-to-firm production networks. Exploiting differential Chinese demand across Chilean commodity products, we measure firms’ exposure to the boom and trace its effects on productivity and resource allocation. We find three mechanisms. First, more exposed firms experience larger revenue increases but no differential productivity gains, channeling revenues into wages and materials. Second, among exposed firms, low-productivity firms expand employment while high-productivity firms do not, hiring workers from more productive employers. Third, domestic suppliers with greater indirect exposure show larger sales and productivity gains. We develop a model with heterogeneous export wedges and labor market frictions in which commodity booms can reduce sectoral productivity by exacerbating input misallocation, consistent with firm-level and aggregate evidence. Calibrated to Chile, this mechanism explains half of the mining TFP decline from 2005 to 2013.

title: Climate Shocks, Debt Defaults and Investment in Climate Adaptation – Squaring an Impossible Trilemma
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Climate Shocks, Debt Defaults and Investment in Climate Adaptation – Squaring an Impossible Trilemma
detail.abstract: Climate disasters tend to be associated with increased sovereign default risk. Countries face an “impossible trilemma”: scale up adaptation investment, keep debt sustainable amidst high borrowing costs and avoid the higher risk of default from delayed adaptation. Using a global panel of disaster event-level shocks, we find that a 1pp increase in disaster related losses as a share of GDP raises the odds of sovereign default by approximately 2-3 percent. An additional US$1 billion in cumulative Official Development Assistance (ODA) is associated with a 0.13 point gain in a country’s adaptive capacity. Using average marginal effects and our predicted margins we then map concessional ODA finance to default probability and translate these relationships into a practical budgeting yardstick for calibrating needed ODA to sovereign default risk reduction targets. In a context of declining ODA, our findings highlight the crucial role of well-designed support in climate adaptation policies.

title: AI and Economic Divergence in Asia
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: AI and Economic Divergence in Asia
detail.abstract: Using a small open economy overlapping generations model, this paper examines how AI can drive economic divergence across and within Asian economies. While AI adoption may promise sizable productivity gains, it could create temporary but potentially longlasting divergence across countries. Structurally-prepared advanced economies tend to adopt AI earlier and see immediate growth gains while emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) face delayed adoption and initial growth headwinds from rising costs of capital. Structural reforms that boost productivity and strengthen human capital not only accelerate adoption in EMDEs but also amplify the growth gains. Within countries, AI adoption could widen inequality along multiple dimensions: across skill groups, as high-skilled workers benefit disproportionately from complementarity with the more capital-intensive technology, and across generation, as the shift of national income toward capital favors asset-rich older households relative to younger workers who rely primarily on labor income. Redistributive policies can help mitigate these distributional pressures, though they entail equity efficiency trade-offs that vary with country-specific fiscal and demographic conditions.

detail.abstract: Firms are reducing staff and, more often, slowing hiring on the strength of what they expect artificial intelligence to do, frequently before that capability has been demonstrated in their own work. This article calls the pattern anticipatory substitution and distinguishes it from substitution that follows demonstrated capability, from augmentation, and from cost-cutting merely attributed to AI. Drawing on recent survey, payroll and experimental evidence, it argues that anticipatory substitution is most likely where savings are visible and waiting looks costly, and least likely where labor is scarce or roles are protected. It also argues that its costs fall unevenly: a firm that freezes hiring can easily reverse course, while the young workers it did not hire bear lasting losses. The article places this concept within a broader argument about AI operated by people as a tool rather than operating in their place, while acknowledging that human control does not by itself preserve employment. It examines why AI's gains may concentrate even as its use spreads, and why firms and states find adoption hard to resist. Resting explicitly on the normative premise that economies exist for people, it proposes human-initiated AI, disclosure of the evidence behind AI-justified workforce reductions, protection of entrylevel pipelines, and a substantial public role in AI, anchored in international rules. The article is conceptual, and it identifies the evidence that would weaken its claims.

title: Integrating Fragmented Networks: Interoperability in Money and Payments
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Integrating Fragmented Networks: Interoperability in Money and Payments
detail.abstract: Payments technologies pose an economic dilemma: network effects can lead to a small number of dominant platforms, but efforts to increase choice can risk market fragmentation. We examine whether interoperability can help resolve this tension, using data from India’s Unified Payments Interface—the world’s largest fast payment system by volume—as well as from a major pre-existing fintech firm. When the two networks became interoperable, overall usage of digital payments rose. Consistent with a model of payment choice that we propose, this increase was driven by regions where digital payments were more fragmented across platforms ex ante. Our model implies that the unification of networks increased total usage of digital payments by more than 50% in the year after integration.

title: Optimal Policy for Financial Market Tokenization
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Optimal Policy for Financial Market Tokenization
detail.abstract: Most tokenized financial assets are on restricted-access (“private”) blockchains and represent underlying assets that brokers deposit at custodians. Trading with tokens unlocks efficiency gains, but unconnected private blockchains also risk fragmenting markets, leading policymakers in several countries to explore interoperability mandates or public-private tokenization partnerships. We provide the first formal model of tokenized market formation and use it to derive optimal policy. Brokers with heterogeneous market power compete to attract investors and execute their trades, which is cheaper within a tokenized market that a coalition of brokers can set up. Partial coalitions divert trades away from excluded competitors, leading to equilibrium coalition structures that can feature excessive investment or insufficient tokenization. Indeed, technological progress that facilitates asset tokenization can increase fragmentation. Neither public-private cost-sharing nor interoperability mandates can guarantee the social optimum when used alone, but their optimal combination does.

title: Sharing with a Rival: Contract Design for Layered Co-opetition in Service Markets
