detail.abstract: Problem definition: We identify and formalize a distinct co-opetition practice-layered co-opetition-in which an asset-controlling firm supplies a downstream rival with a service-enabling input and access to a capacity-constrained complementary asset while continuing to compete with it for end users. Sharing can improve service quality, expand demand, and increase asset utilization, but it can also strengthen the rival, intensify competition, and increase congestion. We study when this arrangement benefits both firms and how procurement contracts allocate value across layers. Methodology/results: Using EV mobility as a canonical application, we develop a game-theoretic model in which consumers choose between the firms based on service prices and congestion. We compare independent competition, where the rival uses an outside supplier and alternative facilities, with coopetition under a uniform wholesale-price contract or a scale-contingent quantity-discount contract. Gross value creation does not guarantee mutual gain: shared access must create enough value to offset the rival's forgone outside option and the competitive and congestion costs of sharing. Counterintuitively, greater complementary-service value can induce the asset owner to lower the rival's procurement price. Because the rival's customers continue to generate procurement and complementary-service revenue, the asset owner also competes less aggressively for them. Quantity discounts can sustain mutual gains where wholesale pricing cannot, but do not uniformly dominate: the expansion they induce can intensify competition and congestion, leaving other settings viable only under wholesale pricing. Within the maintained low-friction domain, firm-level mutual profitability does not determine stakeholder performance, which depends on how the quantity discount is implemented. Managerial implications: Managers should jointly assess complementary-service value, the rival's outside option, competition, congestion, and value allocation. A more profitable complementary layer can warrant softer procurement terms; greater contractual flexibility need not improve performance; and mutual profitability need not imply better outcomes for consumers or the focal system.

detail.abstract: Enterprise cloud migration is frequently divided among security teams that protect systems, data-governance teams that manage meaning and accountability, compliance teams that interpret obligations, and engineering teams that execute transfer. This functional separation creates gaps because the same migration decision can affect confidentiality, data quality, lawful use, retention, residency, auditability, recoverability, and provider accountability. This structured technical review synthesizes scholarly research and authoritative guidance on cloud computing, information security, data governance, distributed systems, privacy, continuity, reliability, and cloud data architecture. It asks how these disciplines can be integrated into migration strategy without turning governance into a late approval exercise. The evidence supports a common control model organized around data journeys and lifecycle states. Classification must connect security sensitivity with business meaning and legal obligations; responsibility maps must connect provider controls with accountable data owners; migration validation must connect technical integrity with semantic and compliance acceptance; and continuous evidence must support both operations and assurance. The paper proposes ALIGN-C: Assess assets and obligations; Link security, governance, and compliance requirements; Integrate ownership and provider responsibility; Guard migration paths and transformed data; Normalize evidence, lineage, and validation; and Continue monitoring, resilience, and exit governance. ALIGN-C is an evidence-derived conceptual framework and has not been empirically validated. Its contribution is a unified decision and evidence model for secure, governable, and demonstrably compliant enterprise cloud migration.

title: Labor Productivity Growth in the Nordics: The Roles of Frontier Firms and Diffusion
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Labor Productivity Growth in the Nordics: The Roles of Frontier Firms and Diffusion
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the drivers of labor productivity growth in the Nordic countries, using both sectoral and firm-level data over the period 2000–2024. The sectoral analysis documents a broad-based slowdown in labor productivity growth, driven primarily by within-industry developments rather than shifts in the sectoral composition of employment. Firm-level evidence shows that productivity growth is increasingly concentrated among frontier firms—the most productive firms within each industry—while the rest of the firm distribution (“laggards”) has experienced weak or stagnant productivity growth. A decomposition of frontier productivity growth reveals that gains among incumbent frontier firms account for most productivity growth at the frontier across countries. The contribution of net firm entry is highly heterogeneous, and is positive mainly in countries where young entering firms exhibit strong productivity momentum upon joining the frontier. The paper finds evidence of productivity diffusion from frontier to laggard firms but shows that the speed of diffusion has declined since the 2010s. The slower diffusion is closely associated with rising persistence at the productivity frontier: when the same firms remain at the frontier for longer periods, opportunities for laggards to catch up are reduced. Overall, the findings highlight that sustaining aggregate productivity growth hinges not only on innovation at the frontier but also on firm dynamism—particularly entry, exit, and turnover at the frontier—to ensure that productivity gains diffuse broadly across the economy.

title: The Diversity Illusion: Representational Dependence in AI-Mediated Collective Judgment

detail.abstract: Organizations aggregate judgments because distinct contributors are expected to bring partly distinct information, interpretations, and errors. Artificial intelligence weakens the correspondence between contributor count and independent judgment-generating processes by making successful representations cheap to replicate, fast to diffuse, and difficult to trace across nominally separate actors. We develop a theory of representational dependence and show how nominal plurality can exceed representational plurality. This separation creates a diversity illusion: consensus can be mistaken for corroboration, and replication of a dominant representation can dilute genuinely distinct judgment. We theorize an endogenous convergence dynamic in which current-regime performance can improve as a common representation diffuses even while the system loses alternative mappings that may become valuable following structural change. We define regime change independently of the focal representation's performance, so a structural break need not imply failure of the dominant mapping. Because the quality of alternatives is difficult to verify before rare states occur, organizations and interorganizational aggregates may preserve less plurality than their cross-regime decision criteria would warrant. Observable judgment paths provide partial, domain-bounded evidence of representational plurality before outcomes accumulate. The theory revises how organizations should understand independence, consensus, and diversity in AI-mediated collective judgment.

detail.abstract: Mining mobilizes metal-bearing minerals through excavation, crushing, waste-rock exposure, tailings storage, drainage, and erosion. Stream sediments integrate these releases over space and time, but high total concentrations do not by themselves establish anthropogenic enrichment, bioavailability, or ecological harm. This structured critical review examines heavymetal accumulation in stream sediments associated with mining and evaluates the strengths and limitations of spatial and ecological risk assessment methods. The synthesis covers catchment processes, sampling design, grain-size and organicmatter effects, digestion and sequential extraction, geochemical background selection, contamination indices, sedimentquality guidelines, multivariate source analysis, and spatial mapping. Evidence supports a weight-of-evidence approach: enrichment factor, contamination factor, geoaccumulation index, pollution load index, potential ecological risk, and guideline quotients answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable. Spatial interpretation should follow hydrological connectivity and depositional environments rather than distance from a mine alone. Total-metal screening is strengthened by sediment properties, mineralogy, chemical fractions, porewater or biota evidence, and toxicity testing. The paper proposes the SED-RISK framework: Source and catchment context; Exposure-pathway mapping; Design of representative sampling; Reference-background definition; Integrated geochemical assessment; Sediment-quality and bioavailability evaluation; Interpretation of spatial uncertainty; and Stakeholder-oriented risk management. The framework provides a transparent basis for monitoring and remediation without claiming new field measurements.

detail.abstract: Modern service platforms often provide customers with real-time congestion information, such as anticipated waiting times, before they decide whether to use a service. This creates an intertemporal tradeoff in service recommendation: directing a customer to a service may generate immediate value, but the resulting congestion can make that service less attractive to future customers. We study this tradeoff through a finite-horizon stochastic optimization problem in which a platform dynamically recommends among multiple services, each represented by a queue, with customers' joining probabilities decreasing with congestion. We first formulate the problem as a Markov decision process and show that optimal decisions generally depend on the joint congestion state, giving rise to a prohibitively large state space. We develop two complementary approximation algorithms that overcome this curse of dimensionality in different ways. First, we provide a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme that uses truncation and rounding of the model primitives to compress the joint congestion state, while carefully accounting for how these approximations affect the stochastic evolution of the system to establish near-optimality. Second, we develop a polynomial-time LP-guided algorithm that replaces the joint-state representation with service-level marginal information and achieves a (1-1/e)-approximation guarantee under substantially more general service and joining dynamics. Finally, we show that monotone joining behavior, whereby customers become less likely to join as a service becomes more congested, marks a fundamental tractability boundary: without monotonicity, the problem is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor. This establishes monotonicity as a key behavioral property that enables tractable dynamic service recommendation despite the complexity introduced by congestion-dependent joining.

detail.abstract: AI governance often treats heterogeneous deployment risks as entries in a single AI risk register, normalizing them to common scales and selecting controls against the resulting aggregate. This paper argues that the practice creates a measurement error. AI deployment risk arises from at least three analytically distinct risk-bearing objects: the model, the operation in which its output is used, and the organization's exposure created by deploying and relying on the system. Because each object generates different failure mechanisms, admits different controls, and belongs to different owners, evidence of strength in one object cannot retire risk in another. The paper names this failure control mismatch and identifies two recurring forms: false retirement and under-ownership. It develops a separated diagnostic that preserves object identity through inherent and residual risk assessment, and a decision matrix that routes each residual to an indomain control, an accountable owner, an explicit disposition, and a continuity owner where risk propagates across objects. A healthcare deployment involving nH Predict serves as the running case, supplemented by employment-screening and platform-work examples. The Risk Lens completes the Four Lenses of AI Measurement by distinguishing adverse-consequence measurement from capability, compliance, and organizational maturity.

detail.abstract: Public institutions often seek to increase trust through clear and reassuring communication. This goal becomes more difficult when residents receive government information through translation, digital interfaces, community organizations, news media, and personal networks. The central problem is not simply whether a message appears trustworthy. It is whether reliance on that message is justified by observable institutional conduct. This article develops a framework for calibrated reliance in multilingual public communication. It draws on a structured qualitative review of 50 scholarly, legal, policy, and institutional sources available by 15 June 2025. The evidence covers institutional trust, migration, language access, risk communication, digital government, public administration, and community mediation. The analysis distinguishes trust from compliance, use, satisfaction, and familiarity. It identifies six tests that allow migrant users to evaluate public information: provenance, cross-language consistency, procedural congruence, explanation of uncertainty, accessible recourse, and safe corroboration. Together, these tests form the Multilingual Institutional Reliance Framework. The framework explains why polished translation cannot compensate for a procedure that contradicts the message, why identical wording may still produce unequal understanding, and why community intermediaries should support verification without becoming substitutes for public accountability. The article proposes a task-based evaluation method. Agencies should compare language versions, observe complete service journeys, record correction performance, and examine whether users can verify the source and challenge an adverse outcome. Institutional trust should not be maximized as a communication metric. Public institutions should create conditions in which people can decide when reliance is warranted, when further verification is needed, and where a decision can be contested.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-autonomous, LLM-based agents that perceive, reason, plan, and act with minimal human oversight-is among the fastest-moving emerging computing technologies, and is now being embedded in operational decision loops such as supply chains, outpacing the governance needed to manage an agent's decision authority, accountability, and failure modes. Existing instruments such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and the EU AI Act address model-and system-level risk, not the operational question of how much autonomy an agent should hold for an individual decision, or who is accountable when it errs. This paper contributes a runtime governance framework for autonomous AI agents and applies it to supply chain decision-making. It defines four governance tiers-Advisory, Supervised Autonomous, Bounded Autonomous, and Fully Autonomous-and, unlike static levelsof-automation taxonomies, an explicit weakest-link rule that computes a tier per decision from its reversibility, financial impact, and stakeholder scope, with monitoring-driven runtime reassignment and a RACI-E accountability model in which the agent executes but a human remains accountable. We evaluate it in a controlled simulation of a last-mile carrier-allocation agent that proposes against the full carrier panel, so governance must genuinely catch three failure modes-anomalies, lowconfidence margins, and budget-boundary breaches-rather than have them designed away. Across 3,000 consignments, governed autonomy resolves 58% of decisions autonomously while cutting the SLA-breach rate from 13.6% under ungoverned autonomy to 5.0% (human-only 3.6%) and eliminating executed boundary violations; an equal-information control further shows that the breach reduction is largely an information effect while boundary enforcement is a pure governance effect.

detail.abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly recognised as a promising solution for food supply chains (FSCs). However, existing DT research has focused mainly on conceptual development, technical applications, and pilot implementations, providing limited empirical evidence on the determinants influencing firms' adoption decisions. Thus, this study examines the determinants of DT adoption decisions in FSCs. Drawing on Diffusion of Innovation theory and the technology-organisation-environment (TOE) framework, the study develops a research model explaining how TOE factors shape firms' adoption decisions. Survey data from 260 respondents in food and technology-related firms across Western economies are analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Results show that compatibility, technology readiness, top management support, competitive pressure, and market uncertainty significantly influence the DT adoption decision, while complexity negatively affects adoption. Findings indicate that the DT adoption decision in FSCs is shaped not only by perceived technological characteristics but also by organisational support and external environmental pressures.

title: Rider Learning in On-Demand Meal Delivery: Diminishing Returns and the Moderating Role of Operating Conditions

detail.title: Rider Learning in On-Demand Meal Delivery: Diminishing Returns and the Moderating Role of Operating Conditions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This study is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grants No. 72301187, 72361137004)

detail.abstract: The rapid growth of on-demand meal delivery has increased the importance of improving delivery efficiency while effectively managing the rider workforce. While prior studies have examined various operational factors affecting delivery outcomes, limited attention has been paid to how riders learn from accumulated delivery experience. Drawing on the learning-by-doing perspective, we examine the effect of rider experience on delivery time and explore the moderating effects of peak periods, traffic congestion, and rider workload (i.e., the number of outstanding orders). Econometric analyses of order-level operational data from an on-demand meal delivery platform reveal a negative, nonlinear relationship between rider experience and delivery time, with significant diminishing marginal performance gains. More importantly, we find that peak periods and higher rider workload strengthen and attenuate the learning effect, respectively, while the strengthening effect of traffic congestion is only partially supported across model specifications. These findings suggest that the performance benefits of delivery experience depend not only on accumulated experience itself but also on operating conditions, offering valuable implications for understanding rider learning and designing experience-aware dispatching and workforce management policies.

detail.abstract: Primal Genesis proposes four recurring configurations of motivation and engagement - Hunter, Gatherer, Nomad, and Farmer - organized around challenge, cooperation, exploration, and structured continuity. This conceptual paper translates the book's framework into hypotheses that can be tested against established dimensional personality models. The configurations are proposed regions of continuous variation, not validated types, inherited essences, or rankings of ability. Their scientific value depends on incremental, out-of-sample prediction beyond the Big Five and related constructs. Three candidate sources of added value are specified: interactions among component traits, discrepancies between preferred and institutionally rewarded expression, and situation-dependent changes in behavior. The paper outlines provisional profiles, a developmental account of conditioning, educational and occupational fit predictions, and a particularly tentative stress-response extension. It proposes scale development, competing dimensional and person-centered models, longitudinal designs, preregistered aptitude-treatment experiments, and cross-cultural replication. Educational applications would be warranted only if the model demonstrates reliable measurement and reproducible advantages over simpler explanations. Its proposed purpose, contingent on such validation, is constructive rather than diagnostic - to help people recognize their own recurring preferences and acquired capacities and to appreciate that others may thrive under different conditions - an aim that motivates the research rather than a demonstrated benefit. Historical subsistence labels supply a vocabulary, not evidence for evolutionary origins. No new empirical data are reported, and neither the four-profile structure nor its applied benefits have been established.

detail.abstract: Financial planning lacks a shared measurement standard: two plans built from identical household data may recommend materially different outcomes, with no common framework to determine which is more efficient. Existing financial measurement standards evaluate historical outcomes, and standards in other fields already evaluate forward looking projections under contested assumptions. Financial planning has no comparable standard for the quality of a plan. This paper proposes the Financial Optimization Standards for Households (FOSH), a mathematically grounded framework that addresses this challenge by identifying what can be objectively measured about a financial plan and separating it from what must be declared. The paper formalizes the Household Financial System Problem (HFSP), the observation that household financial planning constitutes an interconnected, multi-objective optimization system. It then introduces the household's efficient set, the full Pareto-efficient surface in the space of household objective attainments, computed from household facts prior to any preference consideration, as the reference surface against which submitted plans are evaluated. FOSH defines verifiable signals measuring plan efficiency, assumption sensitivity, data reliability, and objective scope, and embeds ethics structurally through signal design. The framework provides the measurement layer that the profession's accountability aspirations require for evaluating plan quality.

detail.abstract: This study examines the effectiveness of traditional econometric models, such as ARMA, GARCH, and EGARCH, in forecasting the implied volatility of crypto derivatives when data history is limited. We compare these models with machine learning approaches, including LASSO and Gradient Boosting, which utilize additional features like returns and rolling volatility. The results show that simpler models like ARMA and LASSO outperform GARCH-based models, which struggle with limited data. Machine learning models demonstrate competitive performance, highlighting their adaptability to the unique characteristics of cryptocurrency markets. These findings provide valuable insights into selecting appropriate forecasting methods for crypto derivatives under data constraints.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the behavioral factors influencing the adoption of environmentally sustainable practices in Artisanal and Small-scale Mining (ASM) communities in Colombia, using the COMB model to identify the capabilities, opportunities, and motivations that shape mining behaviors in specific territorial contexts. Methodology: A sequential mixed-methods approach was implemented across three Colombian municipalities (Istmina, El Bagre, and Santa Rosa del Sur), including 21 semi-structured interviews, 6 focus groups (58 participants), social norms surveys (92 participants), and participant observation. The analysis combined thematic coding based on the COMB model with descriptive statistics for the quantitative data. Results: The assessment revealed marked territorial differences across the three dimensions of the COMB model. Local governance structures (Social opportunity) and cultural identity (Reflective motivation) emerged as determining factors of pro-environmental behavior. Approximately 45% of miners were found to consult experienced peers as their primary source of knowledge, while the gender dimension proved crucial in environmental decision-making. Conclusions: Interventions to promote sustainable mining practices require differentiated approaches that recognize territorial particularities, respect traditional knowledge, and strengthen existing social structures. The COMB model provides an effective framework for designing culturally appropriate policies that integrate technical, economic, and sociocultural considerations into the transformation of mining practices.

detail.abstract: Cross-border e-commerce sellers trade lower sea-freight rates against longer replenishment time, inventory exposure, and service risk. Anker Innovations’ public disclosures motivate the problem but do not estimate or validate the model. This paper develops an auditable static SKU–lane screen for a fixed sea–air share. It separates annual freight, pipeline-inventory, and safety-stock costs, allows correlated lead-time shocks, and limits the RMB value of pipeline plus safety-stock inventory. Under a normal screening approximation, two propositions establish cost monotonicity and convexity, while a feasible-boundary rule identifies the largest admissible share. In the synthetic base, ρ=0.30 and a RMB 2.0 million expected-exposure cap produce 45.2% sea. A 5,000-replication stress test shows cap exceedance in 48.49% of simulated weeks; searching the same random-number stream for no more than 5% exceedance reduces the share to 32.6%. This reliability result is conditional on the simulation design, not a distribution-free guarantee. A separate Shanghai–Los Angeles public-data illustration documents observed and assumed inputs without claiming statistical validation. The resulting reproducible screen distinguishes expected exposure from probabilistic risk while remaining outside dynamic dual-sourcing policy design.

detail.abstract: Accurate yield curve fitting and term structure modeling are central to sovereign debt management, fixed-income derivative pricing, and systemic risk monitoring. Traditional parametric frameworks, such as the Nelson-Siegel and Svensson models, offer parsimonious representations but often struggle to capture localized termstructure non-linearities, abrupt level shifts, and dynamic curvature anomalies during market dislocation. This paper presents a comprehensive machine learning architecture for yield curve fitting, term-structure interpolation, and relative-value arbitrage detection. We implement Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with a customized Matern kernel alongside non-linear Neural Network architectures to reconstruct zero-coupon yield curves across sovereign bond markets. Using fitted yield surfaces, we identify cross-sectional pricing dislocations via residual z-score metrics and design a long-short bond arbitrage strategy. Empirical results indicate that Gaussian Processes achieve superior out-of-sample fitting accuracy compared to classical parametric benchmarks, reducing Mean Absolute Error (MAE) by up to 42% in high-volatility regimes. Furthermore, the systematic relative-value arbitrage strategy generates significant risk-adjusted returns with a Sharpe ratio of 1.94, demonstrating the practical utility of non-parametric machine learning in fixed-income portfolio management. Beyond fitting accuracy, this study contributes to the practical deployment of explainable probabilistic machine learning in regulated fixed-income markets. Unlike black-box deep learning systems, Gaussian Process Regression provides explicit uncertainty quantification through its posterior variance, which is critical for risk management, Value-at-Risk estimation, and compliance reporting.

detail.abstract: Enterprise data migration to the cloud must reconcile two objectives that are often managed separately: scaling the movement and modernization of data across portfolios while preserving security, compliance, ownership, quality, and operational resilience. This structured technical review synthesizes research and authoritative guidance on cloud computing, data governance, information-security management, zero trust, distributed systems, data platforms, continuity, provider risk, and migration assurance. The evidence shows that scale is not achieved by increasing transfer throughput alone. Repeatable migration requires a governed operating model with reusable patterns, federated decision rights, policy-as-code guardrails, automated evidence, standardized data contracts, and risk-tiered approval gates. Security risk is concentrated in transitional states, including incomplete inventories, privileged migration identities, temporary storage, uncontrolled replicas, semantic transformation errors, dual operation, and premature source retirement. Provider certifications and shared-responsibility models do not remove enterprise accountability. The paper proposes GOV-SCALE: Ground migration in business and regulatory obligations; Organize ownership and decision rights; Validate data, dependencies, and target fitness; Standardize secure migration patterns; Control identity, encryption, and movement; Assure integrity, resilience, and cutover; Learn through telemetry and continuous evidence; and Enable governed expansion and exit. GOV-SCALE is an evidence-derived conceptual framework rather than an empirically validated method. It positions governance as the mechanism that makes secure migration repeatable across datasets, domains, platforms, and migration waves.

detail.abstract: Prescriptive methods under uncertainty differ in their treatment of risk, ambiguity, and belief. Criticism based solely on an axiom that a method rejects may therefore establish a difference between theories without identifying a defect in an analysis. This paper proposes a crossmethod framework for evaluating prescriptive systems, including their objectives, information, implementation, and disclosures. Nine conditions concern consequential admissibility, mechanism and timing, plan integrity, mandate fidelity, specification provenance, epistemic compatibility, transparency, and formulation. Three further conditions address vanishing events, learning, and optional information within explicit domains. The conditions are proposed assessment criteria, not a characterization theorem or a claim of universal minimality. Illustrative examples distinguish their roles without claiming a complete logical-independence result. Selected mathematical results make parts of the framework operational: a spectral coefficient measures discontinuity in rare events; support-endpoint guarantees admit no informative uniform confidence bound over an unrestricted distribution class; refinement can worsen true performance on a specified pure-action menu; and certain support-based prescriptions are not uniformly learnable. An evidence table distinguishes mathematical constructions from unverified claims about deployment. The framework permits different authorized attitudes toward uncertainty while requiring that an analysis state what it optimizes, what it assumes, what it can validate, and what policy it will implement.

detail.abstract: Women in India's information technology (IT) workforce face sustained occupational demands and a disproportionate share of household and caregiving responsibilities, yet little evidence describes how these pressures relate to work-life balance (WLB) within a single, well-defined workforce after the acute conditions of the pandemic had passed. This study tested how occupational strain, organizational and family support, and caregiving responsibility relate to self-reported WLB satisfaction among women employed in IT and ITenabled companies in Bangalore, India. A cross-sectional survey was self-administered online via Google Forms to women working in Bangalore's IT sector between September 2023 and September 2024, using a non-probability convenience sample. After removing eight fully blank submissions, 107 responses were analysed. Five Likert items were combined into an Occupational Strain Index (Cronbach's α = .64). Associations were tested with Spearman correlation, the Mann-Whitney U test, and multiple linear regression; 250 open-ended comments across three items were coded thematically to contextualise the quantitative results. Reporting followed STROBE guidance for cross-sectional studies. Mean WLB satisfaction was 3.34 (SD = 0.94) on a five-point scale. Occupational strain showed the strongest association with satisfaction (ρ =-.38, p < .001) and remained the only significant predictor in a regression model that also included family support, leisure frequency, and caregiving status (b =-0.59, p < .001; R² = .22). Women with caregiving dependents reported significantly higher strain than those without (U = 1619, p = .044, r =-.24), although caregiving status alone did not differentiate satisfaction. Formal WLB policy presence, marital status, and workarrangement type showed no significant association with satisfaction at this sample size. The most frequent theme in open-ended responses was a request for greater flexibility in work location or hours (35.2% of substantive comments), followed by childcare provision, commuting relief, and menstrual leave. In this sample, subjective occupational strain, rather than the presence of a formal policy or a particular work arrangement, had the strongest relationship with WLB satisfaction. Interventions that target workload, deadline pressure, and commuting burden directly may therefore reach employee-reported WLB more effectively than expanding the policy menu alone, though the crosssectional, non-probability design limits causal and population-level inference.

detail.abstract: In this study I examine the extent to which the collapse of the Lebanese pound's parallel-market exchange rate against the US dollar is statistically associated with the deterioration of Lebanon's banking sector during the 2019-2023 financial crisis. Lebanon's peg to the dollar held for over two decades before collapsing in 2019, and I test whether the magnitude of the resulting devaluation tracks measurable banking-sector outcomes: US-dollar bank deposits, bank return on assets (ROA), and the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio. Using annual secondary data compiled from the World Bank's Global Financial Development Database, IMF Article IV reports, and Lebanese banking-sector bulletins for the years 2017-2023, I estimate log-linear regressions of each performance indicator on the year-end parallel-market exchange rate. The results show a strong, statistically significant negative relationship between the exchange rate and USD bank deposits (r =-0.989, R² = 0.977, p = 0.0015): deposits fell by 25.1% between 2019 and 2023 as the currency lost more than 97% of its parallel-market value over the same span. The relationship between the exchange rate and bank ROA was directionally negative but not statistically significant (r =-0.536, p = 0.352), and NPL data, available only for 2018-2020, moved together with the exchange rate (r = 0.978), though the sample was too small for formal regression. These findings support the "twin crisis" framework, in which currency and banking crises reinforce one another, and demonstrate that Lebanon's devaluation is empirically, not just anecdotally, linked to the erosion of its banking sector. However, small annual sample sizes, a direct consequence of the breakdown in routine banking disclosure after 2019, limit the strength of causal claims, and future research should extend the series and incorporate bank-level, multivariate data once fuller disclosure resumes.

title: How Can Companies Evaluate ROI of AI Projects Before Implementation? A Pre-Implementation Readiness Assessment Framework

detail.title: How Can Companies Evaluate ROI of AI Projects Before Implementation? A Pre-Implementation Readiness Assessment Framework

detail.abstract: AI project failure is widely documented in the practitioner and industry literature: Gartner, for instance, projected that at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proofof-concept by the end of 2025, citing poor data quality, unclear business value, and escalating cost (Gartner, 2024), and this attrition is reported alongside widely noted executive enthusiasm for AI adoption. Despite this attention, systematic, operationalized frameworks for assessing project readiness before implementation remain limited. This paper addresses the following research question: how can organizations systematically assess pre-implementation readiness factors associated with the likelihood of realizing value from AI projects, prior to committing implementation resources? The paper distinguishes this readiness-assessment objective from the narrower task of forecasting financial ROI directly. Drawing on failure-cause research (Ryseff, De Bruhl, & Newberry, 2024; Sculley et al., 2015) and the organizational-readiness and technology-adoption literature, this study develops the Pre-Implementation AI ROI Assessment Framework (PIAF): a nine-dimension instrument, organized across strategic, operational, and tactical levels, with associated 1-5 scoring rubrics and a Composite Readiness Index (CRI) intended to support structured go/no-go decisionmaking. Following design-science research guidance for building and demonstrating novel artifacts (Hevner, March, Park, & Ram, 2004), the framework is illustrated, not validated, through five composite scenarios constructed from patterns reported in the cited failure-cause and adoption literature rather than from verified primary-source records of named organizations. Two scenarios, modeled respectively on a healthcare radiology deployment and a manufacturing predictive-maintenance pilot, are scored in full dimension-by-dimension detail; three additional scenarios are summarized at outcome level only. In the two fully scored scenarios, readiness scores constructed from the nine-dimension rubric are internally consistent with the outcome each scenario was designed to represent. This demonstrates that the instrument can discriminate between contrasting readiness profiles; it is a design-science demonstration of the artifact's internal coherence, not an empirical test against independently verified, real-world outcomes, and it should not be read as evidence of predictive validity. The paper's contribution is threefold: a theoretical contribution (operationalizing * organizational-readiness and failure-cause constructs into measurable dimensions), a methodological contribution (a literature-grounded derivation procedure and a transparent scoring instrument), and a managerial contribution (a structured diagnostic tool for portfolio prioritization and mitigation planning). The illustrative rather than empirical status of the scenario analysis, the absence of inter-rater reliability testing, and unvalidated scoring weights and thresholds are identified as limitations that require prospective, multi-organization validation before the framework’s specific thresholds and weightings can be treated as established rather than provisional.

detail.abstract: Backtests of intraday strategies can drift away from what the live system actually does; in our case, the drift never showed in summary statistics. We report six defects found while running one intraday US equity system live and comparing its live days with their backtest replay. Three came from data: a default feed that carried a small fraction of real opening volume, historical prices adjusted for dividends that live orders never see, and data the live system downloaded but the backtest never did. Two came from code: a sizing step that exceeded a limit the live account enforces, and UTC timestamps read as New York time. One came from configuration: settings that were switched on but never reached the code that places orders. For each we give the symptom, the size of the error, the cause and the test or control that now guards against it. All six sat where two paths that should agree had drifted apart. We close with a ten-point checklist. We make no claim about whether the system is profitable.

detail.abstract: Death management is simultaneously a transmission-control, diagnostic, surveillance and community-trust function during Ebola outbreaks. We reconstructed province-report episodes from the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with explicit death-alert or available-body counts together with dignified and safe burials (EDS) and post-mortem swabs. Because EDS can process carry-over from previous days, EDS-to-alert ratios were treated as throughput indicators rather than completion probabilities. From SitRep 58 onward, 13 count-compatible episodes represented 624 death alerts or bodies, 517 EDS and 433 post-mortem swabs. Weighted throughput was 82.9% for EDS and 69.4% for swabbing. On 11 July in Ituri, 68 bodies required management, only 36 EDS and 24 swabs were completed, six bodies were buried by families without securitization and 26 were carried forward. In SitRep 80 (reporting date 2 August), 99 death alerts yielded 81 EDS and 60 swabs while only 16/32 health zones reported and nine refusals persisted. Post-mortem response functioned as a queue rather than a same-day closed cascade. detail.abstract: Direct agreements are intended to keep a project alive when the project company cannot. In Saudi public-private partnerships, that commercial logic now sits beside an express statutory regime for assignment of contractual status. The Civil Transactions Law (CTL), particularly Articles 255–258, links contractual substitution to advance consent, discharge of the outgoing party, defenses, and the survival of security. At the same time, the National Center for Privatization & PPP (NCP) guidance templates effective from 1 January 2026 expressly contemplate lender step-in, suspension of termination, and replacement of the project company.2 This paper asks a narrow but consequential question: when does lender intervention cease to be cure and become an assignment of contractual status under Saudi law? Using the controlling Arabic text of the Civil Transactions Law, the PSP framework, the 2026 NCP templates, and comparative project-finance materials, it develops a four-route characterization model—cure, temporary intervention, same-entity rescue, and new-entity substitution—and a Continuity Test for distinguishing an Article 255 transfer from a termination-and-regrant or ownership change. It further argues that Articles 256 and 258 should at minimum operate as anti-silence rules: transaction documents should not assume that outgoing-party liability or third-party support survives a consented substitution without a legally sufficient basis for that result. Private-law consent under Article 255 also remains distinct from regulatory, ownership, qualification, licensing, and project-specific approvals. The resulting Saudi Step-In Paradox is that the drafting that makes permanent replacement commercially credible can simultaneously activate statutory consequences that generic step-in language does not answer. The paper converts that problem into a transaction architecture: a Two-Consent/Three-Gate approval model, a Cure–Substitution Gap analysis, Legacy Liability and Security Continuity Schedules, and a six-part enforceability test. More broadly, it advances a Transactional Characterization Principle: cross-border market labels such as “step-in” and “novation” do not determine legal effect in a codified system; local law attaches consequences to what the transaction actually does..

detail.abstract: The advent and adoption of Artificial Intelligence has come at a cost, with growing construction of AI-oriented data centers and rapidly expanding energy consumption. Demands for regulation have grown in public attention, however, the scale of proper regulation has not been thoroughly reviewed through an economic lens. This paper analyzes the geographic scope of data center externalities and their influence on the level of government responsible for their regulation. Utilizing theories of fiscal federalism and a negative-externality model, this study hypothesizes an association between the scale of the externality and the regulatory scale used to correct it. A quantitative analysis of 947 cases from the U.S. Data Center Fights Tracker confirms a statistically significant association (p< .001) between externality scale and regulatory scope. Localized concerns were associated to municipal action in 94.7% of cases, while spillover externalities saw state or federal action 61.3% of the time. The paper then utilizes comparative case-studies in Virginia and Texas to analyze the mechanisms that dictate regulation scale and devolution. Ultimately, the paper recommends a layered policy framework that maintains local land-use authority for site-specific impacts while leveraging state institutions to coordinate regional grid and spillover costs.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence in agriculture is commonly evaluated through changes in yield, input use, labor cost, profitability, sustainability, or adoption. These measures are necessary, but they can miss a distinct economic effect: a technology may change whether a production configuration is economically viable at all. This paper develops the Agricultural Viability Frontier framework by formalizing the concept of an agricultural frontier introduced in Kao (2026). Building on research on digital agriculture, technology adoption, intensive and extensive supply responses, farm viability, and the economics of autonomous machinery, the paper distinguishes optimization from frontier expansion. Optimization improves a crop-location-scale-production configuration that was already viable; frontier expansion changes membership in the viable set. The framework defines a production configuration, an economically viable set conditioned on technology and the surrounding economic environment, and frontier-expanding technological change. It further proposes a Frontier Expansion Test centered on four questions: whether the activity would occur in substantially the same configuration without the technology, which constraint is binding on viability, whether the technology materially relaxes that constraint, and whether complementary conditions remain sufficient. Recent evidence on autonomous field machinery, labor scarcity, robotic harvesting, and autonomous greenhouse control illustrates why technical success or positive return on investment is not by itself evidence of frontier expansion. The contribution is integrative rather than a claim that viability boundaries or extensive-margin effects are new: the paper extends a prior geographic use of a farm viability frontier into a technology-conditioned, configurationlevel framework for evaluating when AI makes agriculture better and when it makes additional agriculture economically possible.

detail.abstract: Provider rules change evaluation outcomes, but participants also respond to those rules. This paper studies risk choice inside the five fictitious 50K contract systems introduced earlier in this research program: Ideal Basic (I0), Ideal Realistic (I1), Static Discipline (A), EOD Trail (B), and Intraday Guardrail (C). Every system retains a $3,000 evaluation target, $2,000 headline drawdown, and 20-session horizon. Contracts A-C then add minimum days, consistency, daily-loss, trailing-drawdown, buffer, and payout-cap rules. The analysis has two layers. For the static contract, a daily-grid dynamic program supplies an upper numerical benchmark within a finite action set. For the path-dependent contracts, a global optimum would require a much larger state space. The paper therefore compares nine declared policies, selects the best policy on 12,000 training paths, and reports it on 30,000 independent holdout paths. "Best response" for A-C means best in that finite policy library, not globally optimal trading. For a positive-drift, lower-variance trader, fixed baseline risk passes 45.06% under I0 and I1, 43.90% under A, 41.55% under B, and 20.26% under C. The training-selected pass policy raises the figures to 60.64%, 60.64%, 50.60%, 41.55%, and 20.26%, respectively. The static dynamic-programming policy transfers well to I0 and I1, fixed high risk is selected for A, and baseline risk remains best in the tested library for B and C. Rules do not merely subtract a constant probability; they change the participant's response. The paper also reconciles an apparent difference across the research line. Matilla Serrano (2026c) checked both target and loss on a ten-point intraday grid. The original dynamic program in this paper checked both at daily closes. The rule engine in Matilla Serrano (2026d) checks losses intraday but determines qualification at the close. These are different stopping rules, so their numerical pass probabilities need not match. Monitoring is part of the contract model. The extended analysis adds an 80-cell drift-policy-contract surface and 20 fresh holdout replications for each contract. These results test computational robustness under the declared synthetic process; they do not introduce market observations. Recent preprints already analyze contract value, first-passage probabilities, and risk sizing in funded-account evaluations (Lim, 2026a, 2026b; Tomàs Fernández, 2026). The contribution here is the controlled policy comparison after risk becomes a participant choice. Within the program, that comparison is necessary because a contract rule can change both the feasible path and the response selected by the trader.

detail.abstract: The demographic generational transition is frequently associated in housing and real estate debates with an expected increase in future market supply. However, the legal transfer of ownership through inheritance and the actual market activation of a property are separated by a distinct decision-making process. This paper develops an integrated research framework for analysing this process. The Inherited Real Estate Disposition Model (IREDM) combines emotional attachment, intergenerational obligation, family and co-heir dynamics, economic factors, property and location characteristics, as well as information and decision complexity. In addition, the Inheritance-to-Property-Release Lag (IPRL) is proposed as a temporal outcome measure capturing the period from inheritance to the first external market activation of the property. Testable hypotheses are derived from the model, and a sequential mixed-methods design incorporating a competing-risks or multi-state perspective is outlined. The contribution of this paper lies not in being the first to observe delays in property sales following inheritance, but in systematically decomposing these delays and integrating them into an empirically testable research framework specifically designed for inherited residential property in Germany.

title: Aequa: Gap-Certified Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Power-Law Flow

detail.title: Aequa: Gap-Certified Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Incompressible Power-Law Flow

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are attractive surrogates for flows that must be solved many times, but they come with no guarantee: the residual loss they minimise does not bound the error of the trained model. For non-Newtonian flow the problem is harder still. A computable error bound requires a stress that is symmetric and exactly in equilibrium, which penalty-based training cannot deliver, and the three-dimensional parametric studies these surrogates are meant for are precisely where finite element solvers become prohibitively slow. We introduce Aequa, a PINN for incompressible power-law flow whose training loss is its own error bound. Aequa passes two neural potentials through parameter-free differential layers, so that incompressibility, boundary conditions, momentum balance and stress symmetry hold exactly for every value of the weights, and it trains a single weight-free loss, the primal-dual gap. Our contributions are threefold. First, guaranteed error bounds: we prove that the loss equals the energy error of the network at every iteration, so each prediction carries a two-sided enclosure of the energy, a bound in the natural distance with sharp, explicitly computable constants, and a pointwise map of the error. Second, exactness on any domain: we prove that one family of rigid-motion generators per hole or cavity, the classical Michell and Kelvin fields, completes the certified class in two and three dimensions, that omitting them leaves a detectable error floor, and that the class can approximate any finite-energy solution. Third, certified speed in three dimensions: a single trained network covers an entire parameter range and returns each answer together with its bound in about two seconds. On eccentric annulus and spherical-shell flows with shear-thinning exponent r = 4/3, the energy enclosures contain the reference energy at every parameter value, with relative widths from 2 × 10-4 to 7.5 × 10-3 , and the loss density reproduces the true error map without any reference solution. In three dimensions, finite element solves that are six to a hundred times less accurate take one to twenty minutes each and return no bound; matching the accuracy of Aequa would take an estimated several hours per solve. The three hours of training therefore cost about as much as one such solve, and every further certified answer is essentially free.

detail.abstract:
The rapid growth of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) has raised important questions about the role of ETF flows in the pricing and performance of underlying equities. Using the transparency of the ETF structure, we examine the relationship between past ETF flows and subsequent stock returns. While short-term mean reversion effects are well documented, evidence on longer-term effects remains limited. 

Based on a broad dataset covering a substantial share of the global ETF market capitalization, we find that flows from thematic and sectoral ETFs are associated with distinct return patterns across investment horizons, with short-term reversal effects and longer-term trend-following dynamics particularly visible in U.S. equities. Building on these findings, we construct a systematic cross-sectional equity signal that combines shortand long-horizon ETF flow information. The resulting portfolios exhibit meaningful return dispersion and low correlation with traditional equity factors, suggesting that ETF flows may provide a complementary source of information for stock selection and systematic portfolio construction. The effects are weaker in European equities, where ETF ownership remains lower.

title: Speed Limits for Liquidity: Queues, Gates, and Runs in Semi-Liquid Funds

detail.abstract: Semi-liquid funds-non-traded BDCs, interval and tender-offer funds-repurchase shares each quarter at net asset value up to a cap, typically 5% of shares, and ration excess requests pro rata. We develop an equilibrium model of this mechanism. A cap works as a speed limit. If the drain it permits, 𝜅[𝜃 + Λ(1 + 𝜃)], does not exceed the fund's excess return plus costless liquidity, 𝜋 + Λ𝜇, no investor base can run the fund. Above this floor, runs are sustained by the backlog of liquidity-constrained investors they trap in the queue. We characterise the run region in closed form, show that a backlog above a tipping level eliminates the no-run equilibrium, and show that tighter caps can be more fragile. We then characterise all run-proof designs. Among work-conserving anonymous rules, a fund is robust to every investor base if and only if its cap satisfies the speed limit-most cheaply implemented through a fee we show to be minimal-or all liquidity needs are verified and prioritised and requests are withdrawable. Irrevocable, first-in-first-out and last-in-first-out queues are more fragile than withdrawable pro rata, and leverage lowers the floor. Tender-offer filings for 46 funds show that proration, absent in private-credit BDCs before 2026, reached 23% of their offers in 2026 and is highly persistent. detail.abstract: Scientific, public, and institutional recognition of the ecological crisis has not led to a sustained transformation of the practices and forms of activity organization that reproduce anthropogenic pressure on natural systems. One reason for this mismatch lies in the persistent praxeological gap between knowledge of the state, functional organization, and limits of natural systems and the capacity to translate that knowledge into changes in concretely organized activity. Contemporary ecological thought has developed several strong ways of describing the crisis. Earth System Science and the planetary boundaries framework make visible the biophysical limits of human impact; ecological ontologies and new materialist approaches, including the work of Latour, Morton, and Haraway, show that the ecological crisis cannot be described only through the decisions of people, states, and institutions: infrastructures, animals, plants, microorganisms, technical objects, and the relations that emerge between them and human activity also matter; political ecology and ecological Marxism, including Moore and Malm, analyse extraction, fossil capital, and unequal responsibility; social-ecological systems and adaptive governance, developed by Ostrom, Folke, and others, describe institutions, resilience, and learning. These approaches are important because each clarifies a real layer of the ecological situation. Yet none of them, taken separately, resolves the methodological problem at the centre of this article: how to connect knowledge about natural systems with the concrete organization of the activities that transform them and with the consequences that spread beyond the initial site of intervention. As such an analytical resource, the article reconstructs the concept of the activity-natural system proposed by P. G. Shchedrovitsky in 1987 as the praxio-natural system (PNS). From the original model it extracts a set of interconnected analytical distinctions: position and structure of activity, natural material, temporal regimes, field of consequences, interference of activities, and organizational-management superstructures. Their contemporary reconstruction is supplemented by the categories of Afanasyev's systemic account of living systems and Möbius's biocenosis, ecological representation, reflexive governance, and institutional learning. The main claim is that PNS provides a methodological grammar for describing how activity is organized, how natural material is transformed, how consequences are distributed, and how governance can become capable of learning from those consequences and redesigning the activity that produced them.

detail.abstract: This tutorial presents a pedagogical introduction to statistical power analysis in Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). Proper sample size planning requires assessing the probability of detecting overall model misfit, either through analytical methods or simulation-based approaches. Standard analytical tools rely on asymptotic normal theory, which can break down under non-normality or missing data. This tutorial demonstrates both strategies — analytical (using semPower with lavaan syntax) and Monte Carlo simulation (using simsem) — side by side, using the WHOQOLBREF four-factor model as a unifying case study. We illustrate how simulation complements analytical calculations by enabling researchers to evaluate parameterlevel power, coverage, and relative bias under realistic scenarios involving model misspecification, missing data, and non-normal continuous indicators. We argue that analytical methods provide a fast and theoretically grounded starting point for sample size planning, while simulation-based approaches allow those conclusions to be stress-tested against the specific population structure, misspecification form, and data conditions of the study at hand.

detail.abstract: We examine whether quarterly earnings pressure reaches frontline regulatory compliance through performance management systems. We study controlled-substance dispensing, in which pharmacists exercise nondelegable scrutiny and bear personal criminal liability. Using Drug Enforcement Administration data on over 40,000 pharmacies, we find that opioid dispensing is three percent higher when the parent company meets or narrowly beats analyst forecasts and five percent lower when it beats them by a wide margin, a pattern inconsistent with demand. The increase is concentrated in the quarter's final month and larger where nonmedical demand is higher and smaller where external monitoring is stronger. After Oregon's 2012 regulation requiring sufficient staffing and restricted productivity quotas, this association weakened relative to same-chain controls elsewhere. Counties with more pressured pharmacies show higher subsequent overdose mortality. Personal criminal liability does not fully insulate frontline scrutiny from earnings pressure, and regulatory interventions that reshape performance management systems can partly restore it.

detail.abstract: Do changes in environmental legislative stringency affect firms’ real activities and the pollution allocation? We construct a text-based index of U.S. state environmental legal stringency from 2000 to 2021, capturing the breadth and punitive severity of newly enacted or amended environmental provisions, including monetary penalties and jail terms. Linking this index to facility-level pollution, we show that state-level legal stringency reduces corporate pollution; a Bartik shift-share instrument supports a causal interpretation.  This reduction in pollution is associated with higher cost of goods sold, lower gross margins, and greater capital expenditure. Within multi-state firms, increases in HQ-state legal stringency spill over to neighbouring-state facilities, with the pollution response differing by financial constraints and becoming more pronounced in lower-stringency states. Environmental laws therefore shape firms’ operations, internal resource allocation, and the geographic distribution of environmental externalities.

detail.abstract: Background and Objectives: Vision-language models (VLMs) are proposed as operators for image-guided intervention, but how they use the images they are shown is uncharacterised. We present a coronary guidewire-navigation environment as a controlled instrument, and ask whether rendering the vessel lumen into simulated fluoroscopy helps one such operator.,Methods: The environment renders a fluoroscopic projection each step and executes the operator's JSON action. One VLM navigated from ostium to mid-LAD target in two patient-derived left-coronary anatomies, comparing wire-only and vessel-overlay views over 25 seed-matched episodes per arm. An open-loop policy that only advances, run at the operator arms' own timestep, established what the task requires without visual information. Navigation efficiency was primary, analysed over all episodes without conditioning on success; left-main rotation was secondary.,Results: The open-loop policy reached target in 75/75 and 75/75 episodes, 100.0% of both anatomies, so the task requires no visual information. detail.abstract: This paper studies how industrialization reshapes cultural values, using the centrally planned placement of China's "156 Projects", a large-scale industrialization program launched in the 1950s. Drawing on modernization theory, I test whether the transition from an agrarian to an industrial society weakens traditional values and shifts gender norms toward greater equality. Using a nationally representative census sample, I develop a new measure of cultural values by applying a large language model to classify the semantic content of Chinese given names, and combine it with a frequency-based Feminine Name Index. Using a dynamic difference-indifferences design, I compare prefectures that hosted "156 Projects" with other prefectures before and after project establishment. Project-hosting prefectures experienced higher income, a shift from agriculture toward industry, and lower fertility. Confucian values in men's names declined. Gendered naming changed asymmetrically: women' names became less distinctively feminine, driven by a reduced emphasis on physical appearance, while men' names showed no comparable change. At the same time, references to intelligence in men's names increased.

detail.abstract: The non-Gaussian CAPM states that beta and coskewness are the only two systematic risks: beta captures second-order risk, while coskewness captures third-order risk. However, the empirical performance of coskewness is known to be weak. Using a return-moment expansion, I decompose coskewness into a sum of correlations between stock and market moments. If investors care less about higher-order risks, these components should receive unequal prices. In Fama-MacBeth regressions of individual stocks excluding microcaps, only the lowest-order component, the variance-variance correlation, earns a significant premium; higher-order cross-moment correlations do not. Thus, third-order risk is priced, but in a more nuanced way. A strategy combining beta and the variance-variance correlation earns about 9% annually, unexplained by Fama-French factors.

title: Will AI Help or Hurt Work and the Economy? What People Around the World Expect
affiliations: Purdue University - Daniels School of Business, Georgetown University, Bank for International Settlements (BIS) - Monetary and Economic Department, Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and

detail.title: Will AI Help or Hurt Work and the Economy? What People Around the World Expect
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence may augment workers, displace labor, or do both. We elicit beliefs from more than 64,000 adults across 32 countries, covering 65% of the world's population and 85% of global output. Workers are substantially more likely to expect artificial intelligence to facilitate than threaten their jobs. Facilitation is more prevalent in lower-productivity countries, whereas threat is unrelated to productivity. Facilitation and threat often coexist within individuals, indicating that perceived benefits and risks are distinct rather than opposite dimensions. They are also associated with different macroeconomic expectations: facilitation with stronger expected growth and employment, and threat with weaker employment and higher inflation. These heterogeneous beliefs may shape the diffusion and acceptance of artificial intelligence across countries.

title: Organizing Expertise with Externalities: Evidence from Primary Care

detail.title: Organizing Expertise with Externalities: Evidence from Primary Care
detail.abstract: Many modern organizations use knowledge hierarchies, where frontline workers try to resolve tasks and pass those they cannot resolve to experts. But the implications of this organization of expertise are not well understood, especially if firm revenues depend on who resolves each task or the firm generates downstream externalities. We study a knowledge hierarchy (KH) using 500,000 patient cases from an online primary care firm, linked to outcomes and costs across Sweden's healthcare system. We use variation in assignment arising from temporary doctor congestion, controlling for date-by-three-hour windows and flexible case characteristics. Within the KH, nurses resolve 70% of cases and pass the remainder to doctors. Relative to doctor-only care, the KH modestly increases external primary care and ED visits but has no adverse effects on hospitalizations, earnings losses, or mortality. Although the mean effect of KH on systemwide (firm plus downstream) production costs is small, this masks substantial heterogeneity. Compared to using only doctors, the savings from the firm's selective use of the KH equal 1.6% of online primary care costs. However, our main finding is that reassigning cases between the direct-to-doctor and KH routes within 15-minute windows to minimize systemwide production costs would save 6.8% of online primary care costs.

title: Covariances versus Characteristics in General Equilibrium
affiliations: University of Minnesota and Ohio State University - Fisher College of Business

detail.title: Covariances versus Characteristics in General Equilibrium
detail.abstract: We question a deep-ingrained doctrine in asset pricing: If an empirical characteristic-return relation is consistent with investor "rationality," the relation must be "explained" by a risk factor model. The investment approach changes the big picture of asset pricing. Factors formed on characteristics are not necessarily risk factors: Characteristics-based factor models are linear approximations of firm-level investment returns. The evidence that characteristics dominate covariances in horse races does not necessarily mean mispricing: Measurement errors in covariances are more likely to blame. Most important, the investment approach completes the consumption approach in general equilibrium, especially for cross-sectional asset pricing.

title: Inflation Expectations as a Policy Tool?

detail.title: Inflation Expectations as a Policy Tool?
detail.abstract: We assess whether central banks may use inflation expectations as a policy tool for stabilization purposes. We review recent work on how expectations of agents are formed and how they affect their economic decisions. Empirical evidence suggests that inflation expectations of households and firms affect their actions but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear, especially for firms. Two additional limitations prevent policy-makers from being able to actively manage inflation expectations. First, available surveys of firms’ expectations are systematically deficient, which can only be addressed through the creation of large, nationally representative surveys of firms. Second, neither households’ nor firms’ expectations respond much to monetary policy announcements in low-inflation environments. We provide suggestions for how monetary policy-makers can pierce this veil of inattention through new communication strategies. Our results are consistent with firms with more outside purchase contracts using less leverage to decrease the expected costs of financial distress on their explicit and implicit contracting parties.

detail.abstract: We study how Expected Shortfall changes with the holding horizon when volatility combines a mean-reverting diffusive factor with a rough Volterra factor under the physical measure. The asset price remains a continuous semimartingale, so the leading short-horizon scale of returns and tail risk is proportional to √ h; roughness enters through higher-order changes in the shape of the conditional loss distribution. For locally linear exposures, we derive explicit rough-leverage and integrated-variance corrections to Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. Under a weighted Fourier-Edgeworth condition, the rough-leverage correction is of relative order h H , whereas in the no-leverage variance-mixture regime the leading symmetric correction is of order h 2H. We establish perturbation results showing when these expansions survive pricing and linearization remainders, and develop fixed-horizon inference for the risk-functional parameters H and χ R = λ R ρ SR , including a conditional delta method for normalized ES. A controlled Monte Carlo experiment verifies the sign, rate and magnitude of the analytical correction and the finite-sample accuracy of the proposed standard errors. We then formulate a direct-horizon risk engine and a practitioner validation protocol for linear and nonlinear books. The framework is intended as a model-risk, economic-capital and stress-testing tool, not as a replacement for regulatory liquidity-horizon rules.

This overturns the proposition that an investment’s value is independent of the entity considering it. We describe the characteristics that determine the subsidy, quantify its size (which could be large), and identify empirical work supporting our model’s predictions.

detail.abstract: A companion paper, "The Pathogenesis of the Polycrisis," traces a causal chain from a structural flaw in the distribution of collectively produced wealth through psychological insecurity to social and political pathology, but deliberately stops short of treatment. This paper takes up the intervention question directly, arguing that the transfer of accurate structural information — an understanding of how the crisis arises and what can be done about it — functions as a genuine, testable point of leverage on that chain, not merely a preparatory step toward some other remedy. Drawing on appraisal theory, the paper shows why even provisional knowledge that a coping response exists changes the psychological experience of insecurity before any action is taken, and identifies three specific functions structural understanding performs: relieving misattributed shame, widening the cognitive tunnel scarcity imposes, and removing the displaced target that frustration would otherwise seek. The paper's central claim operates at the level of shared paradigm rather than individual psychology alone, following Meadows' account of paradigm as the deepest point of systemic leverage, and it supplies the missing bridge between individual change and collective outcome using threshold models of collective behavior and the theory of common knowledge, explaining why public transmission of understanding succeeds where private transmission does not. The paper states its limits as clearly as its claims — information is a comparatively weak source of agency relative to direct mastery experience, and its effect weakens in populations with an entrenched history of futile action — and closes with explicit, falsifiable predictions distinguishing this account from a general endorsement of "raising awareness."

detail.abstract: The recent arrival of disease-modifying Alzheimer's therapies, lecanemab and donanemab foremost among them, is routinely described as the field's most significant advance in a generation. Less routinely asked is whether the trials that produced this advance were ever built to reach anyone beyond a narrow slice of the Alzheimer's population to begin with. This paper reclassifies an original 200-trial Alzheimer's disease sample, first assembled for a broader monograph comparing global equity in Alzheimer's disease and cancer research, by intervention class rather than by disease stage, and finds that the eligibility barrier problem already documented for Alzheimer's trials generally is not evenly distributed across treatment types. Among the 82 trials, 41% of the sample that could be classified by intervention class, disease-modifying trials targeting amyloid or tau pathology showed a 42.9% biomarker or imaging confirmation requirement, nearly three times the whole-sample rate of 15%, alongside a 78.6% comorbidity exclusion rate and a 71.4% prior-treatment exclusion rate, both well above the 54.0% and 29.0% rates reported across the full Alzheimer's sample. Symptomatic and non-pharmacological trials showed no such elevation on the biomarker dimension, though non-pharmacological trials carried the highest comorbidity exclusion of any intervention class at 82.4%. A parallel classification by disease stage found real but weaker variation, with moderate-to-severe trials showing no biomarker requirement at all, consistent with biomarker confirmation mattering most where a diagnosis is still uncertain. These findings are then read against existing population-based research quantifying just how narrow the disease-modifying eligibility window already is in practice, independent of geography: one prospective analysis found fewer than 15% of real-world individuals with mild cognitive impairment or early Alzheimer's disease would qualify for the pivotal amyloid-lowering antibody trials at all, driven overwhelmingly by cardiovascular disease and anticoagulant use, the same categories this paper's own comorbidity-exclusion finding independently reproduces. Read together, the two results suggest that the newest, most consequential class of Alzheimer's treatment carries an eligibility barrier that is not simply steep everywhere, but steepest exactly where diagnostic and monitoring infrastructure, PET scanners, CSF sampling capacity, specialist neurology access, is already scarcest, with direct implications for how blood-based biomarker rollout and eligibility-criteria reform should be prioritized.

detail.abstract: We build a tractable heterogeneous-firm business cycle model where firms face Knightian uncertainty about their profitability and learn it through production. The higher uncertainty reduces agents' confidence and further discourages economic activity. detail.abstract: This paper examines how three monetary policy instruments—the federal funds rate, forward guidance, and large-scale asset purchases—differ in their distributional effects on U.S. household consumption. Using Consumer Expenditure Survey data for 1992–2019, orthogonal high-frequency shocks, and cell-level local projections, this paper finds that the increase in non-housing consumption following expansionary asset purchases is larger for the lowest income quintile than for the highest, with this differential significant in the Northeast and statistically distinguishable from other regions. Across housing contracts, conventional interest rate policy produces a larger consumption decline among lower-income renters than among mortgagors with the same income, whereas asset purchases produce a larger decline among mortgagors, consistent with a cash flow channel through refinancing rather than a dominant employment channel. The Northeast's prominence is consistent with housing's greater weight in local household budgets. Direct tests show that the three instruments are not interchangeable, and forward guidance has no consistent distributional direction.
