detail.abstract: The mean response in the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) is widely used to summarize individual forecasts. In this paper, we propose a novel summary forecast that enhances the predictive power of the mean response by selectively incorporating idiosyncratic signals. Our framework is motivated by the observation that while individual forecasts are highly correlated-suggesting a factor structure-they also exhibit significant heterogeneity. We treat the mean response as the primary common factor and define heterogeneity as the idiosyncratic component of each individual forecast after accounting for this commonality. Employing a factor-adjusted regularized framework, we integrate informative idiosyncratic components to improve the mean response. Using SPF data from the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and the European Central Bank, we show that incorporating these idiosyncratic components leads to significant predictive gains over the mean response.

detail.abstract: Resilience engineering frames operational continuity as the ability of a socio-technical system to sustain, adapt, and recover performance under disturbance, rather than only preventing failures in a narrow technical sense. Logistics operations are increasingly cyber-physical systems, because transport execution, warehouse automation, port and terminal workflows, and multi-party coordination depend on interconnected information systems, cloud services, and operational technology networks. This interdependence increases exposure to ransomware, malware, denial-of-service disruption, and intrusion events that can propagate across organisations and quickly become service-level agreement breaches, throughput collapse, and multi-node congestion effects. Real-world incidents in maritime logistics and freight forwarding show how cyber events can disrupt booking platforms,corporate and terminal systems, and operational processes at scale, with reported financial impacts reaching hundreds of millions of dollars in some cases. Traditional disaster recovery approaches can remain too IT-centric when they treat restoration as an application recovery problem, and not a system-level problem that joins IT, OT, and operationaldecision-making under time pressure. This study develops a resilience engineering framework for disaster recovery and cyber-incident readiness in logistics operations, focused on modelling disruption propagation, quantifying operational impacts, and translating results into logistics-specific recovery playbooks and recovery targets. The research proposes a hybrid modelling approach combining dependency mapping and disruption simulation to examine cascading failure scenarios involving (i) ransomware disruption of coordination platforms, (ii) cloud or shared digital service unavailability, and (iii) compromise of OT or IoT networks that underpin warehouse and port automation. Empirical baselines from port container throughput statistics and sector threat distributions are used to ground scenario parametersand outputs, and a worked simulation illustrates how short-duration disruption can translate into large throughput losses when recovery is constrained by operational bottlenecks. The contribution is a practical cyberphysical resilience architecture for logistics, including measurement metrics, playbook structures, and benchmarks for recovery time and recoverypoint objectives aligned to operational continuity thresholds.

detail.abstract: A clearing house sets margin from a risk model that reads prices, and the traders who post that margin move the prices the model reads. We close the loop and derive the speed at which a risk model may react before it destabilizes the market it measures. The loop gain is g = λQ/m, the price impact of the constrained position divided by margin per unit, and realized volatility is fundamental volatility divided by 1-g. For a risk model with reaction speed θ and a margin rule with elasticity γ to perceived variance, the dominant eigenvalues have modulus θγg * /(1-g *) and the market is stable if and only if θγg * < 1-g *. The loss of stability is always a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation, so the margin cycle it creates has a period between three and four updating intervals and never a period of two. Two design choices move the limit by more than the lookback length does: an equal-weight window tolerates a quarter of the loop gain of an exponential rule with the same mean lag, and marking capital to market tightens the limit by a further factor of 1-g *. Away from that boundary the loop damps the response of margin to fundamental volatility below what the rule alone implies, and the operative risk is instead a quiet period, in which falling measured volatility lowers margin, raises leverage, and carries the gain toward the point where no price clears. A floor at √ λW removes that possibility exactly. The loop gain is identified from a return series together with the published parameters of the margin rule.

detail.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has begun to reshape the way university students approach writing, research, revision, and academic communication. Among the technologies attracting considerable attention, ChatGPT has introduced new possibilities for generating ideas, explaining difficult concepts, improving language, and providing immediate feedback on written work. These capabilities are particularly relevant to university writing centers, which traditionally provide individualized support through human tutors. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a replacement for writing tutors, writing centers can approach generative AI as a collaborative tool that complements human expertise. This article examines how human-AI collaboration may redefine writing center tutoring practices, student support, and approaches to academic integrity. A conceptual methodology is used to synthesize existing scholarship concerning writing pedagogy, artificial intelligence, automated writing assistance, and academic integrity. The discussion identifies several opportunities, including personalized feedback, brainstorming support, language assistance, accessibility, and improved availability of writing resources. At the same time, significant challenges arise from inaccurate AI-generated information, overreliance on automated suggestions, inappropriate authorship, privacy concerns, and the possibility of students submitting AI-generated text as their own work. The article proposes a human-centered model in which tutors remain responsible for pedagogical judgment while AI functions as a supplementary resource. Such an approach positions writing centers not merely as places where students correct grammatical errors but as environments where students learn how to evaluate, question, revise, and responsibly use emerging technologies. The future role of writing centers therefore depends less on resisting AI and more on developing informed practices that preserve human learning, student agency, and academic integrity.

detail.abstract: Since the late 1970s, comparative family law has formally severed the marital-support obligation from the sex of the spouse who owes it. Orr v. Orr struck down sex-specific alimony statutes in the United States; Germany's 2008 reform recast post-divorce maintenance as an exception to a general principle of self-responsibility; Brazil's 2002 Civil Code addressed spousal support in gender-neutral terms; and English law has never formally distinguished husbands from wives under the Matrimonial Causes Act 1973. Yet across all four systems, the doctrinal proxies that determine who actually receives support-foregone earning capacity, marital standard of living, length of marriage-continue to track a sexual division of domestic labor that formal neutralization did not touch, producing outcomes that remain overwhelmingly one-directional. This article argues that formal gender-neutralization did not deconstruct the marital obligation; it relocated it from a status-based command onto a facially neutral distributive mechanism whose justificatory basiscompensation for relationship-specific sacrifice, on one account, or protection against post-marital need, on another-has never been settled. Courts and legislatures move between these two incompatible rationales opportunistically, producing a "justificatory oscillation" that better explains persistent outcome asymmetry than any residual doctrinal sexism. Using a comparative doctrinal method across the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, and Brazil, the article traces this oscillation through recent reform (Florida's 2023 elimination of permanent alimony, the Law Commission of England and Wales's 2024 scoping report, and the UK Supreme Court's 2025 decision in Standish v Standish) and proposes a modest interpretive heuristic-the compensable-sacrifice test-that would require courts to identify a specific, marriage-attributable economic sacrifice as the exclusive trigger for post-marital support, substituting demonstrated conduct for marital-role stereotype as the operative variable in either spouse's favor. detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve's Summary of Economic Projections (SEP) is usually summarized by its median, although each of the four releases per year since 2012 contains a cross-section of individual projections that can differ substantially in both dispersion and shape. detail.abstract: Contemporary global macroeconomics presents a significant structural paradox: while aggregate indicators such as global GDP, nominal trade volumes, foreign direct investment (FDI) flows, and asset prices in major economies continue to show positive growth trends, the underlying economic dynamics supporting this aggregate expansion are progressively weakening. Traditional macroeconomic analysis often treats sustained positive GDP growth as a sufficient condition for economic health, yet this static focus on output growth may obscure the systematic deterioration in growth quality and the structural erosion of long-term productive capacity. This paper develops a theoretical framework to explain the coexistence of aggregate expansion and declining growth momentum, proposing that the global economy is transitioning toward a paradigm of "high-cost expansion with low-efficiency growth." Within this paradigm, aggregate GDP expansion increasingly relies on fiscal stimulus, debt accumulation, factor-intensive inputs, and redundant capital allocation during supply chain restructuring, rather than on total factor productivity (TFP) improvements driven by technological progress. Through case studies of the United States, China, Vietnam, Germany, Saudi Arabia, and other economies, this paper identifies common patterns of divergence between aggregate output growth and underlying growth quality, and proposes an empirical framework for systematic crosscountry testing.

detail.abstract: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz has long been interpreted as an American monetary allegory of the late 19th century, particularly of the “Crime of 1873” and the free-silver debate. Yet a more fundamental question remains: which combinations of monetary objectives could coexist in a commodity-money system, and which were mechanically unattainable? This paper restates the impossible trinity for a commodity-money system and applies the framework to the transformation of the U.S. monetary regime from the greenbacks to the gold standard. The three policy objectives are defined as (1) a fixed exchange ratio between the dollar and the standard metal(s) (=a fixed exchange rate), (2) the free exchange between the dollar and the standard metals (= free capital mobility), and (3) independent control of the money supply (= monetary policy independence). Using evidence on the composition of the money supply, the legal and market silver-gold ratios, and the price level, the paper examines the trade-offs among these objectives. The analysis shows that the greenback period (1862–1879) combined (2) and (3) at the cost of (1), while the gold standard (1879–1900) restored (1) and (2) as the money supply became increasingly dependent on gold flows. The free-silver movement of the 1890s attempted to combine (1) and (3), but could not sustain this combination under international arbitrage. The analysis therefore identifies the resumption of specie payments in 1879, rather than the Coinage Act of 1873, as the more consequential institutional turning point and interprets the prolonged deflation after 1879 as a consequence of the gold-standard regime. The framework also offers a basis for comparative analysis of other commodity-money systems, including Britain and China.

Credit risk assessment is fundamental to lending profitability and portfolio quality.
Traditional models often fail to capture non‑linear borrower behaviours, while complex machine
learning models remain difficult to interpret. This study develops an explainable machine
learning pipeline to predict loan defaults using Lending Club data, addressing both predictive
accuracy and business transparency. Following a structured analytics workflow – data cleaning,
feature selection via SelectKBest, stratified train‑test splitting, and SMOTE‑based resampling –
three classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) are trained and evaluated.
Rather than relying on accuracy alone (which is misleading in imbalanced datasets), models are
compared using precision, recall, F1‑score, and ROC‑AUC. SHAP analysis provides global and
local interpretability. Results show that XGBoost achieves the strongest performance
(ROC‑AUC = 0.996), and SHAP reveals that payment history and outstanding principal – not
static application features – are the most influential drivers of default risk. This work
demonstrates that high‑performance models need not be “black boxes”; with appropriate
explanation tools, lending institutions can adopt sophisticated analytics while maintaining
regulatory accountability and stakeholder trust.

detail.abstract: How do labor markets in migrant-sending economies adjust when jobs abroad contract? I study Saudi Arabia's Nitaqat program, combining its 2011 enforcement with predetermined differences in Indian districts' historical orientation toward Saudi Arabia relative to other Gulf destinations. Exposure had little effect on employment or labor-force participation, but changed the composition of work: a one-standard-deviation increase in Saudi orientation raised self-employment by 3.5 percentage points and reduced casual and regular salaried work by 2.2 and 0.9 points. The shift was concentrated in own-account and unpaid family work. Complementary evidence from Kerala is consistent with migration adjustment. The results show that external labor-demand shocks can reallocate work without increasing unemployment.

detail.abstract: The growing use of drones by state militaries is reshaping the dynamics of asymmetric warfare across Africa. Governments confronting insurgent movements increasingly rely on unmanned aerial systems for surveillance, intelligence gathering, and targeted strikes. Insurgent groups, however, are not passive recipients of this technological shift: they adapt by developing tactics designed to evade aerial observation or to exploit the same technologies themselves. This article examines how drone proliferation affects the strategic interaction between state forces and non-state armed groups. Comparing four cases with markedly different histories of drone exposure-the Sahel, Somalia, Libya, and the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo-the analysis traces how insurgent movements respond to aerial surveillance through dispersion, concealment, and the adoption of commercial drone technologies for reconnaissance and limited attack operations. The article develops the concept of an adaptation ceiling: the point at which sustained insurgent exposure to aerial surveillance yields adaptive repertoires-evident in Al-Shabaab's decade-long experience in Somalia-that substantially blunt its operational value. Rather than resolving asymmetric conflicts in favour of the technologically superior party, drone proliferation contributes to the emergence of a contested vertical battlespace in which both state and non-state actors compete for control of aerial observation. The findings qualify optimistic assumptions about drone-enabled counterinsurgency in weak-state settings: tactical advantage achieved without addressing the governance failures and political grievances that sustain insurgency tends to yield limited and diminishing strategic returns.

title: Prim-Lex Polar Governance and Development Assessment System: A Five-Prim-Fire, Eight-Dimensional Coherence, and Nine-Nexus Framework for Polar Risk, Resilience, and Investment Decision-Making

detail.abstract:
The polar system is undergoing the most rapid and structural transformation in the Earth system. In 2026, the annual maximum extent of Arctic sea ice reached its lowest value in the 47-year satellite record, and spring sea-ice extent remained at historically low levels. Northern Sea Route cargo traffic hit a record 37.02 million tonnes in 2025 and is projected to increase by approximately 14% in 2026, surpassing 40 million tonnes for the first time. The number of unique ships entering the Arctic Polar Code area increased by 40% compared with 2013, and total distance sailed nearly doubled. At the same time, the institutional gridlock in Antarctic governance continues to deepen. CCAMLR has failed to adopt any new marine protected area since 2012, and the “institutional anti-commons” dilemma under the consensus rule has been rigorously modeled in 2026 through a multi-agent evolutionary game framework. The BBNJ Agreement entered into force on 17 January 2026, introducing new legal tools such as ABMT/MPA and EIA for the approximately 2.8 million km² Central Arctic Ocean ABNJ area, but its practical application in polar regions faces severe challenges from fragmented governance and geopolitical confrontation. Although the Arctic Council, under the Kingdom of Denmark’s Chairship for 2025–2027, has attempted to restore partial dialogue functions through a new “strategic planning consultation” model, diplomatic-level formal meetings have remained suspended since March 2022.

These developments indicate that the core bottleneck in polar governance is no longer “insufficient scientific evidence” but rather the absence of a unified mathematical language capable of integrating the physical processes of ice-sheet melting, the commercial dynamics of shipping growth, the functional changes of ecosystems, the institutional rhythms of governance response, and the risk logic of capital flows into a single quantitative framework. Based on the Five Prim-Fires, Eight-Dimensional Coherence, and Nine-Nexus Guidance theoretical system of Prim-Lex Theory, this paper constructs the Prim-Lex Polar Governance and Development Assessment System (PL-POLAR). The Five Prim-Fires—Physical Prim-Fire, Animal Prim-Fire, Plant Prim-Fire, Mind Prim-Fire, and Earth-System Intelligence Prim-Fire—provide a cross-scale theoretical foundation from energy scales to planetary scales for the polar system. The Eight-Dimensional Coherence framework—Climate-Cryosphere Coherence (D1), Development-Conservation Coherence (D2), Science-Policy-Practice Coherence (D3), Governance-Legal Coherence (D4), Ecological Functional Coupling Coherence (D5), Spatial Coherence (D6), Temporal Coherence (D7), and Information-Knowledge Coherence (D8)—maps polar system states into an eight-dimensional phase vector space through 42 observable indicators. The core index PWCI (Polar-Wide Coherence Index) measures overall system coherence as the modulus of the complex sum of eight phase terms. PDRI (Polar Decoherence Risk Index) and PSRI (Polar Systemic Risk Index) capture decoherence risk and systemic risk, respectively. The Nine-Nexus decision architecture translates coherence diagnostics into a decision algorithm covering “whether it can be done—how to do it—when to do it—how much to invest—when to adjust—when to exit.” The PL-POLAR Three-Color Certification (Green/Yellow/Red), governed by the principle that “composite scores cannot override critical red lines,” provides auditable admission judgments for polar development and investment projects. Using six empirical anchors— normalized Arctic shipping route operations, the CCAMLR MPA negotiation gridlock, the ATCM/CEP environmental impact assessment system, the Arctic Council governance recovery process, the BBNJ institutional interface, and Arctic shipping insurance insurability—this paper systematically demonstrates the application pathway of PL-POLAR in identifying “phase differences” and “critical windows” in polar governance.

detail.abstract: How should a central bank divide its communication between the state of the economy and the way policy responds to that state? I study this question in a monetary model in which the policy decision is itself informative, long-term bond prices affect intermediary net worth, and public losses are backed by taxes. Because the observed decision already reveals part of the policy reaction, information about economic conditions is usually more valuable. Reaction guidance can nevertheless dominate when private information or long-duration exposure makes the decision harder to interpret. Allowing the central bank to combine the two messages weakly improves welfare, although an interior mix is chosen only for a small set of parameter configurations. Forward guidance should therefore be designed around what markets learn from policy actions and how that learning changes private and public balance sheets.

title: Dominant Currency Pricing and Currency Risk Premia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dominant Currency Pricing and Currency Risk Premia
detail.abstract: This paper studies how dominant-currency pricing affects currency risk premia. Empirically, weextract common risk factors from excess currency returns using principal components and relate countries’factor exposures to observable macroeconomic characteristics, with export dollar invoicing emerging as apredictor of carry trade exposure. A small open-economy model with dominant-currency pricing anddollar-denominated liabilities explains why. Dollar export invoicing weakens the exchange rate's stabilizingeffect on external demand, while dollar debt makes depreciation costly for leveraged intermediaries. When thetwo frictions interact, depreciations occur in bad states, local-currency assets become risky, the currencypremium rises, and the risk-adjusted neutral rate increases. Under a standard Taylor rule, this mechanismgenerates persistently higher inflation.

title: Creditors’ Seniority and Sovereign Risk: Evidence From Debt Composition
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Creditors’ Seniority and Sovereign Risk: Evidence From Debt Composition
detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on the de facto seniority structure of sovereign debt. Using a measure of the Relative Percentage in Default (RPID) by creditor group for 119 low-income and emerging market countries over the period 1980–2022, we show that debt owed to the IMF and the World Bank is, on average, the most senior, followed by debt owed to official bilateral creditors. Private creditors, notably bondholders and commercial banks, are on average junior to official creditors, with commercial banks being the least prioritized group for repayments. Beyond characterizing the seniority hierarchy, our empirical analysis shows that creditor composition has economically meaningful implications for sovereign risk. Using an instrumental variable estimation, we show that IMF credit outstanding as a share of GNI is robustly and negatively associated with the probability of a debt crisis. This stabilizing effect weakens progressively as debt stocks rise, suggesting that the IMF's crisis-preventing role diminishes in situations of severe debt overhang. Turning to sovereign borrowing costs, we find that IMF lending is negatively associated with sovereign bond spreads.

title: The Coming Great Repression? New Measures and a Century of Evidence
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: The Coming Great Repression? New Measures and a Century of Evidence
detail.abstract: Governments have historically used financial repression to reduce debt and fiscal pressures, yet few systematic measures of repression exist. To fill this gap, we introduce two quantity-based repression indicators grounded in a structural portfolio-choice model, exploiting the gap in government-bond demand between captive and non-captive investors. A narrow fiscal indicator captures pressure on banks to hold government bonds. A consolidated measure adds the perimeter of central bank liabilities. Applying our measures to a novel dataset of 17 advanced economies since 1920, we find that financial repression has been a persistent feature of modern history, peaking after World War II, receding during the capital account liberalization era, and rising again after the Global Financial Crisis. Our measures correlate with conditions typically associated with repression—such as high debt burdens and restricted capital mobility—along with crowding out of private investment and credit. Using a debt decomposition framework, we show that repression was a major driver of debt reduction after World War II, generating larger fiscal savings than traditional seigniorage, and has again generated fiscal savings since the Global Financial Crisis. With the conditions historically associated with elevated repression present today, our evidence suggests that financial repression may see increased use going forward.

title: Looking for Underlying Structure in WEO Forecasts
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Looking for Underlying Structure in WEO Forecasts
detail.abstract: This paper examines the statistical properties of the IMF’s World Economic Outlook (WEO) projections over 1999–2023 for 29 economies. The optimism of WEO growth forecasts is well established; we confirm it and look behind it at two features of how the forecasts are built. First, the growth of the systemic economies (the United States and China) appears to be underutilized in the projections: forecasts embed less of the cross-country growth comovement present in the data, a gap we term forecast fragmentation that did not narrow over the sample. Second, the conditional growth–inflation link present in the historical data is weakly represented in the projections. These patterns suggest that structural models, in which such cross-country and real–nominal linkages can be verified through estimation, could be a useful complement to expert judgment, serving as a baseline check for medium-term anchors.

title: Financial Shocks in Currency Markets: Evidence from UIP Premia
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Financial Shocks in Currency Markets: Evidence from UIP Premia
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a sign-narrative VAR approach to identifying financial shocks in currency markets. The approach imposes minimal sign restrictions shared across canonical exchange rate models, leveraging their key insights while remaining robust to misspecification relative to structural models typically used in the literature. To sharpen the identification, sign restrictions are complemented with narrative restrictions anchored on episodes of well documented FX market dysfunction. Focusing on two emerging economies (Brazil and Chile), our estimates suggest that financial shocks account for about one third of UIP fluctuations, and contribute less than 10% to the variance of macro variables including output and inflation. While infrequent, when they do materialize, financial shocks trigger sharp declines in output, suggesting economically meaningful spillovers from frictions in currency markets to the real economy.

title: Explaining Income Divergence in the Western Indian Ocean: Evidence from Mauritius, Seychelles, Madagascar and Comoros
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Explaining Income Divergence in the Western Indian Ocean: Evidence from Mauritius, Seychelles, Madagascar and Comoros
detail.abstract: This paper examines the divergent economic development paths of Mauritius, Seychelles, Madagascar, and Comoros since 1980. Despite operating in broadly similar regional and geographic settings, Mauritius and Seychelles achieved significantly higher levels of real GDP per capita, while Madagascar and Comoros saw more limited progress. Combining qualitative analysis with panel econometric methods (FMOLS and DOLS), the paper finds that institutional quality, human capital development, trade openness, and macroeconomic policies are associated with higher levels of real GDP per capita. The results suggest that stronger governance frameworks and investment in human capital are associated with higher income levels in Mauritius and Seychelles, while more persistent institutional and structural challenges are associated with lower income levels in Madagascar and Comoros. Overall, the findings suggest the importance of institutions, human capital, and external integration in economic performance across the four Indian Ocean island economies.

title: Aggregate Gains from AI and Their Distribution: Global Evidence From Usage Data
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Aggregate Gains from AI and Their Distribution: Global Evidence From Usage Data
detail.abstract: How large is the labor cost saved by AI, and how is it distributed across occupations? Using five waves of the Anthropic Economic Index (January 2025 to February 2026), we construct two novel measures from observed AI usage across countries over the world. The AI concentration index (ACI) shows that in developing economies, virtually all AI usage-based value is generated in a small professional enclave (ACI near 1.0); high-income economies average 0.4 to 0.5, with concentration declining in many countries. The labor cost equivalent (LCE) values the time currently saved by AI at $2.7 trillion annually (3.4% of GDP), an indicative measure of the labor cost of that time. Income and regulatory readiness predict concentration; lacking an official English language slows broadening, a barrier for developing countries.

title: Fiscal Populism and Monetary Policy Rules
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Fiscal Populism and Monetary Policy Rules
detail.abstract: We explore the historical link between populist regimes, fiscal monetization, and inflation, and how these links affect monetary policy in the 21st century. Using data for a large set of advanced economies and emerging markets since 1960, we show that, historically, left-leaning populist regimes are linked to increases in central bank lending to the central government, a gauge of deficit monetization. In turn, central bank lending is associated with marked increases in inflation. We show that past exposure to populism that relied on deficit monetization affects the conduct of monetary policy today. Countries with a history of deficit monetization and left-wing populist regimes systematically respond more strongly to deviations of inflation expectations from target. This effect persists even after controlling for the direct effect of past inflation on monetary policy rules. In the context of the literature of experienced learning, this novel finding sheds light on the persistence of past populist policies---central banks operating under the shadow of past populist regimes that relied on inflation-prone deficit monetization continue today needing to send stronger signals of their independence and commitment to price stability to effectively anchor inflation expectations.

title: Global Dollar Exposure and Its Relationship with CIP Deviations
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Global Dollar Exposure and Its Relationship with CIP Deviations
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes a global map of dollar exposures and examines the relationship between net dollar exposures, defined as the difference between dollar assets and liabilities, and covered interest parity (CIP) deviations. We find that the cross-sectional relationship is significantly negative in advanced economies but positive in emerging markets. CIP deviations represent the hedging cost that foreign holders of dollar assets or liabilities incur to manage exchange rate risk. To explain, we develop a model in which the CIP deviations are determined by the demand and the supply side of hedging. The negative correlation in advanced economies can be explained by the variations in hedging demand. Larger net dollar exposures increase the hedging demand, raising hedging costs (reflected as more negative CIP deviations) and producing a negative correlation. In contrast, the positive correlation in emerging markets is explained by the supply side of the hedging market. Limited hedging supply leads to wider CIP deviations (more negative), encouraging firms to borrow in U.S. dollars rather than local currencies, thereby reducing net dollar exposures and generating a positive correlation.

title: Public Debt, Wealth Inequality, and the Burden of Taxation
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Public Debt, Wealth Inequality, and the Burden of Taxation
detail.abstract: Public debt and wealth concentration have co-moved persistently across advanced economies and historical periods, defying standard theories of wealth inequality, particularly given that rising inequality has coincided with falling real interest rates in recent decades. I develop a stylized Diamond model with household heterogeneity and progressive taxation to formalize how public debt, through its tax burden, endogenously dictates tax progressivity and thereby affects the wealth distribution. In this framework, permanent debt shocks alter tax progressivity depending on the macroeconomic regime, with debt expansions increasing progressivity when interest rates are high but reducing it when interest rates are low. The resulting impact of public debt on wealth inequality is nonlinear in the overall level of the tax burden, disequalizing below a threshold and equalizing above it. Cross-country empirical evidence supports these predictions and shows that public debt is a quantitatively important, and often dominant, driver of postwar wealth inequality, with sizable effects transmitted primarily through the tax burden. These findings establish the distribution of the tax burden as a primary driver of long-run wealth inequality, and public debt as a central mediating channel through which structural shocks, such as population aging or artificial intelligence, propagate to the wealth distribution.

title: Monetary–Fiscal Policy Interactions in Korea: A QPM-Based  Analysis
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Monetary–Fiscal Policy Interactions in Korea: A QPM-Based  Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops a quarterly projection model for Korea with an integrated fiscal block, enabling analysis of monetary-fiscal interactions. The model is validated through historical decompositions and forecast evaluation. Scenario analysis comparing dynamics with and without debt-stabilizing fiscal rules reveals a fundamental trade-off: rules generate short-run procyclicality but prevent permanent debt drift. Without rules, temporary nominal GDP movements cause lasting debt-to-GDP changes. For Korea, facing age-related spending pressures, a medium-term fiscal framework could safeguard sustainability.

title: Stablecoins and the Future of Payments: Evidence from Financial Markets
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund

detail.title: Stablecoins and the Future of Payments: Evidence from Financial Markets
detail.abstract: We examine whether financial markets expect stablecoins to play an important role in payments. After the decisive congressional vote on the GENIUS Act, the market value of payment incumbents fell by 1.3% ($21.5 billion) relative to other financial firms, consistent with stablecoins increasing competition in payments. The decline was larger for firms focused on cross-border payments, and smaller for those protected by network effects or offering crypto services. Accounting for anticipation using prediction markets, we estimate that the Act reduced the value of incumbent payment firms by 13–27% ($220–470 billion), exceeding the impact of recent pro-competitive regulatory shocks.

title: Inferring Structural Beliefs from Macroeconomic Expectations: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Inferring Structural Beliefs from Macroeconomic Expectations: Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: I analyze multi-horizon market forecasts for macroeconomic variables in Brazil from 2010 to 2026,using a structural macroeconomic model to interpret stated beliefs as the outcomes of a coherent beliefsystem. This produces time-varying beliefs about policy rules, transmission mechanisms, and structuralshocks. Beliefs about the monetary policy rule vary in two distinct dimensions, with the perceived target andTaylor response coefficients showing independent variation. Monetary transmission is seen as weak; theperceived Philips and IS curves are very flat. Markets see fiscal policy as increasingly unresponsive to higherdebt. The perceived inflation target is unchanged after an unexpected monetary tightening, but the perceivedresponse to inflation increases, with larger effects for monetary surprises and smaller for news shocks.

title: Private Finance and Climate Investment Needs: An Analytical Framework
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Private Finance and Climate Investment Needs: An Analytical Framework
detail.abstract: Achieving climate-related commitments and mitigating related risks to macroeconomic andfinancial stability require improving the conditions for private investment. Raising sufficient private finance ishowever challenging, particularly for emerging markets and developing economies. This paper develops ananalytical framework to assess how reforms shape private climate finance. Key dimensions include macrostructural reforms to lower capital costs, measures to incentivise financing for climate-related investments, andblended financing that leverages public resources to attract private investment. To the extent the resultingexternally-financed investments are resilience- and growth-enhancing, these can also support strengthening ofthe longer-term balance of payments position. Effective implementation may require international support,especially for developing economies

title: Locked Out: Drivers and Economic Implications of Declining Housing Affordability in Europe
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund

detail.title: Locked Out: Drivers and Economic Implications of Declining Housing Affordability in Europe
detail.abstract: Amid sharp house price increases in some parts of Europe, housing affordability has again become one of the main concern of households. This paper conducts three complementary sets of analyses to shed light on the drivers and economic implications of declining housing affordability. First, using a structural VAR, we show that supply-side factors have become increasingly prominent drivers of house prices—a notable shift from the credit-driven price increases that preceded the Global Financial Crisis. Second, drawing on household-level EU-SILC data, we argue that the burden has fallen disproportionately on lower-income urban renters, who face both rising rents and diminishing prospects of transitioning to homeownership. This is especially true for financially more vulnerable renters who have seen their probability of becoming home owners fall by more than half since the pre-GFC period. Third, we provide new empirical evidence that the resulting widening of income and wealth gaps between owners and renters is compounded by the efficiency cost of reduced labor mobility, as high housing costs make it harder for workers to move to more productive locations – quantitively, housing affordability constraints might have led to around one million foregone moves within the EU over the past decade. The analyses underpin the policy recommendations to alleviate housing affordability challenges set out in the IMF’s 2026 Euro Area consultation, including the need to focus on national measures to boost housing supply, with a complementary role for EU-level action.

title: Jurisdictional Capital and AI Regulation: Evidence from The EU AI Act
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Jurisdictional Capital and AI Regulation: Evidence from The EU AI Act
detail.abstract: We study how AI regulation affects firm valuation using the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the world's first comprehensive AI framework. In an event study around the April 2021 proposal, we find firms combining deeper EU presence with faster AI hiring earned higher announcement returns, suggesting markets value “jurisdictional capital”—experience in the EU regulatory environment helps firms navigate the AI regulation. The effect is stronger for high-risk AI, for firms with stable and concentrated EU presence, or prior compliance experience, unexplained by size, foreign exposure, or lobbying. EU-embedded, AI-expanding firms increase within-firm EU revenue share when peers are less embedded.

title: Riding the Global Financial Cycle: How Capital Flows into LIC's
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF) and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Riding the Global Financial Cycle: How Capital Flows into LIC's
detail.abstract: As low-income countries (LICs) gain access to international capital markets, the scope for increased financing rises but so does the risk of shocks. Our empirical results suggest that, after the global financial crisis (GFC), the global financial cycle has been a significant driver of private capital flows to LICs. In particular, a stronger US dollar (against advanced economy currencies) was associated with weaker net inflows. We also find that external government borrowing in LICs had a statistically significant but relatively small counter-cyclical component, inversely related to global financial and economic cycles, complementing policy responses to shocks.

detail.abstract: This is a didactic presentation of  trading costs and effective protection rate (EPR, the relative difference between the rent provided by trading costs protection against competing imports and the additional production costs due to the higher domestic price of inputs) when trade in Glbal Vaue Chains is prevalent. Transaction costs affect not only the competitiveness of goods but also --and perhaps more importantly-- of services sectors. Why? Because one of the most important results of the measure of trade in value-added, in our views, is to fully expose the economic weight of services in today's international trade. Moreover, in a “trade in tasks” perspective, not only the value of nominal tariffs, but also their distribution between unprocessed and processed goods -- a feature of nominal schedules known as tariff escalation -- have a particular importance. By increasing more the domestic prices of finished goods than those of intermediary, tariff escalation creates a significant anti-export bias on complex manufactured goods. Mitigating arrangements commonly used in developing countries, such as Export Processing Zones or draw-back schemes have only limited effects when GVC up-grading through deeper domestic inter-industrial linkages is the policy-makers' main objective.

title: Financing First-of-a-Kind Climate Technologies: Insights from the German Ecosystem
affiliations: , Technische Universität München (TUM) and

detail.title: Financing First-of-a-Kind Climate Technologies: Insights from the German Ecosystem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Achieving net-zero emissions requires commercializing and scaling emerging climate technologies. A crucial milestone is financing a first-of-a-kind (FOAK) project, the first commercial-scale plant of a technology. Yet, despite growing policy attention, there is little agreement on what makes a project first-of-a-kind, and why such projects struggle to receive sufficient investment. Drawing on 28 interviews with investors and operators of FOAK projects in the German climate technology ecosystem, we develop a framework of three types of FOAK projects and identify the challenges in financing them. We find challenges due to unproven technologies or markets, which makes it difficult for FOAK projects to raise the debt needed to scale, often limiting their financing to grants or equity investments. Investors and policymakers can use the presented framework to identify likely investment hurdles by climate technology, enabling more targeted policy support to bridge the gap between constructing a first plant and scaling a technology.

title: Beneath the Aggregate: Subtype-Level Equity Gaps in Global Cancer Clinical Trials

detail.title: Beneath the Aggregate: Subtype-Level Equity Gaps in Global Cancer Clinical Trials

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: Global equity research in oncology clinical trials has typically treated cancer as a single category, which obscures a real possibility: that representation gaps vary by cancer subtype rather than applying uniformly across the disease as a whole. This paper re-examines an original 200-trial sample of oncology clinical trials, first assembled for a broader monograph comparing Alzheimer's disease and cancer, at the level of individual cancer subtypes, and supplements it with a dedicated 882-trial India-sited dataset to trace subtype-specific patterns in sponsorship and research independence. Among the 113 trials, just over half the sample, with a clearly identified cancer subtype, real variation emerged beneath the aggregate picture reported previously. Gastric cancer trials carried markedly higher eligibility barriers than the sample average: a 66.7% biomarker or imaging requirement and full comorbidity exclusion, against roughly 15% and 60% respectively across the whole cancer sample, a pattern that lines up with the same endoscopy and imaging scarcity already documented across low- and middle-income health systems generally. Breast cancer trials showed the strongest low- and middle-income country site representation of any subtype examined, at 13.3% against a near-zero baseline elsewhere. The India dataset drew a sharper line still: cervical and liver cancer, two subtypes carrying disproportionate global disease burden in low- and middle-income countries, showed a predominantly domestic-research pattern, 67.4% and 68.2% India-only, respectively, with correspondingly low industry sponsorship, while breast, lung, and hematologic malignancy trials followed the extractive, multinational pattern already documented at the whole-disease level. Hematologic malignancy trials showed no low- or middle-income country site representation at all, alongside the highest comorbidity exclusion of any subtype, consistent with published eligibility criteria for cell-based and transplant-adjacent trials that routinely exclude patients for infectious markers, HIV, hepatitis B and C, that are themselves more prevalent in the same populations these trials fail to reach. Taken together, these findings suggest a cancer subtype's equity profile tracks its own disease-burden geography more closely than any disease-wide average can show, with direct consequences for where subtype-specific trial reform and research investment would do the most good.

detail.abstract: We argue that consequential effects of AI on the global political economy are already observable, and they follow from a structural shift in the character of technological dependency. Historically, technology transferred to developing countries constituted a stock, a domestically held asset that could be inspected, worked with, learned from, and absorbed through sustained engagement. Frontier AI, by contrast, is consumed as a flow, continuous and externally controlled, foreclosing the learning process and inhibiting capability accumulation. We argue that this shift changes what dependency means for state capacity, in ways that classical dependency and development state theories do not anticipate. The argument is developed though digital dualism, a framework characterizing platform capitalism's effects on accumulation, labour, and the state in Global South economies. We find that the four mechanisms underlying digital dualism cohere under a single upstream/downstream logic under AI: concentrated control of the technology stack upstream shapes the terms on which labour and value are extracted downstream. This sharpens the state's structural double bind-its position as both necessary counterweight to digital capital and the actor most eroded by it-through a mechanism where the two horns are causally entangled. We study the case of China, whose partial success in building domestic AI capability illustrates the dependency's layered structure. We also develop the implications for economic outcomes under digital dualism, with AI intensification likely to worsen the development trap, widen the dual economy, deepen oligarchy, and raise the bar for realizing the developmental state.

detail.abstract: Potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) is an important staple and cash crop in Nepal, yet limited empirical evidence exists on its production economics, marketing efficiency, and value chain performance in Far-Western hill districts. This study analyzed the profitability, marketing efficiency, and value chain dynamics of potato production in Dadeldhura district, Nepal, using primary data collected in 2018 from 60 potato-growing households and key market actors through semi-structured questionnaires. Cost-benefit analysis, market margin analysis, Cobb-Douglas production function, and value chain analysis were employed to assess production and marketing performance. The average potato productivity was 19.53 t ha⁻¹, while the total production cost and gross return were NRs 311,859.53 ha⁻¹ and NRs 661,142.20 ha⁻¹, respectively, resulting in a benefit-cost ratio of 2.12. Moreover, labor (β = 0.403), farmyard manure (β = 0.406), and chemical fertilizers (β = 0.575) had significant positive effects on potato production. Similarly, four marketing channels were identified, among which the Producers-Collectors-Wholesalers-Retailers-Consumers channel handled 59.74% of total potato sales but recorded the lowest producer's share (74.8%) and the highest market margin (NRs 11.32 kg⁻¹). In contrast, direct producer-toconsumer marketing provided a 100% producer's share and the highest marketing efficiency. Furthermore, major constraints included price fluctuation, lack of mechanization, pest and disease incidence, inadequate storage facilities, and high middlemen margins. The findings highlight the importance of improving market coordination, strengthening producer organizations, expanding storage infrastructure, and promoting direct marketing systems to enhance producer returns and support sustainable potato commercialization in Nepal.

detail.abstract:
Knowledge can now be produced, transmitted, and recombined at near-instantaneous speed. Yet the social structures through which knowledge acquires authority — education, credentials, professional jurisdiction, organizational position, standards, and responsibility — are reproduced by people who move through them over time. This paper develops the generational renewal constraint. When a change in knowledge touches the rules by which a field trains, selects, certifies, promotes, authorizes, and sets standards, deep renewal requires a sufficient share of key positions to become aligned with the new knowledge conditions. Alignment can arise through newly formed actors entering those positions and through sufficiently deep conversion by incumbents. Renewal time therefore depends on formation and career lags, succession, selection openness, incumbent conversion, and the decision threshold governing rule change. Under the assumptions stated in Appendix A, it retains a positive lower bound even as individual formation time is compressed toward zero. The constraint is not an age effect, and the paper distinguishes adaptation within a knowledge structure from renewal of the structure's reproduction.

The consequences depend on the type of change. Under accumulative change, successive renewals can proceed independently and the number of changes simultaneously undergoing renewal remains bounded when renewal time is finite. Under substitutive change, a new frontier change can supersede a previous one before its structural renewal is completed; the expected interval between completed renewals then rises exponentially with the product of the arrival rate of structure-touching change and renewal time. Faster knowledge production can therefore widen rather than close the distance between the frontier and socially operative knowledge. Artificial intelligence is examined as a stress test because it can shorten parts of formation and strengthen intragenerational conversion while also increasing the arrival rate of rapid, potentially substitutive change.

detail.abstract: We study the online allocation of indivisible goods among n agents, where each good must be allocated immediately and irrevocably upon arrival. Against an adaptive adversary, Neoh and Teh [2026] proved that no algorithm can guarantee a positive approximation to proportionality up to one good (PROP1) that is independent of the number of goods, and the same holds for proportionality up to k goods (PROPk) for any fixed k. We instead consider an oblivious adversary, which fixes the input in advance. Choo et al. [2026] showed that the uniformly random allocation returns a Θ(1/ log(n/δ))-PROP1 allocation with probability at least 1-δ. We improve this to Ω(1/ log log(n/δ)); our algorithm does not take δ as input, so the same algorithm achieves this bound for every δ ∈ (0, 1). Moreover, with the same probability, a variant of our algorithm gives every agent almost her entire proportional share after adding doubly logarithmically many goods from outside her bundle, and even without adding any good when no single good is too valuable relative to this share. In contrast, for envy-freeness up to one good (EF1), we show that, for every α ∈ (0, 1], every randomized algorithm has an input on which its probability of returning an α-EF1 allocation is at most e-Ω(n). For envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), this probability is at most 1/n! with only n + 1 goods, a bound that is optimal within a factor of (n + 1)/2. For the maximin share (MMS), this probability is at most 5/6, however small α is. Allowing more removals gives a positive envy-freeness guarantee: allocating each good to a uniformly random agent among those with positive values achieves, with high probability, an approximation factor arbitrarily close to one for envy-freeness up to logarithmically many goods, and logarithmically many goods are necessary for this rule.

detail.abstract: In recent years, the digital economy has become one of the factors affecting economic growth, innovation, and changes in production and exchange structures. However, its development path is not the same in countries and depends on a set of technological, human, financial, and institutional factors. The present study aims to identify and comparatively analyze the opportunities and challenges of the development of the digital economy in Iran, with a qualitative approach and a review-analytical and comparative approach. For this purpose, the evidence obtained from domestic and international studies was reviewed and compared in four main axes, including digital infrastructure, human capital, financial and fintech resources, and governance and regulations. The results show that Iran has important capacities such as communication infrastructure, educated human resources, and technical capability in the field of digital and financial services. However, there is a gap between these capacities and their transformation into productivity, innovation, and sustainable economic value. The main finding of the research is that the challenge of Iran's digital economy is due to the lack of coordination and complementarity of the main pillars more than the lack of technology. Therefore, the development of this sector requires coordinated policy-making, strengthening infrastructure and human capital, improving access to financial resources, and creating transparent, stable and appropriate legal and regulatory frameworks in accordance with the country's conditions.

detail.abstract:
As large language models are marketed as compliance assistants, a structural question is often left implicit: what kind of computational artefact can discharge verification functions within EU compliance processes? This article develops a three-pattern taxonomy of compliance automation. Pattern P1 systems are probabilistic classifiers and guardrails; Pattern P2 systems are LLM assistants that draft compliance analyses for human review; Pattern P3 systems execute formally encoded obligations against structured evidence and return a verification result. Here, 'deterministic' describes execution of an explicit, declared rule set over structured evidence. The analysis identifies six architectural properties for an automated layer assigned a compliance verdict of record: determinism and reproducibility, soundness, coverage completeness over encoded obligations, auditability, maintainability under legislative change, and preservation of normative structure (D-S-C-AM -S). The derivation combines EU requirements concerning demonstrable conformity, accountability, documentation, traceability, review and legal change with a stated design premise: the automated layer itself is assigned the verdict of record, rather than serving only as an aid to a human assessor. EU legislation prescribes no particular technology. Reproducibility is necessary, but it does not by itself separate P3 from a tightly controlled P2 pipeline; coverage and auditability depend on an explicit, enumerable and correctable rule-and-evidence representation. The argument draws on the GDPR, the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation, the revised Product Liability Directive, and CJEU automated-decision case law. It also addresses booleanproxy semantic loss in formalising graduated legal standards. A companion source audit of the MAILO v5.2.0 audit snapshot found all nine case-law paragraph mappings traceable yet incorrect. The finding shows that formal traceability can support inspection and correction without guaranteeing substantive legal correctness. The resulting architecture assigns interface and triage functions to P1/P2 and reserves the verdict-of-record function for a formally encoded verification layer within its declared scope. The analysis also cautions against certifying high-risk systems with verification tools whose operative rules cannot themselves be audited.

The P1/P2/P3 taxonomy, the D-S-C-A-M-S framework, argumentative choices, and final source selection were not delegated to these tools. detail.abstract: Matching mechanisms differ in how much of an agent’s preference ranking must be determined and reported to obtain a particular object. A mechanism is singleton-attainable (SA) if every object that an agent can obtain through some report can also be obtained by reporting only that object as acceptable. With an SA mechanism, once an attainable object has been identified, the agent need not rank or report any other object. Singleton-attainability identifies a distinct dimension in matching theory and market design: transparent access to attainable outcomes, separate from incentives, stability, welfare or equity. We establish general conditions for SA and derive its strategic implications. Top-lift invariance and truncation invariance together imply SA, while strategyproofness and stability each imply SA. By contrast, no Pareto improvement over a strategyproof, individually rational, and non-wasteful mechanism is SA. In particular, every Pareto improvement over Deferred Acceptance violates SA. We introduce report width, which measures how many acceptable objects may have to be reported to obtain an object. SA mechanisms have report width one. Report width is unbounded for a large class of efficient mechanisms that Pareto-improve Deferred Acceptance. Stable selection with report-induced priorities has width one when priorities are monotone and maximal width under reverse priority dominance. Rank-welfare maximization has width one when the outside-option rank is fixed and maximal width when it is report-dependent. These results reveal a structural divide, which we call the width dichotomy: across all mechanisms and families in our classification and all structural classes we study, report width is either one or unbounded.

detail.abstract: This qualitative research examines critically the lived experiences of the Dalit (Harijan) community living in Ganaktuli, Dhaka, within the context of Sustainable Development Goal 11 (SDG 11), i.e., making cities inclusive, safe, resilient, and sustainable. Though at the core of urban sanitation services, Dalits are among the most excluded groups in urban Bangladesh, with systemically imposed barriers in housing, water, education, healthcare, and economic mobility. Based on ethnographic eldwork and 100 structured interviews with Dalit households conducted from March to August 2023, this paper provides new empirical evidence to measure the multidimensional exclusion of such communities. The study proposes two principal analytical tools: the Urban Inclusion Index (UII), which rated the community at a low 0.35, and a Multidimensional Exclusion Score (MES), indicating that 80% of households suffer high deprivation in ve fundamental areas. In spite of promises by the government of resettlement and some provision of infrastructure, the research nds an acute governance de cit characterized by eviction without resettlement, poor public services, and everyday struggles for survival. The research concludes that policy discourse has not been translated into effective inclusion and cautions that Bangladesh's SDG 11 path is likely to leave Dalits in its wake unless immediate reforms are implemented. The study adds to the debate regarding caste, urbanization, and social justice in South Asia and offers a replicable method for measuring urban exclusion among disadvantaged groups.

detail.abstract: When does a recommendation reveal an expert's conflict of interest? We study cheap talk with two privately known biases and characterize a two-message equilibrium in which a cautious recommendation identifies the less biased type while a favorable recommendation is used by both types. By contrast, increasing the more biased type's bias can establish this equilibrium but does not affect communication once it exists. Thus, conditions that facilitate conflict revelation need not make communication more informative.

detail.abstract: The rapid global expansion of digital identification systems, biometric authentication, and cashless payment infrastructures has raised questions about the conditions under which individuals can access employment, banking, and public life. This paper examines the extent to which the convergence of corporate and state digital infrastructures could create mechanisms of conditional participation-that is, systems in which access to essential services becomes contingent on compliance with institutional identity or behavioral requirements. It situates this empirical inquiry alongside a distinct hermeneutical thread: the popular association of such systems with the biblical "mark of the beast" (Revelation 13:16-17), treating that association not as an explanatory hypothesis but as a discourse phenomenon worth understanding in its own right. Using a comparative case-study design across jurisdictions with differing digital identity regimes-India's Aadhaar system, the European Union's eIDAS digital identity framework, Sweden's nearcashless economy, and lower-connectivity contexts illustrative of exclusion risk-the paper evaluates evidence for surveillance, exclusion, and coercion risks alongside the efficiency, fraud-reduction, and financial-inclusion benefits these systems are designed to deliver. The paper argues that the empirical risks of conditional participation are real, documented, and policy-relevant independent of any theological framing, and that treating the "mark of the beast" narrative as a serious object of discourse analysis-rather than dismissing or endorsing it-offers a productive way to understand public resistance to digital governance infrastructures.

detail.abstract: Health-related websites combine ordinary interface features-including forms, chatbots, checkout flows, subscription services, and tracking technologies-with activities regulated by health, data-protection, consumer, professional, and product law. Existing function-based regulatory tools and jurisdictional digital-health guides address parts of this problem, but they do not provide a single comparative model that separates baseline safeguards from function-specific triggers across the United States, European Union, United Kingdom, and United Arab Emirates. This article develops such a model through a document-based functional comparison of legislation, regulator guidance, enforcement materials, cases, and selected scholarship. The website function serves as the unit of analysis. The comparison identifies a baseline review and eight functions that may activate stricter legal regimes: health-data collection, disease claims, telemedicine, prescription and pharmacy services, direct-to-consumer laboratory testing, AI medical advice, UAE-facing health services, and non-essential EU/UK tracking. Although the four jurisdictions share some baseline expectations, they allocate function-specific obligations through different institutional structures. The resulting baseline-and-triggers model functions as a first-stage issue-spotting protocol: it identifies when an interface feature requires jurisdiction-specific analysis of licensing, data protection, disclosure, substantiation, localisation, conformity assessment, or professional registration. detail.abstract: Energy typically represents the second-largest controllable operating expense in hospitality properties and a major cost and sustainability driver in multifamily housing. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI), combined with Internet of Things (IoT) sensing, occupancy analytics, and predictive automation, is reshaping energy management and sustainable operations across these two property types. Drawing on a structured review of published industry case studies, vendor performance data, and trade research from 2025-2026, the paper synthesizes reported outcomes across HVAC, lighting, water heating, and load-management applications. Findings indicate that AI-driven energy management systems reduce total energy consumption by approximately 15-30% within 12 months of deployment in hospitality settings and 15-26% in multifamily settings, with HVAC optimization accounting for the largest share of savings in both sectors (18-31% system-level reduction). Reported payback periods range from 12 to 36 months. Beyond direct cost savings, documented benefits include reduced equipment maintenance burden, improved occupant comfort scores, and measurable greenhouse-gas reductions supporting environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting requirements. The paper concludes that AI energy management is transitioning from a pilot technology to a standard operational practice, with HVAC-first implementation strategies offering the fastest return on investment for property owners and operators in both sectors.

detail.abstract: India's agricultural sector faces persistent challenges arising from the energy-water-agriculture nexus, including groundwater depletion, rising energy demand, and environmental degradation. In response, national policies like the Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan (PM KUSUM) have emerged to integrate solar energy to ensure energy security and diversify rural livelihoods. This study systematically reviews the evidence on the effectiveness, sustainability outcomes, and implementation challenges of solar energy applications in Indian agriculture. This study adopts a systematic review framework with a narrative synthesis approach to review existing empirical and policy-oriented literature on solar energy applications such as agrivoltaics (AV), solar-powered irrigation systems (SPIS), and floating solar photovoltaics (FSPV) in agriculture in India. Findings reveal that integrated solar-agriculture models generate synergistic benefits, including higher farm profits, rural employment, micro-entrepreneurship, and CO 2 mitigation. However, these outcomes are constrained by structural and institutional barriers. The review also finds significant gaps in the literature, including limited longterm evaluations, overreliance on descriptive and technology-centric studies, weak causal designs, and underrepresentation of Empowered Action Group states. The findings highlight the need for integrated policy approaches that combine technological innovation with institutional strengthening, capacity building, and sustainable resource governance.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the "Accountability Gap" at the entry point (intake) of police administration: a structural state in which the absence of an initial record prevents external oversight from functioning. Drawing on research on police discretion, on accountability and oversight, and on architecture as a mode of regulation, it develops a framework centred on the "record trigger", the event on which the rules of a system require an official record to be created. Official replies from Japanese police and a prefectural public safety commission show that the formal acceptance of a written criminal complaint can remain undetermined, and the governing rules require no entry in the register of criminal cases while it does. Because statutory oversight takes formal records as its input, a "pending evaluation" becomes indistinguishable from "no complaint filed", and the one external oversight path examined declined review on the ground that the matter concerned criminal procedure. Rather than attributing this gap to the aptitude or intention of individual officers, the paper treats it as a property of system architecture. It contrasts the Japanese design with published instruments of US police intake: Computer-Aided Dispatch and Records Management Systems, the New York City Civilian Complaint Review Board, and federal consent decrees. The comparison isolates one design principle: the factual generation of a record must be decoupled from the evaluative decision to accept a case. Unbundling intake in this way allows system-forced record generation and external oversight access, so that discretion is exercised on an existing record rather than through the non-creation of records.

detail.abstract: This paper empirically explores the pass-through channel of inflation expectations to inflation by looking at a real-time macroeconomic forecasting exercise conducted by an exogenous observer. Models that are informed either by households’ updated beliefs about future inflation or, especially, by services firms’ expected changes in their own prices can systematically predict core inflation more accurately – and do so in a stable way – than a class of commonly used models that do not use this information. Qualitative updates in households and firms price surveys emerge as relevant signals of consumer and firm behavior, since they influence aggregate inflation dynamics. These results point to an economically meaningful pass-through channel of short-term inflation expectations to inflation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how bank behaviour affects aggregate credit dynamics. It develops a simulation model of a credit market with three banks, risky one-period loans, equity backing based on Value-at-Risk, customer switching and discretionary changes in interest margins. The simulations suggest that weaker customer attachment among borrowers and more frequent strategy innovation by banks tend to increase the volatility and persistence of aggregate credit. The paper then derives model-based country hypotheses about relative customer attachment and strategy-innovation propensity from observed credit-series properties. The hypotheses are compared with historical evidence on bank-firm relationship intensity and interest-rate spread variance, which are used as proxies for customer attachment and strategy innovation. These consistency checks are broadly compatible with the view that bank-customer relationships and banks' strategy innovation may contribute to differences in aggregate credit dynamics.

detail.abstract: We study how policy expectations affect the estimated natural rate of interest (r*) for the United States and the euro area. To discipline policy expectations, we incorporate information on future policy rates and long-term yields in episodes when the Fed and ECB provided forward guidance. For the post-Covid period, we find that r* rises much more than in an otherwise standard specification that omits yield-curve observables. By implication, the post-Covid tightening of the monetary policy stance was not nearly as large as standard r* models imply, which helps explain why economic activity did not slow much when nominal policy rates were raised dramatically in 2022 to fight inflationary pressures. Yield-curve information pins down anticipated policy innovations and alters r* estimates and, thus, the monetary policy stance.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the IMF’s systemwide stress testing approaches, which cover multiple financial sub-sectors and their clients. Developing these tools is crucial for identifying cross-sector and cross border amplification channels and enhancing policy responses, as recognized by the international financial stability community. The paper reviews classic and modern theories and operational methods for analyzing systemic liquidity risks that impact numerous institutions simultaneously, illustrating how shocks can spread through banks, nonbank financial institutions (NBFIs), and market-based finance via runs, redemptions, margin and collateral calls, fire sales, price dynamics, and disruptions in core markets. It details two base IMF tools—an Excel-based flow-of-funds framework and investment fund liquidity analysis with fire sale and market-impact dynamics—and their application and enhancement within Financial Sector Assessment Programs (FSAPs) across various countries.

title: Optimal Corporate Taxation Under Financial Frictions

detail.title: Optimal Corporate Taxation Under Financial Frictions
detail.abstract: This paper studies the optimal design of corporate taxes when firms have private information about future investment opportunities and face financial constraints. A government whose goal is to efficiently raise a given amount of revenue from its corporate sector should attempt to tax unconstrained firms, which value resources inside the firm less than financially constrained firms. We show that a corporate payout tax (a tax on dividends and share repurchases) can both separate constrained and unconstrained firms and raise revenue, and is therefore optimal. Our quantitative analysis implies that a revenue-neutral switch from profit taxation to payout taxation would increase the overall value of existing firms and new entrants by 7%. This switch could be implemented in the current U.S. tax system by making retained earnings fully deductible.

detail.abstract:
Small states routinely rely on larger states and international institutions for markets, monetary stability, administrative capacity, security, and regulatory access. Dependence is therefore often treated as a constraint on sovereignty. Yet formal independence and external dependence can coexist for long periods, while a legal right to withdraw from an arrangement may provide little practical freedom when alternatives are prohibitively costly.

This paper develops an adjustability-centered framework for analyzing sovereignty under dependence. It distinguishes formal authority from practical sovereignty and argues that the relevant question is not whether a state is dependent, but whether consequential external relationships remain politically adjustable through negotiation, redesign, substitution, or, at the limit, exit.

Liechtenstein provides a structured case. Its postwar and European integration history shows repeated dependence on larger systems alongside episodes of reorientation, treaty modification, differentiated integration, and externally induced policy adaptation. The paper introduces the concepts of relationship adjustability and practical choice, and proposes a qualitative Adjustability Test focused on authorization, voice, redesign, substitution, and transition costs.

The contribution is diagnostic rather than classificatory: dependence becomes sovereignty-thinning when formal choice persists but feasible alternatives and credible adjustment mechanisms collapse.

title: State Capacity Without Self-Provision: Separating Political Authority from Capability Provision in Small States

detail.title: State Capacity Without Self-Provision: Separating Political Authority from Capability Provision in Small States
