detail.abstract:
Small states are commonly analyzed through a capacity problem: they face high fixed costs, thin administrative pools, and vulnerabilities that make it difficult to reproduce the institutional apparatus of larger states. Yet this framing can obscure an important distinction between possessing a capability, directly providing it, and retaining political authority over the arrangements through which it is obtained.

This paper develops a provision-authority separation framework for small-state capacity. It argues that a state can access monetary, customs, administrative, security, or other capabilities through durable external arrangements without thereby transferring all political authority over the relevant policy domain.

Liechtenstein provides a structured case because its statehood combines extensive external provision with continued international sovereignty and demonstrable instances of policy divergence from its principal partner, Switzerland. The paper distinguishes three analytical questions: whether a capability is reliably accessible, who supplies or administers it, and where politically meaningful authority remains. It introduces the concepts of provision-authority separation and externalized state capacity, together with a qualitative capability-architecture test.

The contribution is integrative rather than a claim that dependence, delegation, or external shelter are new phenomena. The central claim is that state capacity and state self-provision are not the same thing: the institutional location of a capability does not by itself determine where political authority resides.

title: Pricing Power in Advertising Markets: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: Stanford University, Harvard University, Stanford University and Stanford University

detail.title: Pricing Power in Advertising Markets: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: Existing theories of media competition imply that advertisers will pay a lower price in equilibrium to reach consumers who multi-home across competing outlets. We generalize, extend, and test this prediction. We find that television outlets whose viewers watch more television charge a lower price per impression to advertisers. This finding helps rationalize well-known stylized facts such as a premium for younger and more male audiences on television. A quantitative version of our model whose only free parameter is a scale normalization can explain 35 percent of the variation in price per impression across owners of television networks, and aligns with recent trends in television advertising revenue. We use the model to quantify the impact of mergers and the effect of Netflix ad carriage on prices for linear television advertising. We then extend our analysis to social media markets where we find evidence of a premium for older audiences (who multi-home less), and we discuss implications for competition across ad formats.

detail.abstract: Energy-linked finance often upgrades evidence too quickly. A variable that tracks an economic target is treated as support for a specific claim; a certificate proving generation is treated as backing; a deterministic smart contract is treated as settlement; and a constrained claim is called money. This paper develops a claim-conditioned method for determining which evidentiary burdens a claim actually invokes and whether those burdens are closed. It separates four non-substitutable boundaries: measurement admissibility, claim qualification, constraint closure, and monetary performance. Boundary invocation is conditional rather than universal: direct metered or contractual evidence need not first be a macroeconomic indicator. Closure is conjunctive: evidence at one invoked boundary cannot compensate for a deficit at another. Applying the method to revised companion evidence produces four results. Taiwan semiconductor electricity is physically and sectorally specific but fails as a short-run production proxy in 2023 and sharply understates the 2024-2025 output rebound; physical specificity therefore does not establish target validity. A cumulative Bitcoin mining-cost ratio is matched by an elapsed-days placebo and fails robustness tests, so physical expenditure does not itself constitute a financial constraint. Renewable PPAs can be coupled with Guarantees of Origin, correcting a stronger earlier claim, but attribute and obligation remain separate records whose quantity, time, location, cancellation and shortfall terms must be explicitly coupled. Finally, transparent pricing and deterministic execution do not establish closure when the risk model is physically misspecified or governance and legal settlement remain untested. The result is a theory of claim-conditioned evidentiary sufficiency: stronger claims invoke additional boundaries, and no boundary can be passed by borrowing evidence from another.

detail.abstract: In a 2019 analysis, Han, Arcand and Lauer linked projected health improvements ('achieving UHC by 2030') to economic output through an augmented Solow model. This response, by a co-author, reassesses that contribution using archived manuscripts, spreadsheets and source exports. Alongside an inconsistent capital valuation and a questionable balanced-growth calibration, this audit also establishes a disease-category mismatch in the archived material: Across all 120 inspected countryyear-scenario inputs, the series labelled 'NCD deaths' reproduces the source workbook's all-cause deaths series, not deaths that are NCD specific. In several countries, most of the difference in all-cause deaths between the baseline and ambitious UHC scenarios occurs among children under five, and cannot be interpreted as deaths averted through NCD interventions. Thus, using this difference to infer reductions in working-age NCD mortality and disability can produce productivity gains not supported by the underlying data. Holding reconstructed health inputs and archived spending assumptions constant across simulations, the alternative specifications tested here do not reproduce the magnitude of published GDP benefit. Under the preferred reconstruction, the ten countries show US$223 billion of additional GDP during 2019-2023, or 0.19% of cumulative baseline GDP, compared with the reported US$578 billion and 0.54%. Nine countries show positive gains in the reconstruction, compared with 10 in the original paper. These findings warrant qualification of policy-facing claims about the spending-health-growth chain and also show the importance of the establishment of a clear chain of provenance, reproducibility, auditability and contestability for complex model estimates.

detail.abstract: This paper aims to resolve the systemic inconsistencies, undue judicial deference, and unprincipled exercises of administrative discretion plaguing Irish Social Welfare adjudication. This deficit is operationalised through a proportional allocation formula bounded by statutory budget caps. The framework operates as an objective decision-making index for administrative officers while providing the Superior Courts with a structured standard of review for unreasonableness.

detail.abstract: This study estimates the economic value of irrigation water using a process-based simulation framework that produces field-level estimates by comparing irrigated and rainfed net revenues. The weighted average value of irrigation water is $0.38 per m 3 and we find substantial spatial heterogeneity in values. Irrigation water values rise during dry years and exhibit diminishing values as irrigation volumes increase. We use the framework to assess the economic benefits of adopting more flexible water allocation policies under different environmental conditions. Under historical conditions, flexible allocation yields average gains of 18% to 35% depending on the crop mix. Under a future 20% precipitation decline scenario, the gains are largest in dry and average years and smallest in wet years, and they remain largest when higher-value, irrigation-dependent crops are included in the rotation. These estimates provide a quantitative basis for designing tradable water rights, setting volumetric prices, and evaluating irrigation infrastructure investments.

detail.abstract: The Theory of Dynamic Adaptive Warfare (TDAW), originally formulated in Portuguese as the Teoria da Guerra Dinâmica Adaptativa (TGDA), is a Brazilian post-classical theory of war developed from a research trajectory that can be publicly traced to 2022 and was systematically consolidated in 2026. Its point of departure is not the obsolescence of classical or modern strategic thought, but the increasing difficulty of explaining contemporary conflict through analytical traditions that are often applied separately even when force, strategic choice, legal constraint, economic coercion, information, technology, legitimacy, institutional interdependence, and adaptation operate simultaneously. TDAW responds to this problem by integrating three foundational bodies of thought-war theory, game theory, and international law-and by translating their interaction into the force-decision-norm triad. From that core, the theory conceptualizes war as a dynamic, adaptive, multidomain, strategically interactive, and legally conditioned system in which actions alter the environment of subsequent decisions, actors learn from resistance and feedback, instruments reinforce or substitute for one another, and pressure may migrate across domains when costs or constraints change. The theory also develops conditional predictability as a disciplined form of strategic inference that organizes intention, capability, vulnerability, opportunity, legal cost, political cost, escalation risk, adaptive capacity, adversarial response, domain migration, and stabilizing forces without claiming deterministic foresight. This foundational article reconstructs the intellectual genesis of TDAW, clarifies its relationship with the traditions from which it draws, develops its central mechanisms, defines its scope conditions, and specifies how its propositions may be subjected to comparative analysis, process tracing, and prospective calibration. The resulting architecture is intended to function neither as a universal theory of all political competition nor as a replacement for established strategic thought, but as an integrative analytical system for conflicts in which coercion, decision, normativity, technology, information, and adaptation are inseparable from one another.

detail.abstract: Indian households hold very little in equities, whereas they are heavily exposed to physical assets such as gold and real estate. Structural factors cannot fully explain this puzzle, so the reason may be behavioural. A survey was conducted among urban savers residing in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (plus Pune). Loss aversion and ambiguity aversion were measured using behavioural elicitation, by presenting hypothetical choice ladders for each. Risk tolerance was included as a control. Data were analysed using logistic regression. Loss aversion was independently associated with non-participation across all robustness checks. In contrast, ambiguity aversion was associated bivariately but carried no independent association in the regression once loss aversion and risk tolerance were controlled. The findings point to a behavioural dimension of the puzzle rather than structural explanations. Urban Indian savers tend to weigh losses more heavily than uncertain outcomes.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a purchase method that is an alternative to traditional Dollar Cost Averaging (DCA), incorporating valuation information through a composite, customizable indicator-the Super Score-built from technical and fundamentalist metrics normalized on a 0-to-100 scale. Unlike approaches that react continuously to any oscillation in valuation, the proposed method preserves traditional DCA as the default behavior for most of the time, restricting the adjustment of allocation between equities and fixed income to statistically rare percentiles of the Score's distribution. This choice draws on both the literature on valuation-based tactical allocation, which associates multiples such as Shiller's CAPE with superior returns when used to adjust equity exposure, and the classical literature on portfolio rebalancing under transaction costs, which demonstrates the existence of an optimal no-trade region around the target allocation. The method thus seeks to avoid the cash drag characteristic of excessively reactive strategies, while addressing the main weakness of traditional DCA: the absence of any response to extreme valuation swings. As an open framework, both the composition of the Super Score and the parameters defining the neutral band and the intensity of the response at the extremes can be freely calibrated by the investor, making the method adaptable to different assets, horizons, and risk profiles. At this stage, this is a theoretical proposal that combines elements already individually validated by the literature; its empirical verification as an integrated method is left as a direction for future research.

title: STaR-DRO: Stateful Tsallis Reweighting for Group-Robust Structured Prediction

detail.title: STaR-DRO: Stateful Tsallis Reweighting for Group-Robust Structured Prediction
detail.abstract: Structured prediction with large language models requires more than accurate labels: outputs must satisfy ontology constraints, preserve valid structure, and ensure evidence-grounded decisions under label imbalance and heterogeneous group difficulty. To resolve these challenges, we present a unified framework for robust ontology-constrained generation. First, we introduce a modular prompt-engineering architecture combining XML-style structure, expert disambiguation rules, chain-of-thought reasoning, metadata-aware decision logic, schema contracts, and a self-validation gate. This targets recurrent in-context structured generation failures, including format drift, label ambiguity, evidence hallucination, and metadata-conditioned confusion. Second, we propose STaR-DRO, which combines Tsallis mirror ascent with sparse entmax-style primal mapback, EMA-smoothed group-loss tracking, rescaled ascent signals, and bounded excess-only multipliers. This upweights only persistently hard groups without suppressing easier ones, addressing conventional DRO’s dense Shannon-entropy exponentiated-gradient updates, high-variance stochastic reweighting, positive adversarial mass on groups that are not persistently hard, and performance costs from simplex competition. We evaluate the framework on EPPC Miner, a carefully chosen, clinically grounded representation of high-stakes structured prediction requiring hierarchical label prediction and evidence-span extraction from patient-provider secure messages. Across Llama models spanning 1B to 70B parameters, our prompt engineering improves zero-shot extraction, with an average label F1 gain of +14.46 and a +17.40 Span F1 gain. Building on supervised fine-tuning, STaR-DRO further improves accuracy and robustness, increasing average label F1 by +1.08/+2.20 and reducing average group-wise validation cross-entropy by 21.3%/14.8% relative to SFT and standard DRO, respectively. These findings significantly advance the reliability of automated communication mining for patient-centered clinical care analysis.

title: Climate Treaties, Lock-In, and Increasing Returns
affiliations: Columbia University - School of International & Public Affairs (SIPA)

detail.title: Climate Treaties, Lock-In, and Increasing Returns
detail.abstract: I present an approach to limiting climate change that differs from the main UN negotiations by focusing on sectors rather than economy-wide measures, on technology-fuel switching rather than emission reductions, and on global systemic change rather than national action. Though lock-in makes even small reductions in emissions costly and difficult for a treaty to enforce, increasing returns makes switching a tipping game with enforcement “built in.” Switching treaties need only specify the new technology-fuel combination; incorporate trade measures and/or R&D funding to bolster increasing returns, where necessary; and provide the “big push” needed to assure selection of the superior equilibrium.

title: IS INTERNATIONAL FREE-RIDING INHERENT TO TRANSBOUNDARY SPATIAL CONSERVATION?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: IS INTERNATIONAL FREE-RIDING INHERENT TO TRANSBOUNDARY SPATIAL CONSERVATION?
detail.abstract: This study examines whether international free-riding manifests itself in the citizens’ stated preferences and constitutes a meaningful barrier to transboundary conservation of biodiversity and ecosystem services. Despite the continued expansion of transboundary protected areas, effective cross-border cooperation in environmental stewardship often remains limited. A common explanation points to free-riding incentives arising under centralised international decision-making. Focusing on two European transboundary protected areas—Białowieża Forest and Fulufjället National Park—this paper empirically tests whether such incentives are reflected in citizens’ stated preferences for conservation. Using a merged dataset of survey responses from Belarus, Norway, Poland, and Sweden, the analysis focuses on respondents who would be expected to benefit from conservation efforts undertaken abroad, and thus have an incentive to free-ride. Attitudinal indicators are used to construct effect-coded variables capturing free-riding tendencies, while controlling for use values, socioeconomic characteristics, and incentive compatibility of the survey design. The results provide no evidence of systematic international free-riding in stated preferences. This finding is robust across alternative model specifications and sampling strategies. The study suggests that barriers to transboundary conservation may lie less in citizen-level preferences and more in institutional or governance constraints, with methodological and practical implications.

title: Exploring the energy complexity nexus in the global economic production space
affiliations: University of Groningen, University of Groningen, University of Groningen and University of Groningen

detail.title: Exploring the energy complexity nexus in the global economic production space
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between production-network complexity and national energy intensity by applying motif-based analysis to multi-regional input-output (MRIO) networks. While energy efficiency improvements are widely promoted as a pathway to reduce energy demand, historical evidence suggests that energy use and economic complexity remain closely coupled, partly due to rebound effects that offset expected savings. Conventional economic complexity indicators, which quantify product sophistication and export diversification, show limited and inconsistent associations with energy intensity. To address this limitation, we construct weighted directed production networks from EXIOBASE3 and apply random-walk motif analysis to capture recurring local supply-chain configurations. We develop four motif-based complexity indicators combining different motif-weighting schemes and country-level aggregation strategies. Results show that selected motif-based indicators, particularly those incorporating reciprocity, exhibit stronger statistical associations with national energy intensity than established complexity indices including ECI, EF, GENEPY, and VXF. These findings suggest that production-network structure captures energy-relevant information beyond what is reflected in product- or export-based complexity measures. The motif-based framework offers a complementary perspective for linking economic complexity with environmental-energy research and provides a potential approach for assessing structural rebound effects in production systems.

title: The best of all possible worlds? Government by promises in the biorefinery bioeconomy
affiliations: and University of Reims Champagne-Ardenne

detail.title: The best of all possible worlds? Government by promises in the biorefinery bioeconomy
detail.abstract: The dominant model of bioeconomy, the integrated biorefinery, which the European Union promotes as the winning technology of the ecological transition, has long been contested within ecological economics: neither absolute decoupling nor sufficiency, but growth preserved. That critique, however, says little about how the regime of promises holds at bay the critical tensions of its own agenda — and the model’s trajectory does not bend. Extending Joly’s economics of techno-scientific promises, we follow that regime across three articulated institutional levels — European programmatic discourse, intermediary networks, and the flagship site of Bazancourt-Pomacle — through a documentary reading of the 2011–2025 period. Read along four operations — legitimation, credibility, governance, irreversibility — the promises take a distinct form at each level. These forms converge and reinforce one another. The European narrative holds the site up as a model, and the site, which runs and can be visited, relegitimises the narrative. Four tensions are thereby held at bay without being resolved. Beyond the biorefinery, what makes a future weigh is its capacity to organise the present. What is at stake is government by promises: for as long as the convergence of promises stands in for proof, the reckoning with biophysical limits is deferred, and the alternative pathways (sufficiency, agroecology, decentralised models) are pushed, little by little, to the margins of what the promises leave disputable.

title: Beyond the Scan: Biomarker Access, Diagnostic Equity, and the Case for a Shared Regulatory Path in Alzheimer's Disease and Cancer

detail.abstract: Two earlier papers in this research program each touched on biomarker access briefly, once while explaining why disease-modifying Alzheimer's trials carry unusually steep eligibility barriers, once while explaining why gastric cancer trials do the same. Neither paper had room to ask the larger question sitting underneath both findings: whether the diagnostic technology deciding who gets tested, and therefore who gets treated, is itself built and regulated in a way that reaches the people who need it. This paper takes up that question directly, across both diseases at once, and finds a pattern that neither disease-specific paper could have surfaced on its own. Alzheimer's disease and oncology are, right now, walking the same path a few years apart. Both fields built their diagnostic gold standards around procedures that are invasive, expensive, and geographically concentrated: amyloid-PET and cerebrospinal fluid sampling for Alzheimer's disease, and tissue biopsy for cancer, and both are now in the middle of a transition toward a blood-based alternative that could plausibly reach almost anywhere a blood draw is possible. For Alzheimer's disease, that transition already has an international regulatory home: a 2024 consensus effort has begun setting minimum performance standards for blood-based amyloid tests specifically because specialist access is limited or absent across much of the world. Oncology's equivalent, circulating tumor DNA testing, already has approved assays and a growing evidence base, but no comparable coordinated push to make sure it reaches low-and middle-income settings as it matures, despite a systematic review already proposing exactly the kind of implementation framework Alzheimer's disease diagnostics has begun to build. This paper lays out the shared shape of that problem across both diseases, the human and technological solutions already documented or actively proposed for each, and argues directly that oncology does not need to reinvent this regulatory path from nothing. It could, with deliberate effort, borrow one that Alzheimer's disease research has already started building.

detail.abstract: Spectral-spatial analysis (SSA) of a single biopsy estimates a tumor cell diffusivity D and a proliferation rate γ by fitting the solution of a reaction-diffusion (RD) equation. A recent in silico validation study observed that, when the tumor age is unknown, only the ratio D/γ can be recovered and the product Dγ cannot. We show that this is a consequence of an exact one-parameter scaling symmetry of the RD equation, (D, γ, t) ↦ → (nD, nγ, t/n). We prove that (i) for the exponential-growth model with a Dirac initial condition on the whole plane, the orbits of this symmetry are exactly the sets of parameters producing the same snapshot, so that the identifiable quantities from a snapshot are precisely Dt and γt; (ii) the dispersion length √︁ D/γ is, up to reparametrization, the unique age-free identifiable biomarker built from (D, γ), while the front velocity 2 √ Dγ is completely undetermined without age information; (iii) the symmetry itself (that is, invariance of the snapshot along orbits) persists for arbitrary reaction terms, bounded domains with parameter-independent boundary conditions, the paper's normalization, and any downstream statistic of a biopsy, whereas the converse statement that fibers equal orbits is proved only for the whole-plane exponential model; and (iv) the empirical "t-cohort" conversion laws can be interpreted as gauge fixing. We also derive testable predictions for the conversion law of D and quantify how age uncertainty limits the accuracy of the velocity biomarker.

title: Quantifying Non-Tariff Barriers: Brexit, Input Sourcing and Firm Performance
affiliations: , Bank of England, University College London and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Quantifying Non-Tariff Barriers: Brexit, Input Sourcing and Firm Performance
detail.abstract: How successful is European integration in removing non-tariff trade barriers? We study how Brexit affected UK firms' input sourcing and sales. The post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) reduced sales and input expenditure at firms with higher pre-Brexit EU trade exposure. It also caused firms to switch towards domestic and non-EU inputs. Through the lens of a trade model, the switch in input sourcing implies the TCA increased trade costs on EU imports by 21% and raised unit production costs by 3.1% for the average UK importer. Our results indicate EU membership secures large reductions in trade costs.

title: Convergence in exergy intensity of GDP: Global and North–South analysis at the primary, final, and useful stages (1971–2019)
affiliations: Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC, University of Leeds - School of Earth and Environment, Calvin University - Engineering Department, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Instituto Nacional de Investigação Agrária e Veterinária (INIAV, I.P.) - MARETEC

detail.title: Convergence in exergy intensity of GDP: Global and North–South analysis at the primary, final, and useful stages (1971–2019)
detail.abstract: Energy intensity, or energy used per unit of economic output, is a key indicator in energy and climate policy, including SDG 7.3. Understanding its cross-country convergence is critical, as global energy and climate progress depends on whether high-intensity countries are reducing intensity faster than low-intensity ones. Existing studies focus on conventional primary or final energy metrics. This paper advances the literature along two dimensions: it incorporates energy quality via exergy analysis; and decomposes convergence across the full energy conversion chain (primary, final, and useful stages). Using the Country-Level Primary-Final-Useful (CL-PFU) database, we apply five complementary methods (kernel density estimation, σ-convergence, the Phillips-Sul log-t test, β-convergence, and γ-convergence) with alternative GDP measures and energy carrier sets. We find robust evidence of global convergence across all 54 specification combinations examined: cross-country dispersion in exergy intensity has fallen by 38-40% since 1971, a single global convergence club is identified, and β-convergence half-lives of 16-19 years confirm systematic catch-up by high-intensity countries. Convergence has, however, been non-monotonic: two divergence episodes are identified (1984-1995, driven by widening dispersion within the Global South, and 2008-2019, driven by divergence within the Global North) with strikingly different geographic signatures. Convergence is consistently strongest at the useful stage across all methods, pointing to end-use technology diffusion as a more powerful equalizer than upstream energy system transformation. These results caution against assuming uniform or persistent convergence, underscore the value of stage-specific exergy-based indicators for long-run energy-economy analysis, and suggest careful consideration of convergence dynamics in policy and baseline modelling frameworks.

title: Collateral Advantage: Exchange Rates, Capital Flows, and Global Cycles
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Collateral Advantage: Exchange Rates, Capital Flows, and Global Cycles
detail.abstract: We construct a two-country New Keynesian model in which the U.S. enjoys an “exorbitant privilege” as its government bonds are desired by banks both in the U.S. and abroad as superior collateral. In times of global stress, the dollar appreciates since the demand for high quality collateral drives up the “convenience yield” earned by U.S. government bonds. There is “retrenchment” - each country reduces its holdings of foreign assets - a critical determinant of which is the endogenous response of prices and returns. The model can account for the observed exchange rate and external position behavior of the U.S. While the model incorporates only a small change from a workhorse New Keynesian model with segmented financial markets, it synthesizes and reconciles three major perspectives: on exorbitant privilege, global financial intermediation, and convenience yields.

detail.abstract: Threshold-based travel behaviour research has generally examined services in familiar contexts, rather than ones outside respondents' lived experience. This paper documents a survey instrument that directly elicits one attribute threshold, acceptable travel time, for a hypothetical rail service. The design includes three ex-ante elements intended to mitigate hypothetical bias and one response-quality mechanism to discourage satisficing. The instrument was piloted using five hypothetical high-speed rail corridors in New South Wales with 22 Sydney-based train commuters, yielding 107 interval-censored observations analysed using log-normal interval regression. The pilot establishes that the instrument runs and produces interpretable output: for each corridor, a maximum travel time meeting the acceptability threshold of a stated proportion of respondents. Without a control condition, the elements' effect on bias is untested. Design faults are diagnosed with corresponding recommendations. Acceptable travel time thresholds may serve in the shortlisting framework for transport solutions, before discrete choice experiments and economic appraisal.

detail.abstract: Data centers provide the physical infrastructure for digital services, yet their local presence raises questions that resemble familiar disputes between neighbors: Who makes the noise, who uses shared resources, who pays the bills, and who keeps their promises? This paper develops a Good Neighbor Framework for data centers in U.S. communities. It combines a selective review of research and public documents with an institutional comparison between household neighborliness and industrial responsibility. Eight expectations organize the analysis: introduction, quiet enjoyment, fair cost allocation, resource stewardship, land-use compatibility, community contribution, communication, and accountability. The framework distinguishes national digital benefits from local burdens, construction activity from permanent employment, electricity demand from household electricity prices, and resource efficiency from absolute resource use. It translates these distinctions into a proposed public commitment register with measurable obligations, responsible parties, verification schedules, and corrective actions. The contribution is conceptual and practical; the paper does not estimate causal effects or validate a composite score. Its central argument is that community acceptance should be earned through observable conduct and credible commitments, while recognizing that some locations or designs may remain unsuitable. The neighbor analogy provides an accessible starting point for evaluating coexistence without presuming either universal approval or universal opposition.

title: From the Countryside to the Streets: Masculinities in Crisis and Illicit Drug Use Among Urbanized Young Rural Workers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidade Federal de Campina Grande, Universidade Federal da Paraíba and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From the Countryside to the Streets: Masculinities in Crisis and Illicit Drug Use Among Urbanized Young Rural Workers
detail.abstract: Abstract Background: Illicit drug use has increased in rural settings, particularly among young men, but the social and gendered processes underlying this phenomenon remain poorly understood. This study examined how illicit drug use among young rural workers relates to transformations in masculine identities associated with the urbanization of rural populations in Northeastern Brazil. Methods: This qualitative study was conducted in Boqueirão, Paraíba, Brazil, with young rural men experiencing problems related to illicit drug use. Data were generated through participant observation involving 40 participants in a public psychosocial care service for people with alcohol and other drug-related needs and in the surrounding community. Seven men aged 18–24 subsequently participated in open-ended life-history interviews. Fieldnotes and interview transcripts were analyzed using an interpretive Reflexive Thematic Analysis informed by gender and masculinity studies. Results: Participants' trajectories revealed adverse childhood experiences involving paternal violence, abandonment, loss, and exposure to substance use. As participants moved between rural and increasingly urbanized social contexts, traditional expectations of masculinity centered on work, provision, strength, and family authority coexisted with urbanized forms of masculine recognition associated with consumption, risk-taking, violence, sexuality, and public displays of economic status. Illicit drug use, particularly crack cocaine use, became embedded in these processes as a means of managing suffering and accessing male sociability, pleasure, and recognition. When drug use became problematic, however, loss of autonomy, material resources, and social status was experienced as a threat to masculinity. The psychosocial care service also emerged as an alternative setting for socialization, emotional expression, mutual care, and the construction of less harmful masculine relationships. Conclusions: Illicit drug use among young rural men should be understood in relation to broader transformations in gender, territory, work, and social life rather than solely as an individual or clinical phenomenon. Substance use and addiction treatment services serving young rural men may benefit from gender-responsive approaches that address masculine norms, social vulnerability, emotional expression, and opportunities for nonviolent forms of socialization and care.

title: Borrowed Claws: Weaponizing "Childless Cat Ladies" as Transnational Misogyny in China's Neo-authoritarian Manosphere

detail.abstract: This study focuses on how a representative Chinese misogynistic manosphere group, Sunba, appropriates U.S. Senator J.D. Vance's rhetoric of the "childless cat lady," adapting and reproducing it within China's localized context. It examines how this reconfigured discourse serves the Chinese Communist Party's agenda of promoting extreme nationalism under the guise of leftist terminology in discussions on gender issues. Through feminist critical discourse analysis, we identify three key mechanisms that explain this crossideological resonance: strategic appropriation of Marxist terminology to construct a "double moral transgression" framework, transformation of reproduction into a marker of political qualification, and deployment of identical friend-enemy binary distinctions that target the same "enemies" despite geopolitical antagonism. These findings contribute to understanding neo-authoritarianism by expanding its gender dimension, revealing how transnational misogynistic discourse can be localized to serve nationalist agendas. The ease with which "childless cat ladies" rhetoric crosses ideological boundaries demonstrates how patriarchal control functions as a highly adaptable technology of rule that transcends conventional political divides.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly moving from systems that generate predictions and recommendations toward systems that can initiate consequential actions. This transition exposes a governance and systems-engineering gap that is not fully captured by conventional model-centric notions of trustworthiness. A model can be accurate, explainable, robust, fair, and validated, yet a particular action based on its output can still be unjustified because the relevant evidence is stale, the operating context has changed, authorization is missing, policy conditions are not satisfied, system health has degraded, or the action exceeds the approved scope of use. This paper calls that gap the last-meter problem of artificial intelligence: the final transition from an AI-generated output to an institutionally permitted real-world action. We separate prediction, recommendation, decision, and execution; define decision-time assurance as a distinct systems layer; introduce a decision-gate abstraction; formalize temporal evidence, authority, policy, systemhealth, and revocation constraints; and propose a taxonomy of failure modes that occur after model inference but before or during execution. The paper relates the proposal to trustworthy AI, human-in-the-loop systems, AI governance, runtime assurance, agentic AI, and emerging regulatory frameworks. It further proposes a research and evaluation agenda for testing whether decision-time assurance can reduce execution risk without making high-consequence AI unusably slow or rigid. AICOS CORE is presented only as one experimental reference implementation direction rather than as evidence that the broader concept has already been validated. The central claim is deliberately narrow: trustworthy models are necessary, but high-consequence AI additionally requires trustworthy decision permission at the moment an action is allowed to affect the world.

title: Information Design, Verification Protocols, and Bargaining

detail.abstract: We study a model in which a sender tries to persuade a decision-maker by committing to a signaling strategy (Kamenica and Gentzkow, 2011). The decision-maker observes this and either commits to an interim verification strategy or delays until the signals are realized (ex post verification). Verification reveals the true state of the world with an endogenously determined probability. We show that interim verification leads to weakly more information disclosure, while ex post verification may result in less or more disclosure. The sender is always strictly better off under interim verification. When ex post verification equilibrium is more informative, the decision-maker prefers it. If it is less informative, the welfare ordering is ambiguous. Thus, interim commitment creates an informational advantage, whereas ex post verification creates a targeting advantage by conditioning verification on the realized posterior. We then study the externalities generated by verification. Coasian bargaining eliminates these externalities and induces full revelation, while Nash bargaining over the surplus between the two protocols determines the direction and size of the equilibrium transfer according to the relative gains from each regime.

detail.abstract: This paper provides an introductory overview of the principal instruments of capital markets, explaining their economic functions, contractual features, valuation principles, and risk-return characteristics. It begins with equities and bonds, distinguishing ownership rights from creditor claims and outlining major security types, credit ratings, and issuance procedures. Common equity valuation indicators and the components of investment returns are introduced alongside the calculation of bond yields. The discussion then examines investment funds, including their organizational features, professional management, value and growth investment styles, and the opportunities and limitations of diversification. The treatment of derivatives distinguishes futures and forwards, swaps, and options, explaining their contractual obligations, payoff structures, and uses in hedging, speculation, and arbitrage. Particular attention is given to the determinants of option prices and the sensitivity measures used to assess changing exposures. The chapter also addresses leverage, liquidity, and the risks associated with instrument complexity. Building on these foundations, it explains the design and investment characteristics of index, bonus, and discount certificates and outlines the process through which structured products are developed. A worked example illustrates the construction of a capital-guaranteed certificate by allocating funds between a zero-coupon bond for repayment at maturity and a performance component comprising options or futures. The example shows how interest rates and maturity affect the funds available for the performance component after financing capital protection. Through definitions, comparative tables, payoff diagrams, and numerical illustrations, the chapter connects basic financial concepts with practical product design and provides a foundation for understanding and comparing investment alternatives.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This study investigates the level of green marketing awareness among college students in India and examines how such awareness influences their attitudes toward, and intentions to purchase, eco-friendly products. It further explores the barriers that inhibit green purchasing behaviour despite high environmental concern. 

Design/Methodology/Approach: A descriptive, cross-sectional survey design was employed. Primary data were collected from 120 undergraduate and postgraduate students across Indian colleges using a structured questionnaire administered via Google Forms. Convenience sampling was used. Frequency analysis, percentage distributions, and cross-tabular comparisons form the basis of the data analysis. The study is grounded in the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), the Value-Belief-Norm (VBN) Theory, and the Green Purchase Intention (GPI) model. Findings: 

Findings indicate that while a substantial majority of respondents demonstrate awareness of green marketing concepts, awareness does not translate uniformly into green purchase behaviour. Price sensitivity, scepticism regarding green claims, and limited product availability emerge as the dominant barriers. Peer influence and social media exposure are identified as significant facilitators of pro-environmental attitudes among youth. Female respondents exhibit marginally stronger green purchase intentions than male counterparts, consistent with prior literature on gender and environmental concern. 

Originality/Value: The study contributes to the green marketing literature by providing empirical evidence from an underexplored demographic-Indian college students-and by systematically mapping the attitude-intention-behaviour gap in an emerging market context. Theoretical and managerial implications for marketers, educators, and policymakers are discussed.

title: Hedging Trade-Cost Uncertainty

detail.title: Hedging Trade-Cost Uncertainty
detail.abstract: This paper studies how international firms hedge against trade-cost uncertainty. We analyze two margins of adjustment: foreign market entry (exporting versus foreign investment) and invoicing in free-on-board (FOB) or cost-insurance-freight-inclusive (CIF) prices. Under oligopolistic competition and price rigidity, trade-cost volatility jointly shapes entry and invoicing choices. Firms with small market shares prefer exporting and FOB-price invoicing, while firms with large market shares favor foreign investment and CIF-price invoicing. Using a novel measure of trade-cost volatility constructed from French customs data, we provide empirical support for these mechanisms and document the joint determination of entry and invoicing decisions. Counterfactual analyses based on the structurally estimated and calibrated model indicate that trade-cost uncertainty has sizable effects on these decisions.

detail.abstract:
This chapter explores the challenges that emerge when allegations of corruption related to investor-State contracts are raised during arbitration proceedings. It explores key issues such as tribunal jurisdiction, the standard and burden of proof for corruption claims, and the legal consequences of corruption findings. 

Drawing from empirical data based on 19 contract-based disputes from a survey of 91 cases, the chapter provides insights into tribunal practices, highlighting the use of red flags and circumstantial evidence in corruption-related disputes. It underscores the lack of consistency in corruption allegations and proposes recommendations for more coherent approaches. 

The chapter advocates for the introduction of corruption due diligence mechanisms, consistent application of international anti-corruption standards, and the development of clear guidelines for arbitrators. It calls for a more proactive approach to addressing corruption in investor-State relations, with an emphasis on transparency and accountability throughout the arbitration process.

detail.title: Asymmetric Reversals
detail.abstract: Short-term return reversal is one of the most robust asset-pricing anomalies, and is commonly linked to liquidity provision. We decompose individual firm stock returns into two distinct components: SYS, the component of returns that can be linked to systematic risk and public information releases; and an orthogonal residual RES. The RES component reverses, while the SYS component exhibits continuation. Moreover, the residual reversals are highly asymmetric: positive residual shocks reverse much more slowly than negative shocks. A return factor based on asymmetric idiosyncratic reversal subsumes the idiosyncratic volatility factor and a broad set of other short-horizon anomalies. Our findings suggest that asymmetric idiosyncratic reversal (AIR) is the primary driver of short-term return predictability.

detail.abstract: High automation exposure need not imply a high share of labour-augmenting tasks. Using the 2026 Global Automation Atlas cross-section of 124 countries, we benchmark Türkiye's pure-augmentation share against its exposure level. Economic exposure reaches 52.8 percent, above the upper-middle-income mean of 47.9 percent, but only 8.8 percent of exposed tasks are classified as labour-augmenting. detail.abstract:
Digitalisation will have a profound effect on labour markets. Far beyond merely replacing jobs,  digitalisation would also alter the fundamental nature of employment relationship. From a game-theoretical point of view, the main concern is that digital platforms have changed the rules of the game. Historically, employment has been conceived of as an infinitely repeated game, which encourages cooperation since players will probably meet each other again. Now, work might consist mostly of one-shot transactions, regulated almost exclusively by the platform. Reputation scores, a feature that is supposed to act as a signal of trust, are actually tied to one particular platform and privately owned. Once workers leave, they are held up by intangible transfer penalties at the platform’s mercy. Furthermore, the increasing network effects tend to increase market power. These potential Stackelberg leaders are thus able to set their own terms and trigger a “race to the bottom” in wages, working conditions, etc. The problem, therefore, is the lopsided power in digital labour markets, featuring locked-in mobility, externalised social costs, and algorithmic opacity. 

I propose a framework based upon three main pillars, each addressing one aspect of platform power: market power through portability, cost externalisation through the benefit pool, and information power through transparency. The three pillars work as a connected portfolio, which would be based on evidence, identifying a concrete path forward.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes and develops a single concept-the Individual Accountability Gap-to explain persistent governance challenges in Papua New Guinea. The concept refers to the absence of cultural infrastructure for individual responsibility: mechanisms enabling persons to be held accountable as individuals rather than as nodes within collective networks. Approximately 50,000 years of tropical environmental adaptation selected for sophisticated collective coordination technologies but did not select for individual accountability, because continuous resource availability and extensive kinship networks removed the survival pressures that drive personal responsibility elsewhere. The paper traces the environmental logic of this gap, demonstrates that Papua New Guinea developed rigorous collective accountability through systems like the Wantok System, identifies specific institutional failure points where the gap collides with imported governance structures, and documents early evidence that economic pressures are slowly generating individual accountability capabilities across generations. The analysis reframes what external observers label corruption or governance failure as an infrastructure mismatch between two legitimate accountability systems, and argues that effective reform requires building individual accountability from within rather than importing it from outside.

detail.abstract:
This paper focuses on current changes in the regulation of the digital economy and new approaches to the distribution of risks and revenues arising from the development of digital platforms and artificial intelligence. The paper focuses on three main topics: support for marketplace sellers affected by drone attacks, protecting jobs in the face of automation, and redistributing revenue from digital platforms in favor of content creators.

With regard to platform-based commerce, the paper examines support measures for Wildberries and Ozon sellers whose goods were damaged as a result of drone attacks, including tax deferrals, compensation, and incentives provided by the marketplaces. The paper analyzes the specifics of determining the extent of damage and the allocation of liability among the platform, the seller, the insurer, and the state. The Russian approach is compared with foreign mechanisms for compensating businesses for losses resulting from military and terrorist risks, and the possibility of establishing a permanent insurance system and government participation in covering such losses is also examined.

With regard to the regulation of artificial intelligence, the article analyzes new initiatives in the United States and Brazil aimed at mitigating the impact of automation on the labor market. It examines proposals to introduce taxes and mandatory contributions for AI developers and companies that replace workers with technology, with the proceeds directed toward retraining and the creation of new jobs. Special attention is given to measures to encourage the hiring of workers who have lost their jobs due to automation, as well as to the challenge of establishing a link between the adoption of AI and job losses.

The paper also examines the trend toward redistributing revenue from the largest digital platforms in favor of content creators. Using Australia as an example, it analyzes a new mechanism for levying a levy on major media platforms and search engines to fund news publications. The Australian approach is compared with mechanisms for compensating publishers in Italy and for funding national audiovisual production in the EU. The paper also separately assesses the possibility of applying similar tools to support the media and other creative industries whose revenues are declining due to changes in content consumption patterns driven by digital platforms and AI.

title: How Many More Disasters Will It Take for Climate Action?

detail.abstract:
On 26 August 2026, a huge section of rock and glacier ice broke away from Langtang Lirung, a mountain on the Nepal–China border, triggering a flood that travelled some 200 kilometres downstream in under seven hours. More than 1,300 people died, around 5,000 remained missing, and over 84,000 were affected. Scientists found that human-caused warming had made the region’s summer about 1.5°C hotter and that thawing ground and retreating glaciers had probably weakened the mountain over decades. They cautioned, however, that they could not determine whether this particular collapse would have occurred without climate change. 
That caution is warranted, and this essay does not treat Langtang alone as proof. But the disaster belongs to a wider picture. In 2021, a similar rock-ice avalanche struck Chamoli in the Indian Himalaya. In 2025, global fossil fuel consumption reached another record, and emissions rose by a further 1.1%. At that rate, the remaining carbon “budget” for limiting warming to 1.5°C would be exhausted in about four years. The lead scientist behind the estimate stated plainly that keeping warming below 1.5°C “is no longer plausible”. Seven of the nine planetary boundaries—the limits within which Earth’s systems remain safe for people—have now been crossed. Warm-water coral reefs appear to have crossed their first major tipping point, while the Amazon rainforest, the great ice sheets and a key Atlantic ocean current may be approaching theirs. 
These changes are measured and reported every year. Yet our overall socio-economic direction remains unchanged. That raises an uncomfortable question: if a disaster that kills more than a thousand people in an afternoon does not change our course, how many more will it take?

detail.abstract:
The recent decision of the U.S. Supreme Court in Moody v. NetChoice, holding that social media companies’ core content moderation decisions constitute protected First Amendment expression, has triggered questions about the future of user free speech rights online. If most speech occurs on privately owned digital platforms and corporate expressive rights are the focus of First Amendment protection, many have questioned how individual’s speech interests can be protected in the digital realm.

In a world of rapidly evolving technology in which regulation and ethical frameworks are often missing, it is unsurprising that there are gaps in the protection of individual rights. We believe it is timely to assess the work of the largest, worldwide human rights oversight experiment for platform content moderation and its implications for free expression in the digital age.

This article provides the first comprehensive review and analysis of over five years of work of Meta’s Oversight Board in applying global standards of free expression and corporate human rights responsibility to content moderation decisions on Facebook, Instagram, and Threads. We assess the extent to which application of these standards have – or have not – been helpful in protecting users’ expressive rights in platform content moderation. Ultimately, we conclude that human rights standards do provide a helpful normative framework – in contrast to the skepticism of some scholarly critics of this approach – but we identify specific areas where additional work needs to be done in translating these norms to private sector content moderation.

detail.abstract:
Background: First-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) monotherapy has shown an early survival deficit relative to chemotherapy in individual randomized trials, but reproducibility across solid tumor types remains unestablished.

Methods: In this meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov for phase III randomized controlled trials from Jan 1, 2009 to Dec 31, 2025 comparing first-line ICI monotherapy with chemotherapy in NSCLC, HNSCC, and urothelial carcinoma, requiring Kaplan-Meier curves with numbers-at-risk. Individual patient data were reconstructed using the Guyot algorithm. Pooled curves were generated by two-stage random-effects meta-analysis. Treatment effects were quantified using segmented hazard ratios and restricted mean survival time differences (RMSTD). The study protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/2SZEY).

Findings: We identified a total of 16 eligible trials, comprising 10,104 patients. All pooled curves violated proportional hazards, rendering a single aggregate hazard ratio insufficient. Pooled curves crossed between 5·7 and 11·5 months across tumor types and endpoints. Early segmented hazard ratios significantly favored chemotherapy for PFS; late hazard ratios favored immunotherapy for both endpoints. RMSTD remained negative through early follow-up in every indication, with breakeven point ranging from 10·8 months in NSCLC PFS to 62·4 months in HNSCC PFS.

Interpretation: This meta-analysis quantifies the time to benefit of first-line ICI monotherapy across tumor types and endpoints, using RMSTD rather than a single hazard ratio to capture the temporal relationship between immunotherapy and chemotherapy. The early survival disadvantage of immunotherapy is a recognized phenomenon, but pooling Kaplan-Meier curves across trials converts it into a concrete timeframe clinicians can use to estimate when benefit over chemotherapy may be expected.

Background: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a global health emergency with West Africa disproportionally affected. We aimed to describe bloodstream infection (BSI) species distribution, AMR and its association with clinical outcomes in patients with suspected infections presenting to the sole tertiary hospital in The Gambia.

Methods: Patients (all ages) presenting with suspected infection and an indication for parenteral antibiotics were prospectively included by convenience sampling from September 2024 to December 2025. Blood culture positivity-rate, species and AMR were described. Associations between BSI and presence of AMR, defined as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) production, with mortality or hospitalization at 30 days (composite primary outcome) were investigated.

Findings: We enrolled 585 patients with a median age of 1 year (IQR 0-11, range 0-90) of which 263 (45%) were female. The blood culture positivity-rate was 210/585 (36%) and the contamination rate 42/585 (7%). Overwhelmingly, S. aureus (n=139) was the most common BSI, followed by pathogens of the Enterobacterales order (n=48) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (n=10).The composite primary outcome occurred in 117/585 (20%). MRSA was reported in 21/119 (18%) and ESBL in 21/44 (48%). Patients with vs. without AMR had worse outcome (12/42 (29%) vs. 14/121 (12%), p=0·01), with no difference seen in patients with vs. without BSI (41/210 (20%) vs. 76/375 (20%), p=0·83).

Interpretation: Aureus was the dominant cause of community-acquired BSI. Prevalence of MRSA and ESBL were higher than previously reported regionally and associated with poor clinical outcome. The tertiary hospital study setting limits the generalisability of findings.

detail.abstract: Density neural MIDAS models report sizeable gains for nowcasting US GDP growth, measured against members of their own model family. We ask what happens when the comparison set is not chosen that way. We implement a published QRNN-MIDAS model to its authors' specification, place it in a three-tier comparison set anchored by a quarterly-updating autoregression, and score every arm separately at each monthly origin inside the target quarter, under a pre-specified protocol. The published model performs worse than the autoregression in all eighteen prespecified headline cells, and so does the structured neural estimator this paper set out to evaluate. Post-hoc analyses then measure what the sample can support. A model confidence set retains the historical mean and the random walk in every cell; at the headline origins the design resolves CRPS differences of roughly twenty per cent of the benchmark's loss, while the best point estimate there is 15.9 per cent; three of 64 target quarters carry seventy to eighty per cent of the squared loss difference behind each competitive comparison; and a stability-targeted fluctuation test rejects nowhere. Defensible design choices-the composition and size of the comparison set, the resolution of the horizon axis, and the loss-each move what the comparison reports. On samples of this size the ranking of density mixed-frequency nowcasts is a joint property of the models and the comparison design.

detail.abstract:
Background: Mortality among children under 5 years in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) has declined substantially since 2000, but progress in the developmental status of surviving children under the Sustainable Development Goals, 2015-2030 (SDGs) remains unclear. This paper examines mortality and disability among children under 5 years in SSA to inform regional global health priorities.  

Methods: We conducted a sub-regional and national analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2023 for all 48 countries in SSA to compare changes in all-cause mortality, developmental disabilities, and Years Lived with Disability (YLDs) between 2000 and 2023. The prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, developmental intellectual disability, epilepsy, hearing loss, vision loss and aggregate disabilities in 2023 was also analysed. Estimates are reported with 95% uncertainty intervals.

Findings: Whereas child mortality declined by 31.1% (30.0 to 32.2) from 3.8 million (95% UI:3.8–3.9) in 2000 to 2.6 million (2.6–2.7) in 2023, the number of children with a disability rose by 67.0% (22.9–127.1) from 7.0 million (6.0–8.5) in 2000 to 11.6 million (9.6–15.9) in 2023, representing a 6.4% (5.3-8.7) prevalence. YLDs rose by 74.3% (1.5–199.2) from 0.8 million (0.6–1.1) to 1.4 million (1.0–2.3) within this period. In 2023, the prevalence of developmental disabilities and YLDs was greatest in Eastern SSA. Some 61.2% of children with disabilities resided in the ten top countries, collectively accounting for 67.2% of the region’s child mortality. Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Ethiopia accounted for the most overlapping burden of child mortality and disability.  Hearing loss was the most prevalent disability (2.4% [2.1-2.6]), affecting 4.3 million (3.8–4.8) children. Epilepsy was associated with the greatest YLDs.

Interpretation: The growing burden of developmental disabilities in SSA calls for global action to place the affected children on a trajectory for optimal development and inclusive learning, as mandated by the SDGs. Improved primary data sources and surveillance systems are also required for more precise disability estimates.

Background: Chronic central nervous system (CNS) infections, remain a major cause of mortality and neurological disability in sub-Saharan Africa. Long-term survivorship remains poorly characterized in resource-limited setting. We assessed mortality and functional outcomes at one year among adults with CNS infections in Mozambique.

Methods: We conducted a prospective cohort of adults with neurotuberculosis, cryptococcal meningitis, or cerebral toxoplasmosis admitted to Mozambique’s referral hospital between September 2024 and August 2025. Clinical and laboratory data were collected. Vital outcomes were assessed at discharge and at 30 days, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months.

Results: Among 122 patients, 42 (34.4%) had neurotuberculosis, 40 (32.8%) cryptococcal meningitis, and 40 (32.8%) cerebral toxoplasmosis. Median age was 40 years (IQR 32.0–46.8), 49.2% were male, and 88.5% were living with HIV; median CD4 count was 132 cells/mm3 (67–210). In-hospital case-fatality was 39.3%, increasing to 52.5% by 6 months, with no further deaths recorded through 12 months. In multivariable Cox regression, a higher level of consciousness was independently associated with lower mortality (aHR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75–0.93; p<0.001). Being male (aHR 3.57, 95% CI 1.69–7.55; p<0.001), having admission fever (aHR 2.41, 95% CI 1.14–5.12; p=0.022), and HIV (aHR 4.92, 95% CI 1.04–23.30; p=0.044) increased the risk of death.

Conclusion: Chronic CNS infections were associated with high 6-month mortality in this Mozambican cohort, particularly among those with HIV, fever, male sex, and greater admission neurological impairment. These findings highlight the need for earlier recognition, timely diagnosis and treatment, and strengthened longitudinal care in resource-limited settings.

detail.abstract: A long-standing intuition in finance is that competition should eliminate all opportunities for alpha. This paper models a market equilibrium in which the opposite holds. Building on two companion papers showing that innovative interpretation of the public record earns alpha but, by improving prices, simultaneously erodes that opportunity, the model makes the production of new interpretations endogenous. Investors search because better interpretation has private value, and successful ideas are then disseminated and competed away. Yet the opportunity set as a whole does not dissolve because available interpretive methods remain improvable, through innovation, while new forecasting problems continually arise. When the expected reward from discovery of new methods exceeds the marginal cost of search, the resulting stationary equilibrium contains a positive stock of open opportunities for alpha even though each individual opportunity has a finite half-life and eventually becomes uneconomic to exploit. Competition therefore eliminates particular opportunities without exhausting the general set and converges to an equilibrium paradoxically characterised by a positive stock of open opportunities for alpha.

detail.abstract: We estimate the labor market effects of Italy's statutory priority to work from home (WFH) for parents of children under age twelve. Using population-wide administrative data and a sharp regression discontinuity design, we find that eligibility raises mothers' annual earnings by 1.6-2.3 percent in high-WFH-intensity firms, alongside increases in paid days and weeks. detail.abstract: Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies are central to most climate mitigation pathways, yet their future availability risks weakening current abatement efforts — a phenomenon known as mitigation deterrence. This paper develops a transparent two-period benchmark model to explore how political economy forces and behavioral biases shape intertemporal climate choices. We allow for general functional forms as well as uncertainty about climate damages and CDR costs. We further demonstrate the framework’s flexibility by extending it with a simple political-economy module in which lobbying over mitigation and future CDR systematically depresses abatement. The model provides a useful starting point for future research on the complex interactions between CDR expectations, current mitigation efforts, and climate policy.

detail.abstract: We develop standardized time-series measures of shocks and uncertainty for output growth and inflation across 14 Asia-Pacific economies using data from Consensus Economics survey of professional economic forecasters. They are based on changes in mean forecasts and standard deviations, adjusted for intra-year patterns that arise from the annual-average percent changes basis of the data. As an example of how our shock measures may be used, we apply the vector autoregression method of sign restrictions to decompose output growth and inflation shocks into fundamental demand and supply shocks. Those shocks and our uncertainty measures align well with major economic events such as the Asian Financial Crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and geopolitical conflicts. We show that our uncertainty measures most closely reflect the concept of macroeconomic uncertainty, with apparent differences to established economic policy uncertainty measures across all comparable economies, but a close relationship with two well-known macroeconomic uncertainty measures produced only for the United States. Hence, extending the measures of macroeconomic uncertainty to all 14 economies in our analysis, along with the shocks for those economies, creates a valuable dataset for economic policy setting and empirical research.
